data.title: GH, KH, and TDS: Which Number Decides What?
data.excerpt: KH prevents pH from crashing, GH determines water suitability for species, and TDS doesn't compensate for either. Why stability matters more than the ideal number.
data.content:
Three Measurements Everyone Confuses

Hardness isn't a single number. Three different measurements are often mentioned together and assumed to be the same thing, yet each one determines something different in your aquarium:

MeasuresDetermines
KH Carbonate HardnessThe ability to neutralize acids (alkalinity)Whether pH remains stable or crashes
GH General HardnessPrimarily calcium and magnesiumWater suitability for species, and the health of scales and shells
TDS Total Dissolved SolidsEverything dissolved, collectivelyA general indicator only — does not compensate for the other two

A common confusion: high TDS means high hardness. Not necessarily. TDS measures salts, minerals, and organic matter indiscriminately; it can rise for reasons unrelated to calcium or carbonates.

KH: The Number That Prevents Disaster

KH is important not because it changes pH, but because it prevents pH from fluctuating. Think of it as a buffer that absorbs acids formed in the tank. When the buffer is depleted, pH doesn't just drop slowly—it crashes.

Here's the critical intersection: the biological filtration process itself consumes alkalinity. This means a tank undergoing cycling with low KH can experience a pH crash mid-cycle. The bacteria may stop working, leading you to believe the filter has failed, when the real issue is depleted buffer capacity.

Specialized sources indicate that a KH below approximately 3 degrees makes a pH crash a likely possibility during cycling, and bacterial activity significantly weakens as pH drops, nearly stopping around 6.0. We present this as a warning sign rather than a definitive limit, as it's widely circulated but we haven't traced it to an original study. The cycling process is explained in the nitrogen cycle guide.

GH: Suitability, Not Quality

GH is not a measure of "cleanliness" or "quality." It's a measure of suitability: soft water fish like tetras and discus prefer low GH, while fish like guppies, mollies, and African cichlids prefer it higher. Shrimp and snails require sufficient calcium for shell and skeletal development.

Here's the most important practical rule: stability is more important than the ideal number. Most ornamental fish adapt to a wide range if it's stable, and they suffer from fluctuations even if they are within the "ideal range."

What We Know and Don't Know About Iraqi Water

We cannot tell you the GH or KH values for your tap water because we don't have a reliable source for this data—and values vary significantly between cities and water sources. The only honest answer: test it yourself.

  • Test your tap water and your aquarium water. The difference between them tells you what your aquarium is doing to the water.
  • If your aquarium's KH decreases over time, it's being consumed, and regular water changes are what replenish it.
  • pH alone is not enough—a stable pH with low KH is a fragile stability. Details on pH are in our article on pH Level in Iraqi Tap Water for Fish.

Don't Chase Numbers

Most harm in this area comes from attempting to adjust numbers with chemicals. Products that "raise" or "lower" pH provide a quick change, after which the water reverts to its natural state, leading to fluctuations—which is worse than the non-ideal number you started with.

  • Choose fish that suit your water instead of trying to modify the water to suit fish you've already chosen. This is the most successful strategy in the hobby.
  • If adjustment is necessary, make it slow and steady using substrate, driftwood, or water mixing, not a shock dose.
  • Monitor the effect with regular testing—refer to our guides on reading aquarium test kits and performing water changes.

Symptoms of Fin Rot

Symptoms of fin rot in ornamental fish appear as:

data.title: Dwarf Cichlids (Ram & Apistogramma): Cichlids Sized for the Community Tank
data.excerpt: The intelligence and substrate-dwelling behavior of cichlids in just a few centimeters. And why the Blue Ram dies quickly for many – plus an easier alternative that offers a nearly identical look.
data.content:
Cichlids Sized for the Community Tank

When a beginner hears the word "cichlid," they think of Oscars and Flowerhorns – large, aggressive fish requiring massive tanks. However, the family has an entirely different branch: dwarf cichlids. These are fish no larger than a few centimeters, possessing the same intelligence and substrate-dwelling behavior, but in a space manageable for a standard home aquarium.

SpeciesPreferred Water ParametersDifficulty Level
Blue Ram (Ramirezi)Warmer than usual, relatively softMost difficult — sensitive to unstable water
Bolivian RamWider range, cooler temperatureClearly easier — a practical alternative to the Blue Ram
ApistogrammaTends towards soft and acidicMedium — requires stability
CrebensisTolerates harder waterThe hardiest of the group
If this is your first cichlid, start with the Bolivian Ram or Crebensis, not the Blue Ram. The Blue Ram is more beautiful but punishes any water fluctuation; most who fail with it fail within the first month.

Why Blue Rams Die Quickly for Many

This point is frankly worth discussing, as it's frequently repeated and often misinterpreted as "bad luck."

  • Requires a mature tank, not a new one. The fish is more sensitive to ammonia and nitrite than average, so introducing it to a tank that hasn't completed its cycle is almost a guaranteed failure — see the biological cycle.
  • Prefers a higher temperature than the rest of the community tank. This creates a real conflict with species that prefer cooler water, forcing a choice: either adjust the tank for it or don't buy it.
  • Usually arrives stressed. Many available specimens undergo a long transport chain and arrive with weakened immunity, making quarantine non-optional here.
  • Stability is more important than the number. A stable reading is better than an ideal but fluctuating reading — refer to the water test guide and GH and KH water hardness guide.

In the Iraqi summer, the equation becomes even more challenging: high temperatures reduce dissolved oxygen, and sensitive fish are the first to be affected — see Protecting Fish in Iraqi Summer Heat.

"Peaceful" Until They Pair Up

Dwarf cichlids are sold as peaceful community fish, which is true – with one condition: that a pair does not form. When a pair bonds and chooses a territory, their behavior completely changes, and they become fiercely protective of their space, exceeding their size.

  • Territorial Defense, Not Tank Defense. Aggression is confined to the vicinity of the chosen spot. Breaking lines of sight with plants and driftwood resolves most of the issue — similar to the logic in Aquarium Fish Aggression and Chasing.
  • Competition at the Bottom. Dwarf cichlids are bottom-dwellers, competing with Corydoras for the same layer and food.
  • Apistogramma Harems. Typically, one male with several females is recommended, not two males – males will fight.
  • And before any mixing, consult the Tank Mate Compatibility Guide.

Where They Fit Among Other Cichlids

The distinction between American and African cichlids dictates expected water parameters and behavior. Dwarf cichlids are found on both sides: Rams and Apistogrammas are South American, while Crebensis are West African. Details can be found in American vs. African Cichlids: The Differences and Best Types and Colors of African Cichlids.

This is a practical, not academic, difference: mixing a dwarf cichlid that prefers soft water with an African cichlid that prefers hard water is a recipe for failure from the start, regardless of similar sizes.

Before You Buy

  1. Is my tank truly mature? If it's only a few weeks old, postpone the purchase.
  2. Can I maintain the temperature it requires without harming other inhabitants?
  3. Do I have a substrate with hiding places and broken lines of sight, or an open tank?
  4. Am I prepared for the behavioral change if a pair forms?

If symptoms appear after introduction, start with the water, not medication — see the Fish Disease Symptoms and Diagnosis Guide. And calculate the load before adding fish by checking How Many Fish Your Aquarium Can Support.

data.title: Reasons for Sudden Ornamental Fish Death and How to Save Your Aquarium

data.content:
Introduction

Keeping ornamental fish is a popular hobby in Iraq, with aquariums found in many homes and businesses. However, these fish can face serious problems leading to sudden death. In this article, we will discuss the reasons for sudden ornamental fish death and how to save your aquarium.

Reasons for Sudden Ornamental Fish Death

There are many reasons that can lead to the sudden death of ornamental fish, including:

  • Sudden temperature fluctuations: Sudden changes in temperature can stress fish and lead to their death.
  • Water quality: Polluted water or water containing high levels of chlorine can cause fish death.
  • Stress: Stress caused by changes in the fish's environment can lead to their death.

Sudden Temperature Fluctuations

Temperature is one of the most important factors in keeping ornamental fish. High or low temperatures can stress fish and lead to their death. In Iraq, temperatures can reach 50 °C in the summer, increasing the risk of fish death. Aquarium owners should use temperature control systems to ensure stable temperatures in the tank.

Water Quality

Water quality is another important factor in keeping ornamental fish. Polluted water or water containing high levels of chlorine can cause fish death. In Iraq, pure water is rare, and most water sources contain high levels of chlorine. Aquarium owners should use water purification systems to ensure water quality.

How to Save Your Aquarium

If you notice your ornamental fish are dying suddenly, you must take the necessary actions to save your aquarium. You can do this by:

  1. Checking the temperature: Ensure the temperature in the tank is stable and there are no sudden changes.
  2. Checking water quality: Ensure the water is clean and free of chlorine.
  3. Providing a safe environment: Make sure the tank is free from any sources of stress.
A golden tip from AQUAVO: Aquarium owners should use temperature control systems and water purification systems to ensure stable temperatures and water quality in the tank. We can deliver products throughout Iraq, and all products come with warranties.

Conclusion

Sudden death of ornamental fish is a common problem in Iraq, but it can be prevented by taking the necessary actions. Aquarium owners should use temperature control systems and water purification systems to ensure stable temperatures and water quality in the tank. Remember, you should always prioritize the health of your ornamental fish.

A Fish Died — What Exactly Should You Do Now

A moment every hobbyist goes through, and in which actions make a difference:

  1. Remove it immediately. A dead fish decomposes quickly and raises ammonia levels; a small tank is affected within hours — Ammonia Spike Emergency Treatment.
  2. Examine it visually before discarding. Spots, cloudiness, eroded fins, sunken belly — information that will help you with the rest.
  3. Test the water immediately. The most common cause of sudden death is not disease but the water — Reading Your Water Test.
  4. Observe the rest closely for a few days: breathing, appetite, behavior.
  5. Do not treat the tank by guessing. Adding medication after one fish dies without a diagnosis does more harm than good — The Correct Treatment Protocol.

Wash your hands after any handling, and cover any wounds before putting your hand in — Aquarium Hygiene and Your Safety.

Ceramic rings are a type of filter media used in aquariums to enhance water quality. These rings are made of porous ceramic materials, allowing water to pass through them, which allows oxygen and nutrients to reach the fish. Ceramic rings are characterized by their unique properties, such as:

  • Large surface area allowing for a large colony of beneficial bacteria.
  • Improving water quality by removing organic impurities.

What are Bio-Balls?

data.excerpt: Overfeeding is the root cause of most aquarium problems. The two-minute rule, feeding schedules based on conditions, and the practical differences between pellets, flakes, and freeze-dried foods.
data.content:
Overfeeding is the Root Cause of Most Aquarium Problems

If you look back at most problem articles on this site — cloudy water, algae, ammonia spikes, post-travel cloudiness — you will find a common recurring cause: more food than is consumed.

Unconsumed food decomposes, raises ammonia, feeds free-floating bacteria and algae, and consumes oxygen. Therefore, reducing food is not stinginess — it is the cheapest preventative measure in the entire hobby.

How Often, and How Much

ConditionFrequencyQuantity
Healthy adult fishOnce daily is perfectly sufficientConsumed within two minutes
Fry and growing fishTwo or three timesVery small amounts each time
New tank cyclingLess than usualThe minimum — bacteria are not yet established
HeatwaveReduce or stop temporarilyMetabolism is high and oxygen is low
After introducing a new fishNothing for the first 24 hours—
The two-minute rule is the only practical measure that holds up: give an amount that disappears within two minutes. If food remains on the bottom afterward, you have given too much — and the excess will not be eaten later, but will decompose.

A weekly fasting day is a common and beneficial practice, especially for round-bodied species prone to digestive and buoyancy issues.

Food Types: Each Has a Role

TypeAdvantagesNote
PelletsComplete daily nutrition, sink to reach mid-water and bottom-dwelling fishChoose a size that fits the mouth
FlakesFloat, suitable for surface-dwelling fishBreak apart and pollute if overfed
Freeze-dried (Artemia)High protein, excellent appetite and color stimulantSoak for a few seconds before feeding
Boiled vegetablesFiber for herbivorous and bottom-dwelling speciesRemove leftovers within hours
Sinking bottom foodActually reaches Corydoras and bottom dwellersSurface fish sometimes snatch it before it sinks

The rule: A daily base of good quality pellets or flakes, with limited variety. Variety is beneficial but not a substitute for a balanced staple diet. AQUAVO offers pellets and specialized foods for betta, goldfish, shrimp, and fry, as well as freeze-dried artemia, in the fish food section.

Read the Package, Not the Advertisement

The most important indicator of food quality is the order of ingredients: food starting with fish or shrimp meal is better than food starting with wheat or grain fillers. The expiration date is truly important — vitamins degrade, and in Iraq's heat, storing the container in a hot place accelerates this. Store it in a cool, dry place, sealed.

Signs You Are Overfeeding

  • Food on the bottom after more than two minutes.
  • Water becomes cloudy a day after cleaning — Diagnosing Cloudy Water.
  • Algae stubbornly returns despite adjusting lighting — Algae Guide.
  • Nitrates climbing week after week — Water Change.
  • Any ammonia reading above zero — Reading the Test.

If the number of fish itself exceeds the tank's capacity, reducing food helps but doesn't solve the problem — How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Hold. When traveling, do not burden anyone with estimation responsibilities: Traveling and Leaving Your Aquarium.

Variety in food does not necessarily mean higher cost: homemade vegetables are a real option for herbivores — Feeding Vegetables. For a comparison of commercial versus budget food, see Food Brands Comparison.

Live and Frozen Foods: Benefits and Precautions

Variety is indeed beneficial, but each form has its handling requirements:

  • Live food stimulates appetite and natural behavior, and many use it before breeding — Breeding as a Decision. However, it is also a known pathway for introducing pathogens if its source is unknown; a reliable source makes the difference.
  • Frozen food is safer in this regard and easier to store. Thaw in a small amount of tank water in a small cup; do not drop frozen pieces directly into the tank.
  • Do not pour the thawing water into the tank — it contains liquids that pollute the water without nutritional benefit.
  • Do not refreeze thawed pieces.
  • And the rule remains: Variety does not mean increasing the quantity. Overfeeding remains the root cause of most aquarium problems.

data.title: Aggressive Black Beard Algae (BBA): Two-Step Removal Guide
data.excerpt: Black Beard Algae (BBA) is aggressive! But it can be eliminated with two simple steps. Here's the proven method.
data.content:
What is Black Beard Algae (BBA)?

Black Beard Algae is a type of algae that appears on the walls and surfaces of the aquarium, characterized by its dark black color. These algae are considered a nuisance that can negatively affect the health of fish and other aquatic animals in the tank.

Causes of Black Beard Algae Appearance

  • Excessive light: Too much light can cause algae to grow rapidly.
  • High nitrogen and phosphorus levels: These excess nutrients can contribute to algae growth.
  • Insufficient aeration: Inadequate aeration can lead to carbon dioxide buildup, which supports algae growth.

Steps to Remove Black Beard Algae

Black Beard Algae can be removed with the following steps:

  1. Adjust aquarium conditions: Light and aeration levels in the tank should be adjusted to prevent algae growth. The duration of light operation can be reduced, or low-intensity lights can be used instead.
  2. Apply chemical treatments: Reliable chemical products, such as those offered by AQUAVO, can be used for algae removal. Product instructions must be followed precisely to ensure safe and effective results.
AQUAVO Golden Tip: Always reduce the use of untreated local water in the aquarium due to high chlorine levels, which can harm both fish and algae. Instead, use treated or distilled water to ensure the health and well-being of your fish.

Importance of Choosing the Right Products

When choosing products to deal with Black Beard Algae, product quality and safety should be considered. AQUAVO can provide water treatment products and algae removers, along with customer service. Additionally, AQUAVO offers shipping services to 18 governorates in Iraq, making it the ideal choice for users across the country.

Conclusion

Removing Black Beard Algae in the aquarium does not require extensive expertise, only a good understanding of the basic steps and consistent application. With AQUAVO's products and services, you can maintain a healthy and beautiful aquarium free from harmful algae.

data.title: Raising Fry: From Hatching to Sale Size
data.excerpt: Most fry don't die of starvation—they die because the food is too large for their mouths. Stunted growth is permanent damage that cannot be compensated for, even with excellent conditions later on.
data.content:
The First Problem Isn't Food—It's Mouth Size

Most fry don't die of starvation because their owner didn't feed them. They die because the food provided is too large for their mouths. A fish the size of a pinhead cannot eat a food pellet, no matter how good it is, so it remains amidst abundant food and weakens day by day.

StageSuitable FoodNote
First days after hatchingYolk sac still presentDo not feed—fry do not eat yet
Smallest fryVery fine and liquid foodsThe most difficult stage, where most losses occur
After a few daysNewly hatched brine shrimpThe most widely used and most effective for growth
After weeksFinely ground foodGradual transition to adult food
Livebearer fry are relatively larger at birth and can eat ground food almost from day one, which is why they are easier—see Livebearer Fish. Egg-layer fry, however, are much smaller and require the delicate stage described above.

Fry Tank Water Degrades Faster Than You Think

This point causes more deaths than starvation. Fry tanks are usually small, feeding is frequent, and fry are sensitive. The result: rapid ammonia buildup in seemingly clean water.

  • Frequent small meals, not one large meal. Excess food spoils within hours in a small water volume.
  • Daily siphon of the substrate. Food remnants and waste accumulate quickly—see Ammonia Spike.
  • Small, frequent water changes with water matched in temperature and parameters, as fry are less tolerant of sudden changes—see Water Change and Treating Tap Water for Fish.
  • The tank must be cycled before introducing fry. A new tank without beneficial bacteria is the worst place for the most vulnerable creature in the home—see The Nitrogen Cycle.

The Filter: The Most Important Technical Detail

A standard filter with strong suction will literally suck in the fry. The common solution is an air-driven sponge filter: its suction is gentle, and its sponge surface collects fine food particles that the fry can pick up themselves.

If you must use an existing filter, cover the intake with a sponge. Details in Which Filter Suits Your Tank and Filter Media, and aeration with Air Pumps.

Stunting: Irreversible Damage

This is the most crucial point in the article. Overcrowded fry or those kept in poor water conditions permanently stop growing, and this cannot be compensated for later, even if moved to excellent conditions. They become adult fish smaller than normal and with weaker health.

  • Increase space as they grow, not after the problem appears—see How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Hold and Calculate Aquarium Capacity.
  • Sort by size. Size differences within the same batch grow rapidly, and larger fry may take the smaller ones' share or even prey on them.
  • Monitor temperature in summer—small tanks heat up faster than large ones—see Summer Heat.

The Honest Question in the End

Not all fry can be raised. A single batch may produce dozens, and your tank cannot accommodate them all at their adult size. Realistic options: expand your space, find hobbyists to take them, or reduce breeding from the start by separating sexes.

Ignoring the question is not a neutral choice—it ends with an overcrowded tank, degraded water, and stunted fish, which is worse than all alternatives. The full background in Breeding as a Decision, and before transferring any group to another home, review Transporting Fish and Aquariums.

data.title: Algae Guide: Diagnose the Type Before Treating
data.excerpt: Algae are a symptom of excess light or nutrients, not a disease to be killed with medication. A diagnostic table by type, and why brown algae in a new tank should be left alone and not treated.
data.content:
Algae are a Symptom, Not a Disease

No aquarium is completely free of algae, not even those of professionals. Algae grow when you have an excess: more light than the plants need, or more nutrients than they consume. So the right question is not "What kills them?" but "What do I have in excess?".

This is why products labeled "algae remover" are a deceptive solution: they kill the visible algae within a couple of days, don't address the cause, and the algae return stronger — and sometimes the mass of dead algae itself raises ammonia, creating a bigger problem than the original.

Diagnose the Type First

TypeAppearanceLikely CauseSolution
Green on GlassSoft green spotsLong lighting + high nitratesMechanical removal, reduce lighting hours
Brown (Diatom)Brown dust covering everythingNew tank, silicates, weak lightingDisappears on its own within weeks
FilamentousLong green threadsImbalance between light and nutrientsManual removal + balance lighting
Green WaterThe water itself is cloudy greenExcess light or direct sunlightComplete darkness for 3 days
Black Beard AlgaeHard black tufts on edgesFluctuating current and nutrientsThe most difficult — dedicated guide

Brown Algae: Do Nothing

This is the type that scares beginners the most and is the least dangerous. Diatoms appear in new tanks because silicates are available and the tank has not yet stabilized. They cover gravel, glass, and plants with brown dust within days.

The treatment is patience. They disappear on their own when the silicate source is depleted and the tank stabilizes — usually within a few weeks. Any chemical attempt here will harm the new tank more than it helps, as it is in the middle of cycling.

If your tank is new, this is a natural sign of the cycling process, not a sign of failure — read about the biological cycle.

Green Water: Primarily a Light Problem

Green water is microscopic free-floating algae; it cannot be removed by the filter because its size is smaller than the pores of the filter floss. Complete darkness for three days will eliminate it because it relies entirely on light, and the fish can tolerate darkness without issue.

Steps and details for differentiating it from white bacterial cloudiness can be found in Diagnosing Cloudy Water by Color.

The Four Root Causes

  1. Long lighting hours. 6–8 hours is sufficient for any home aquarium. More than that feeds algae, not plants.
  2. Direct sunlight. A sunny window alone is enough to perpetuate the problem, no matter what else you do.
  3. Accumulated nitrates from infrequent water changes, too many fish, or overfeeding.
  4. Overfeeding. The root cause of most water problems, including this one.

Algae Eaters: A Help, Not a Solution

Some fish and invertebrates eat specific types of algae — Otocinclus for diatoms, Amano shrimp for filamentous, and Nerite snails for green algae on glass. But pay attention to two points:

  • They don't solve the cause. If the excess remains, algae will grow faster than they can eat.
  • A living creature, not a tool. Adding fish to solve a problem increases the bioload on an already stressed tank, and each species has its own requirements. Do not buy a creature for a single function and then neglect it.

Note on UV sterilizers: they are effective against green water specifically because they kill free-floating cells, and are not effective against algae attached to surfaces.

The Practical Plan

  1. Set lighting to 6–8 hours with a timer, and keep the tank away from sunlight.
  2. Change 20–25% of the water weekly and regularly.
  3. Reduce feeding so it's finished within 2 minutes.
  4. Clean mechanically with a magnet or brush — manual removal is always part of the solution.
  5. Wait two weeks before judging. The tank responds slowly, and changing everything at once prevents you from knowing which factor was the cause.

Use the calculators to determine your tank size and weekly water change volume.

Live plants are direct competitors with algae for the same nutrients, which is a fundamental difference from artificial ones — Real or Artificial Plants. Fast-growing, large-leafed species like the Amazon Sword are among the best at consuming excess nutrients.

Filamentous and Hair Algae

Long green threads that attach to plants and decor and can be pulled off by hand like a clump. They differ from Black Beard Algae in that they are longer, softer, and green in color.

  • Their usual cause is excess nutrients with more light than the plants can consume — the same equation as other algae.
  • Manual removal is particularly effective for them: wrap them around a stick and pull them off. This immediately reduces the biomass while you address the cause.
  • Review lighting hours before increasing intensity — Lighting Guide.
  • Amano shrimp are among the best at dealing with them, within the limits that algae eaters are a help, not a solution — Shrimp and Snails.

data.title: Natural vs. Artificial Plants for Aquariums in Iraq?
data.excerpt: Natural is environmentally better, but power outages sometimes change the equation. An honest comparison between natural, silk, and plastic plants, and when artificial is the right decision, not a compromise.
data.content:
The Short Answer

Natural plants are undeniably better for the environment: they absorb nitrates, compete with algae for nutrients, and provide real hiding places. However, in Iraq, there's a factor that sometimes changes the equation — power outages. Natural plants depend on regular lighting, while artificial ones don't die when the power goes out.

So, the right question isn't "Which is better?" but rather "Which one suits your aquarium, your fish, and your electricity situation?"

NaturalSilkHard Plastic
Absorbs NitratesYesNoNo
Competes with AlgaeYesNoNo
Affected by Power OutagesYes — requires regular lightingNoNo
Safe for Long FinsYesYesNo — sharp edges can tear fins
Requires MaintenanceTrimming and fertilizingRegular washingRegular washing

When Artificial is the Right Decision

It's not a compromise, it's a decision. There are situations where natural plants fail for reasons unrelated to your skill:

  • Fish that uproot plants. Large cichlids and goldfish will dig through the substrate searching for food. Any plant rooted in the substrate will be uprooted.
  • Large predatory fish like Oscars and Arowanas — robust decor is more suitable for them.
  • Long and frequent power outages. Plants requiring strong lighting will wilt and rot, and rotting plants raise ammonia levels. Sometimes, artificial plants in a stable aquarium are better than dead natural plants.
  • Lack of time. Maintaining a planted aquarium is a real commitment: trimming, fertilizing, monitoring.
A warning about artificial plants: Cheap hard plastic plants have sharp edges that can tear the fins of long-finned fish like Bettas and Guppies. Choose soft silk varieties and wash them thoroughly before introducing them to the aquarium.

If You Choose Natural Plants: Start Here

Most failures with natural plants begin with choosing the wrong type. These are low-maintenance (low-tech) varieties that grow under medium lighting without CO2 injection:

  • Anubias — attach them to rocks or driftwood; do not bury their rhizomes in the substrate, or they will rot.
  • Java Fern (Microsorum pteropus) — same rule: attach, don't plant.
  • Java Moss — attach to any surface and forms a green carpet.
  • Vallisneria — plant in the substrate; it grows quickly and absorbs more nitrates.

Important note on Anubias and Java Fern: Burying the rhizome is the primary reason they die, not the lighting. If the rhizomes do rot, see Aquatic Plant Root Rot Treatment.

Plants Are Not a Substitute for the Nitrogen Cycle

This is the most misunderstood point. Natural plants consume nitrates and help, but they do not replace biological filtration, nor do they allow you to skip the tank cycling phase. Ammonia and nitrite are primarily the job of bacteria. Read about the Nitrogen Cycle before relying on plants to clean your aquarium.

If you're considering an aquarium without a filter, plants are part of the answer, but not the whole story — details are in Fish That Live Without a Filter.

Practical Conclusion

Start with Anubias and Java Fern attached to driftwood or rocks. They don't require special substrate, strong lighting, or initial fertilization, and they tolerate neglect better than any other type. If your fish uproot plants or your electricity is unstable, silk plants are a respectable option — provided they are soft. For attaching plants to wood and rocks, AQUAVO offers threads, nets, aquascape glue, and substrate for planted tanks.

data.title: White Spot (Ich): Why Isn't the Medication Killing the Spots You See?
data.excerpt: Only one stage of the parasite is exposed to medication, and the spot you see is not it. This explains why spots increase after starting treatment and why their disappearance doesn't mean recovery.
data.content:
Why the Medication Isn't Killing the Spots You See

This is the most crucial piece of information in the entire subject, and the one most people fail to grasp when treating white spot: The white spot you see on the fish is protected, and the medication cannot reach it.

The causative parasite (Ichthyophthirius multifiliis) goes through several stages, and only one stage is exposed to medication:

StageLocationAffected by Medication?
Trophont — The White SpotUnder the fish's skin layer, feeding on itNo — Protected by the fish's tissues
Cyst StageDetaches from the fish and attaches to gravel and decor within a cyst, where it divides into hundredsNo — The cyst protects it
Free-Swimming Larval StageExits the cyst and swims in search of a fishYes — Fully exposed

This means the entire treatment targets only the third stage. This leads to two seemingly strange occurrences:

  • Spots sometimes increase after starting treatment. This is normal — these are stages that were already inside the skin and emerged, and the medication couldn't reach them.
  • Disappearance of spots does not mean the end of the disease. Their disappearance means the parasites have dropped to the substrate to multiply. If you stop treatment here, the new generation returns stronger.
Practical rule: Continue treatment for 3 to 5 days after the last spot disappears, not from the day it disappears. This is the difference between a successful treatment and one that recurs.

Why Raising the Temperature Works

Raising the temperature does not kill the parasite; instead, it accelerates its life cycle, causing it to reach the exposed stage faster and remain under the medication's effect for a longer duration relative to its lifespan. The free-swimming stage lives for about 48 hours at 24 °C, and less time as the temperature rises.

  1. Raise the temperature gradually to 29–30 °C — one or two degrees every few hours, not all at once.
  2. Increase aeration significantly. This is a mandatory step, not optional: warmer water holds less oxygen, and a sick fish is already stressed. The mechanism is explained in Protecting Fish from Heat.
  3. Use a dedicated medication — Methylene Blue or a white spot treatment, both available at AQUAVO under water treatments. Follow the dosage on the package and do not deviate.
  4. Do not raise the temperature above 30 °C unless you know the tolerance of your specific fish species.

How to Know if It's White Spot and Not Something Else

  • Appearance: Small, raised white salt-like grains scattered on the body and fins — approximately the size of a pinhead.
  • Behavior: The fish rubs its body against the gravel and decor, sometimes days before the spots appear. Rubbing without spots is an early sign.
  • Lethargy and loss of appetite, and rapid breathing if the gills are affected.

If the symptoms are rapid breathing with absolutely no spots, it's likely a water quality issue, not a parasite — test for ammonia and nitrite first, and see Sudden Ammonia Spike Emergency Treatment.

Why It Spreads in Iraq in Spring and Autumn

The reason is not seasonal in itself, but behavioral: many people turn off the heater when the weather warms up during the day, while nights remain cold. This daily fluctuation weakens the fish's immunity, and the dormant parasite takes advantage of it.

The solution is simple: keep the heater on year-round with a thermostat set to 26 °C. It will automatically turn off in summer and only operate on cold nights. Details on choosing a heater and its wattage can be found in the Heater Guide.

Prevention is Cheaper Than Cure

  • Stable temperature — Fluctuations are the primary trigger.
  • Quarantine new fish before introducing them to the main aquarium. Most infections enter with new fish.
  • Do not transfer store water to your tank with new fish.
  • Stable aquarium — Fish stressed by high ammonia or nitrite levels get sick faster. The basics are in the Biological Cycle Explained Simply.

A final, serious note: Do not use human medications on fish, and do not guess the dosage — details are in The Dangers of Human Medicine for Fish.

data.title: The Biological Cycle for Aquariums (Nitrogen Cycle): A Simple Explanation in Arabic
data.excerpt: A complete guide to the biological cycle: the two oxidation steps and who performs them, a table explaining every test reading, why the danger of ammonia levels varies with pH, why the cycle stops, and how to restart it.
data.content:
The Biological Cycle: What Actually Happens Inside the Tank

Most new aquariums fail not because of disease, but because of chemistry. Fish constantly release ammonia directly from their gills, and additional ammonia comes from waste, excess food, and decaying dead plants. This ammonia is toxic and doesn't disappear on its own. The only thing that gets rid of it is bacteria that live on the surfaces of the filter and substrate and feed on it.

Here we need to correct a common misconception: bacteria do not produce ammonia; bacteria consume ammonia. Ammonia comes from the fish and from decomposition. The biological cycle is simply about building up sufficient numbers of these bacteria to consume ammonia as quickly as it is produced.

Two Steps, Not Three Stages

The conversion happens in two oxidation steps, each carried out by a different group of bacteria:

  • Step One: Ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (classic name Nitrosomonas) convert ammonia into nitrite.
  • Step Two: Nitrite-oxidizing bacteria (Nitrospira) convert nitrite into nitrate.

Correctional note: Most Arabic articles name the bacteria for the second step as Nitrobacter. In freshwater aquariums, Nitrospira is practically dominant, not Nitrobacter. Recent research on home aquarium filters has shown that a type of Nitrospira called comammox can complete the entire process from ammonia to nitrate within a single cell, and it is one of the most prevalent types in freshwater filters. This doesn't change your daily tasks, as your test kit measures ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate anyway, but it explains why nitrite sometimes doesn't appear as clearly as expected.

Nitrate, at the end of the chain, is much less harmful but accumulates. The only way to reduce it in a typical tank is through regular water changes.

Test Readings: What They Mean and What to Do

ReadingMeaningFirst Action
Ammonia present, nitrite zeroThe tank is at the beginning of cycling, and the first bacteria are still multiplyingStop adding any new fish, reduce feeding
Ammonia decreasing, nitrite increasingThe first step has worked, but the second hasn't caught up yetPartial water change, and patience — this is the most dangerous stage for fish
Ammonia zero, nitrite zero, nitrate presentThe cycle is completeYou can gradually add more fish, one or two per week
Ammonia and nitrite rising after weeks of stabilityFilter crash: washed with tap water, prolonged power outage, or medication killed bacteriaWater change, and treat as an uncycled tank
Consistently high nitratesWater changes are insufficient or the tank is overstockedReview the water change schedule and fish count

Why the Same Ammonia Level Can Be Lethal in One Tank and Safe in Another

This is the point most articles miss. Ammonia in water exists in two forms: NH₃, the un-ionized form, which is truly toxic, and NH₄⁺, the ionized form, which is much less harmful — the difference in toxicity between them is about a hundredfold. The ratio between the two forms depends on pH and temperature, and it increases as the pH rises.

Percentage of un-ionized ammonia out of total ammonia, according to US EPA tables:

pH LevelAt 25 °CAt 28 °C
6.50.18%0.22%
7.00.57%0.70%
7.51.77%2.17%
8.05.38%6.56%
8.515.3%18.2%

Read the table vertically: the same ammonia reading on the test kit becomes about ten times more dangerous with every degree of pH increase. This means an ammonia reading that is acceptable in a tank with a pH of 6.8 could be an emergency in a tank with a pH of 8.2. If the pH in your tank is 7.5 or higher, interpret any ammonia reading as more dangerous than it appears on the test kit. If it is 6.8 or lower, the danger is much less at the same reading. We cannot know your tank's pH from your location on the map — it varies from city to city and source to source, so test it with a kit or strip before interpreting any ammonia reading. See pH Level in Iraqi Tap Water for Fish.

An important practical consequence: Do not raise the pH suddenly if you have ammonia in the tank. Raising the pH converts some of the relatively safe ammonia into the toxic form within minutes. Treat the ammonia first with water changes. Details on handling a sudden spike are in Emergency Ammonia Spike Treatment.

Nitrite: Why Fish Suffocate with Clear Water

Nitrite enters the bloodstream through the gills and binds to hemoglobin, converting it to methemoglobin. This form cannot transport oxygen. This means the water is full of oxygen, but the fish suffocates internally. The blood turns brown, which is why it's called brown blood disease.

Signs to watch for: rapid breathing, fish gasping at the surface or near the filter outlet, lethargy, dark or brown gills.

First action: Immediate and sufficient water change, and stop feeding for a day or two, as food increases ammonia. Increased aeration helps the fish breathe while you lower the nitrite.

Chemical information to help you understand: Chloride ions compete with nitrite for the same absorption sites in the gills, so the presence of chloride in the water reduces nitrite uptake. However, the chloride concentrations used for this purpose come from raising fish in farms at sizes and densities completely different from a home aquarium, and we do not publish any dosage here. Water changes remain the guaranteed and safe procedure for hobbyists. If additional disease symptoms appear, start with Fish Health Diagnosis.

Cycling Without Fish, and Cycling With Fish

Without fish is the cleaner method: run the filter and heater on an empty tank, add an ammonia source, and test every two days until ammonia and nitrite are zero and nitrates appear. No living creature suffers during the process.

With fish means the fish live amidst ammonia and nitrite while the bacteria multiply. If you are forced into this: a very small number of hardy fish, minimal feeding, and daily testing with water changes at any ammonia or nitrite reading.

Approximate timing for cycling without fish: Nitrite often starts to appear between day 14 and 20, and a complete cycle takes six weeks or more. This is a range, not a deadline — it varies greatly with temperature, ammonia quantity, and whether you introduced media from an established filter.

The fastest legitimate way to shorten the process is to transfer filter media or substrate from a cycled and healthy tank. This is precisely why quarantine is important: anything you move from another tank carries its contents with it.

Why the Cycle Stops

  • Chlorine or chloramine in tap water. It kills bacteria just as it kills germs. A water conditioner is necessary before any addition. If your water utility uses chloramine, a conditioner that only removes chlorine will leave the ammonia component behind — pay attention to the type of conditioner. Details in Treating Tap Water for Fish in Iraq.
  • Low pH and weak carbonate hardness. Bacterial activity is severely inhibited as pH drops and nearly stops around 6.0. Low KH — below about 3 degrees — makes pH crashes during cycling a possibility, as the oxidation process itself consumes alkalinity.
  • Very high nitrite. Above approximately 5 mg/L, nitrite itself begins to inhibit the bacteria that are supposed to treat it, creating a closed loop. The solution is a water change to lower the level, not adding more ammonia.
  • Washing media with tap water. The most common mistake. Wash the sponge with water removed from the tank itself, not under the tap.
  • Medications and antibiotics. Many of them harm beneficial bacteria, so expect ammonia to return after any treatment course in the tank.
  • Prolonged power outages. Filter bacteria are aerobic. If water flow stops for many hours at high temperatures, some bacteria will die.

Specific Iraqi Conditions

Three local pressures converge. Summer heat increases fish metabolism, leading to more ammonia production, while simultaneously reducing oxygen solubility in the water and increasing the proportion of toxic ammonia. Power outages stop the filter precisely when the tank needs it most. And treated tap water requires an appropriate conditioner before every water change.

Practical conclusion: In summer, reduce feeding, reduce fish stocking density, increase aeration, and make water changes smaller and more frequent instead of one large sudden change. To calculate your tank volume and the actual amount of water you are changing, use the calculators.

Common Mistakes That Break the Cycle

  • Adding all the fish in one day after cycling is complete. Add them gradually so the bacteria can keep up.
  • Replacing all the media at once. Replace only a portion and leave the rest to host the colony.
  • Relying on water clarity. Clear water does not mean zero ammonia; ammonia and nitrite have no color. If the water is cloudy, the cause is something else, see Causes and Solutions for Cloudy Aquarium Water.
  • Overfeeding. The biggest source of ammonia that the keeper can directly control.
  • Rushing to judge a fish species before knowing its requirements. Consult the Fish Encyclopedia before purchasing.

Conclusion

The biological cycle is not a stage you complete and forget; it is a continuous balance between the amount of ammonia entering the tank and the bacteria's ability to consume it. Anything that increases the first part — more fish, more food, higher temperature — or decreases the second part — washing with chlorine, medication, power outage — sends you back to square one. Regular testing is the only way to see this balance before you see it in the fish's behavior.

And the cycle is the first thing to collapse when the tank is set up incorrectly — Setting Up Your First Aquarium explains its correct place among the stages. If it collapses suddenly in a running tank, review Causes of Sudden Fish Death. As for ready-made bacteria products, they speed up the start but do not eliminate it — see Filter Bacteria Liquid.

data.title: Which Filter Suits Your Aquarium? Choose by Size, Not Price
data.excerpt: A filter doesn't clean water; it houses the bacteria that treat it. A guide to choosing by tank size, comparing the three main types, and the actual turnover rate that matters.
data.content:
The Filter Doesn't Clean Water — It Houses Bacteria

Most beginners think the filter's job is to suck up visible dirt. This is only one of three functions, and the least important:

  • Mechanical — Traps suspended particles. This is what you see.
  • Biological — Beneficial bacteria colonize the media and convert ammonia. This is what keeps fish alive.
  • Chemical — Activated carbon and similar media absorb odors, tannins, and medications. Optional.
This is why washing filter media with tap water is the most common fatal mistake: chlorine kills the bacterial colony, returning your stable aquarium to a new tank state without you realizing it. Wash the sponge with water taken from the aquarium itself. The full mechanism is explained in the Biological Cycle.

Choose by Aquarium Size First

Aquarium SizeBest FitWhy
Under 40 L, or Betta tankSponge filterGentle current that doesn't stress the fish, and excellent biological filtration
40–100 LInternal, or Hang-On-Back filterStronger mechanical filtration at a reasonable price
Over 150 LExternal (Canister) filterLarge media capacity, and doesn't take up space inside the aquarium
Breeding or isolation tankSponge filterDoesn't suck up fry or shrimp

Comparing Types

Sponge FilterInternal FilterExternal Filter
Biological FiltrationExcellentAcceptableExcellent
Mechanical FiltrationWeakGoodStrongest
Safe for Fry and ShrimpYesNeeds a cover on the intakeNeeds a cover on the intake
Requires Air PumpYesNoNo
Takes Up Space Inside AquariumYesYesNo
MaintenanceEasiestApproximately every two weeksLeast frequent, and longest duration

Turnover Rate: The Number That Actually Matters

Rule of thumb: The filter should process between 4 and 6 times the aquarium volume per hour. A 100 L aquarium needs a filter with approximately 400–600 L/h flow rate.

However, be aware: The number on the box is the filter's flow rate *in a vacuum*. With media, hoses, and head height, the actual flow decreases. Choose a higher rating than your calculation suggests. For fish that dislike strong currents—like Bettas—direct the output towards the glass to break up the flow, rather than choosing a weaker filter.

Mistakes That Break the Filter

  • Washing media with tap water. The number one mistake, hands down. Details on tap water treatment in Treating Tap Water.
  • Replacing all media at once. If you must replace, replace a portion and leave it for two weeks for the new part to establish.
  • Turning off the filter for long periods. Bacteria need water flow to bring them oxygen and food. After a long outage, rinse the media in aquarium water before restarting — see Emergency Aquarium Tools.
  • Filter smaller than the aquarium. It runs non-stop and is insufficient, shortening its lifespan.

Conclusion

Choose the type based on your aquarium size and fish species, not the price. The sponge filter is a very respectable option for small tanks and breeding tanks, and the external filter is best for large aquariums. Whatever your choice, biological media is the real value — details on types in Filter Media, Ceramic Rings, and Bioballs, and a comparison between sumps and external filters in Sump vs. Canister Filter Comparison. AQUAVO offers sponge filters, filter media, filter floss, and ceramic rings in the filter and purification section.

UV Sterilizer: Do You Need It?

A common question, and the answer for most home aquariums is: No.

  • What it does: Treats microorganisms passing through it *in the water* — hence its mention specifically for green water.
  • What it doesn't do: It doesn't treat what settles on the fish, substrate, or glass, nor does it compensate for poor water quality or an overstocked tank.
  • It doesn't replace quarantine or water changes — see Quarantine New Fish Guide.

In summary: A tool for a specific situation, not a general upgrade. A balanced aquarium doesn't need it, and an unbalanced one won't be fixed by it.

data.title: Nitrite Spike: Suffocation in Clear Water
data.excerpt: Nitrite does not reduce oxygen in the water but prevents blood from carrying it. Symptoms of suffocation with clear water and good aeration mean you should test for nitrite immediately.
data.content:
Suffocation in Clear Water

A nitrite spike presents a confusing picture: fish gasp at the surface and appear to be suffocating, yet the water is clear and the aeration is running. The aquarium owner then searches for an oxygen problem that doesn't exist.

The reason is that nitrite does not reduce the oxygen in the water—instead, it prevents the fish's blood from carrying it. Oxygen is present, but the fish cannot utilize it. This is why simply increasing aeration alone does not solve the problem, although it remains beneficial.

Rule: Symptoms of suffocation + clear water + good aeration = test for nitrite immediately. This is the most commonly misdiagnosed scenario in home aquariums.

Do This Now

#ActionWhy
1Stop feedingStops the production of ammonia, which converts to nitrite
2Perform a water change with treated water of the same temperatureDilution is the only immediately effective measure
3Increase aerationDoes not solve the cause but reduces stress on affected fish
4Do not clean the filterThe bacteria that oxidize nitrite live there
5Retest after a few hoursTwo readings provide direction

Why Did Nitrite Appear in the First Place?

Nitrite is an intermediate stage: bacteria convert ammonia into it, and then other bacteria convert it into nitrate. Its appearance means that the first step is working, but the second has not caught up.

  • New tank cycling: Completely normal. The nitrite peak follows the ammonia peak and is a sign of progress, not failure. The nitrogen cycle.
  • Suddenly unstable tank: Something damaged the colony—cleaning the filter with tap water, medication, a prolonged power outage, or a sudden increase in fish load.
  • Overstocking: New fish or overfeeding increased production beyond the system's processing capacity—How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Hold.

A Note on Chloride

Sources mention that chloride competes with nitrite for absorption sites in the gills, thereby reducing its effect. The mechanism is known, but the commonly cited ratios are taken from aquaculture in production tanks—different types and scales than a home ornamental aquarium. Therefore, we will not publish a ratio or dosage: the reliable home remedy remains water changes.

Difference from Ammonia Poisoning

The symptoms are very similar, and the difference is revealed by testing, not by observation:

  • Ammonia: Often accompanied by red gills and visible burns—Ammonia Spike Emergency Treatment.
  • Nitrite: More pronounced suffocation symptoms with less external damage.
  • Both may rise together in a new tank or after filter collapse.

Always test for both together—Reading Aquarium Test Kits and Fish Disease Symptoms and Diagnosis Guide. After the crisis has passed, review stocking and feeding: Aquarium Water Changes.

data.title: Livebearing Fish (Molly, Platy, Guppy, Swordtail): Breeding and Population Management
data.excerpt: The female stores what she needs and gives birth to successive batches after a single mating—the challenge is population management, not producing fry. The male-to-female ratio is not a minor detail.
data.content:
Livebearing Fish: One Family, Four Faces

Mollies, Platies, Guppies, and Swordtails are sold as separate species, but they share the same mechanism: they are livebearers—they give birth to ready-to-swim fry, rather than laying eggs. This changes everything in planning, as the question is not "how do I breed them" but "how do I deal with breeding that happens whether I want it or not".

SpeciesSizeNote to consider before buying
PlatySmallThe easiest and most tolerant—an excellent start
GuppySmallMales with long fins attract nipping from tank mates
MollyMediumHigher biological load and more sensitive to water deterioration
SwordtailLargest among themNeeds more swimming length, and males compete amongst themselves

For guppies, there is a separate detailed guide in the Guppy Care Guide, and for beginners, check their place among the 5 Hardy Fish for Beginners.

The Fact That Surprises Most: One Female is Enough

The most important practical point on this topic: a female can store enough sperm for fertilization and give birth to successive batches after a single mating. This means buying one female from the store can result in several batches of fry in your tank without any male present at all.

This flips the question: the challenge is not producing fry—the challenge is population management. Plan for overcrowding before it happens, because it happens much faster than you expect. Refer to How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Support.

Male-to-Female Ratio is Not a Minor Detail

Male livebearers constantly chase females as a reproductive behavior. If the numbers are unbalanced, the chasing focuses on one female, exhausting her, stressing her, and weakening her immunity.

  • Common Rule: One male to two or three females, not the other way around.
  • Swordtails Specifically: Two adult males in a small tank will compete—one male is better. This is the same observation found in the hardy fish guide.
  • And if you want to avoid breeding altogether: Keep only one sex—sexing is explained in How to Sex Aquarium Fish. But be aware of the storage point above: a purchased female may already be pregnant.
  • To understand the logic of chasing in general, refer to Aggression and Chasing in the Aquarium.

Rescuing Fry: Plants Are More Successful Than Nets

Fry are preyed upon by their mother and the rest of the tank within hours. The solutions are not equal:

  1. Dense plants and floating surfaces—the simplest and most practically successful. Fry hide on their own, without moving or stress.
  2. A separate tank for fry—best for results, but requires an independent biological cycle. A new tank without bacteria will kill fry with ammonia—see the Nitrogen Cycle Explained.
  3. The hanging breeder box—it works, but keeping the female in it for too long stresses her. Use it for a short duration only.

Fry are fed with small, frequent meals of finely ground food; overfeeding here quickly fouls the water because the size is small—see the Fish Feeding Guide and Water Change Guide.

Iraqi Conditions: Temperature Above All Else

Livebearers are generally hardy, but two points can break them locally:

  • Summer heat. High temperatures reduce dissolved oxygen and speed up metabolism, and a tank crowded with fry is the first to collapse—see Protecting Fish in Iraqi Summer Heat (50°C) and Air Pumps: Decoration or Necessity?.
  • Power outages—see Emergency Aquarium Tools for Power Outages.
  • Tap water must be treated before use—see How to Treat Tap Water for Fish in Iraq.

Mollies in particular tend to prefer slightly harder water than Platies, so know your water hardness from the GH and KH Water Hardness Guide before making your choice beyond its limits.

data.title: How Many Fish Can Your Tank Handle? And Why the Inch-Per-Gallon Rule is Wrong
data.excerpt: The common rule ignores body mass, filtration, surface area, and behavior. The five factors that truly decide, and the test that gives you the answer for your specific tank.
data.content:
The "Inch Per Gallon" Rule is Wrong, and Here's Why It's So Widespread

The common rule states: one inch of fish per gallon of water. It's simple, easy to remember, and found everywhere — yet it's unreliable because it ignores everything that truly matters.

What the Rule IgnoresWhy It Matters
Body MassA plump 12-inch fish produces far more waste than twelve slender 1-inch fish.
MetabolismThe biological load follows mass and metabolic rate, not length.
Filtration PowerThe same tank can support more fish with a powerful external filter than with a simple sponge filter.
Surface AreaGas exchange happens at the surface; a shallow, wide tank can support more than a tall, narrow one of the same volume.
BehaviorA territorial fish needs space unrelated to pollution, and schooling fish need a minimum number or they get stressed and sick.

Any rule that simplifies five factors into one number will be wrong. This is why serious calculators use multiple methods simultaneously instead of relying on just one.

The Five Factors That Truly Decide

  1. Adult Size, Not Purchase Size. A fish that is 3 cm long in the store can reach 30 cm. Plan for the adult size from day one — goldfish are the most common example, with details in Goldfish Mistakes.
  2. Biological Load. A plump, greedy fish pollutes many times more than a slender fish of the same length.
  3. Filtration Capacity. See Choosing a Filter — the filter determines how much ammonia your tank can process per hour.
  4. Surface Area and Temperature. Warmer water dissolves less oxygen, so an Iraqi tank in summer can support fewer fish than the same tank in winter. The mechanism is explained in Summer Heat.
  5. Behavior and Compatibility. Minimum school size, territorial needs, and compatibility of temperature and pH among species.

The Practical Answer: Let the Tank Tell You

We won't give you a formula, because there isn't one that holds up. But there is a definitive test that gives you the answer for your specific tank:

Your tank is not overstocked if ammonia is zero, nitrite is zero, and nitrate remains stable between your usual water changes. If ammonia rises or nitrates climb week after week despite water changes, you are exceeding the tank's capacity — no matter what any rule says.

This isn't dodging the question; it's the most accurate answer possible: the readings measure the actual result of all five factors combined. Test strips and ammonia/nitrite test kits are available at AQUAVO under testing and monitoring.

Signs of Overstocking Before the Numbers Show It

  • Fish gasping at the surface, especially in the morning before the lights turn on.
  • Water quickly becoming cloudy after cleaning.
  • Algae returning stubbornly despite adjusting lighting — chronic high nitrates.
  • Aggression and torn fins: a space issue, not a water quality issue.
  • Recurring diseases with no clear cause — overstocking causes chronic stress that weakens immunity.

Start with Fewer Fish

The only rule we confidently recommend: start with fewer fish than you think you need, and add gradually in small batches spaced weeks apart. For two reasons:

  • The beneficial bacteria colony grows to meet the load, and it needs time. Adding a large batch at once will spike ammonia before the bacteria can catch up — the mechanism is explained in The Biological Cycle.
  • You can always add a fish. You can't easily remove one after you've become attached to it.

To accurately calculate your tank size before making any decisions, use the Calculators. If you're considering a filterless tank, the limit is much lower — see Fish That Live Without a Filter.

The calculations are often broken by fish that are bought small and grow very large: Oscars and Arowanas, and outdoors, Koi, which belong in ponds, not tanks. Before anything else, confirm your tank's actual capacity by calculating its volume in liters.

The Calculation Breaks Down at Purchase

Everything above assumes you know the adult size. This is where the calculation practically breaks down: the store displays juveniles, and the decision is based on the size you see, not the size it will become.

  • Ask about the adult size before buying, not after — changing your mind while standing in the store costs nothing.
  • Fish do not grow to fit their tank. The idea that they "stop growing to fit the tank" is common and incorrect.
  • If you already have this problem, your options are limited, and all are more difficult than a one-minute decision in the store.

Species where this commonly occurs and realistic options are discussed in Fish That Outgrow Home Tanks.

data.seoDescription: Learn why the inch-per-gallon rule is flawed and discover the 5 key factors for stocking your aquarium correctly. Get practical advice for a healthy tank.

data.title: Fish Sold Small That Are Unsuitable for a Home Aquarium
data.excerpt: The fish does not grow to fit its tank—it becomes stunted, and stunting is permanent damage. Species where this is common, and realistic options if you already have this problem.
data.content:
The Store Tank Hides the Truth

A fish you see the size of your finger might be the juvenile of a fish that grows longer than your arm. This is not a rare exception—it's a complete sales pattern: large riverine species are displayed small, in small tanks, at a low price, with no indication of their adult size.

And before anything else, let's correct a myth: A fish does not grow "to fit its tank." A small tank does not produce a healthy small fish—it produces a stunted fish, and stunting is permanent, irreparable damage, explained in Raising Fish Fry.

Species Where This Is Common

Sold AsBecomes
"Freshwater Shark" / PangasiusA huge, active riverine fish—one of the most commonly sold under misleading descriptions
Common PlecoMany times the sale size, and a large waste producer
Redtail CatfishOne of the largest to enter the ornamental trade
OscarLarge, messy, and long-lived
ArowanaRequires an exceptionally long tank
Clown LoachGrows very large and lives for many years—details
KoiA pond fish, not a home aquarium fish

We are not publishing centimeter measurements for each species: sources vary, and conditions change the outcome. A practical rule is more accurate than any number—ask about the adult size before buying, and assume it will be larger than it appears.

Why This Is Worse Than Just "A Small Tank"

The problem is not just aesthetic. A fish that outgrows its tank pays the price in multiple ways:

  • Biological load doubles with size. A large fish produces significantly more waste, turning the tank into a constant ammonia battle—Ammonia Spike Emergency Treatment.
  • Insufficient swimming space for active riverine species, leading to lethargy or glass-bumping.
  • Aggression increases with maturity towards tank mates that were suitable when the fish was small—Aggression and Chasing.
  • Strain on equipment not designed for this load—Aquarium Placement and Stand.

To calculate what your tank can actually handle in numbers, refer to How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Hold—this article is about the purchase decision, that one is about the calculation.

The Two Questions Before Buying

  1. What is its adult size? Ask the seller, then check a second source. The seller might not know, and it's not necessarily bad faith.
  2. How long does it live? Many of these species live for many years. You are not buying decor for a season—you are committing to a living being for years, which includes moving, travel, and rehoming.

If the answer does not suit your current aquarium, the honest choice is another species—not "I'll buy it and see." Refer to Choosing Healthy Fish in Store and 5 Hardy Fish for Beginners.

You Already Have This Problem—What Are the Options?

If you are reading this late, this article does not blame you. The seller didn't inform you, and the information wasn't readily available. Realistic options:

  • A larger aquarium if possible—the direct solution, with associated costs, space, and weight.
  • Another hobbyist with a suitable tank. Local hobbyist communities are the best route, and healthy large fish are usually sought after.
  • A specialized store might take it back or help find a home. Ask—the answer varies from place to place.
And one option is completely unacceptable: Do not release fish into a river, lake, or waterway. Invasive species harm the local environment, and the fish itself often dies. This is not compassion—it is double harm.

If you move it to another home, the move itself requires preparation—Transporting Fish and Aquariums.

data.title: Barbs: Which Species Are Safe for a Community Tank?
data.excerpt: Fin nipping is a group behavior, not a personal trait. Increasing the number of fish reduces the problem, rather than exacerbating it. Certain tank mates will inevitably pay the price first.
data.content:
Barbs Are Excellent Fish — Provided You Know Which Kind

Barbs are among the most active and hardy freshwater fish, and at the same time, among the most misrepresented. The problem is that the name "barb" covers species with entirely different behaviors: some are peaceful and suitable for any community tank, while others are known for fin nipping. The buyer hears "barb" and assumes they are all the same.

SpeciesBehavior in a Community TankPractical Verdict
Tiger BarbVery active and a known fin nipperSuitable — but with a sufficient school and carefully chosen tank mates
Cherry BarbPeaceful and smallerThe easiest choice for a community tank
Odessa BarbActive but less intense than the Tiger BarbIntermediate — requires swimming space

Fin Nipping: Behavior, Not Malice

The Tiger Barb does not nip fins because it is "aggressive" in a personal sense. This is group behavior: barbs interact with their own kind through constant social ranking — chasing and competition within the school. When the school is incomplete, this activity finds no internal outlet and is directed at the nearest available target.

This is why the seemingly counterintuitive solution is the correct one: increasing the number of fish reduces the problem, rather than exacerbating it. A small school of Tiger Barbs is more dangerous to its tank mates than a large school. The same principle is explained in Aggression and Chasing in the Aquarium and Schooling Fish: Minimum Numbers.

However, do not rely on numbers alone. Numbers reduce the probability, they do not eliminate it.

Tank Mates Unsuitable for Tiger Barbs

The rule is simple: any slow-moving fish with long fins is a potential target.

  • Betta — Long fins and slow movement, the worst possible combination. See Betta Tank Mates.
  • Angelfish — Their long, flowing fins will be gradually nipped, as explicitly stated in the Angelfish Care Guide.
  • Gourami — They have sensitive thread-like appendages, and their breathing method causes them to ascend to the surface slowly, leaving them exposed.
  • Discus — Slow eaters and already stressed, barbs will steal their food before they can eat it. See Discus Fish Care Guide.

Conversely, suitable tank mates are active fish of similar size with short fins, and bottom dwellers like Corydoras that occupy a different layer of the aquarium. Before mixing any species, consult the Compatibility Guide.

What Barbs Truly Need

  1. Length over Height. Barbs are long-distance swimmers, so horizontal swimming space is more important than just the total liters — see How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Hold.
  2. Current and Oxygen. Active fish consume more oxygen, and in the Iraqi summer, this is the first point of failure — see When Air Pumps Are a Necessity and Protecting Fish in the Iraqi Summer Heat (50°C).
  3. Broken Lines of Sight. Plants, driftwood, and rocks break up chasing paths, calming the aquarium without increasing the liters.
  4. Varied Diet in Controlled Portions. Barbs are greedy and eat quickly, which can lead to overfeeding — see Aquarium Fish Feeding Guide.

If Fin Nipping Actually Occurs

A nipped fin is an entry point for infection, not just a cosmetic damage. Observe the edge: if it becomes white or gradually erodes, you have a second problem — Fin Rot Treatment Guide. Always start with the water before medication, according to the Fish Disease Symptoms and Diagnosis Guide and Reading Your Water Test Kit.

If nipping continues despite a sufficient school and adequate space, the honest solution is to separate the species rather than continue hoping. Some combinations simply do not work, no matter how well conditions are managed.

data.excerpt: The Arowana fish is the queen of large aquariums. Learn about its specifications, prices in the Iraqi market, and the best fish that can live peacefully with it.
data.content:
Introduction to the Arowana Fish

The Arowana fish is one of the most beautiful and popular fish in Iraq, known as the "money fish" or "gold fish" due to its beauty and high price. This fish is found in a variety of colors, including silver, gold, and bronze, and is considered one of the most intelligent and beautiful fish in the world.

Arowana Fish Specifications

The Arowana fish is characterized by several unique specifications, including:

  • Beauty: The Arowana fish is considered one of the most beautiful fish in the world, with its silver, gold, and bronze colors.
  • Size: The Arowana fish ranges in size between 20-30 cm and is considered one of the largest fish in Iraq.
  • Lifespan: The Arowana fish reaches 10-15 years in the wild and is considered one of the longest-living fish in Iraq.

Rearing Arowana Fish in Iraq

Rearing Arowana fish in Iraq requires special care to ensure its health, due to the extreme summer heat reaching 50 °C, frequent power outages, and heavily chlorinated tap water. The fish keeper must provide a suitable environment for the Arowana fish, with appropriate temperature, good nutrition, and constant monitoring.

Arowana Fish Prices in Iraq

Arowana fish prices in Iraq range between 50,000 to 200,000 Iraqi Dinars, depending on size, color, and quality. The Arowana is a fish that reaches large lengths and requires a long aquarium with a secure lid because it is a strong jumper. These two factors are much more important than the price of the fish itself.

Golden tip from AQUAVO: The fish keeper should choose the Arowana fish carefully, ensuring its health and quality before purchasing, and providing a suitable environment for its rearing.

Fish Compatible with Arowana

The Arowana fish is compatible with many other fish, including:

  1. Gourami: The Gourami fish is considered one of the most compatible fish with the Arowana fish, due to its beauty and calmness.
  2. Platy: The Platy fish is considered one of the most popular fish in Iraq and is well-compatible with the Arowana fish.
  3. Neon Tetra: The Neon Tetra fish is considered one of the most beautiful fish in the world and is well-compatible with the Arowana fish.

Using the Arowana Fish in the Aquarium

The fish keeper must use a large, high-quality aquarium to rear the Arowana fish, ensuring a suitable environment and constant monitoring. Calculate the aquarium size and filtration requirements before anything else: Arowanas produce a large amount of waste and require regular filtration and water changes.

Conclusion

Rearing Arowana fish in Iraq requires special care and a suitable environment to ensure its health. The fish keeper should choose the Arowana fish carefully, ensuring its health and quality before purchasing, and providing a suitable environment for its rearing.

data.title: Best Types of African Cichlids and Their Amazing Colors
data.excerpt: Stunning colors and strong personalities! Discover the most beautiful types of African Cichlids and how to choose the most suitable for your aquarium, with care tips.
data.content:
Introduction to African Cichlids

African cichlids are among the most popular fish in the ornamental fish world, due to their great diversity and stunning colors, ranging from bright colors like blue and red to light colors like beige and gray. These fish are considered among the most adaptable in aquariums, as they can adjust to different water conditions.

Best Types of African Cichlids

There are many different types of African cichlids, and each type has unique characteristics. Some of the best types include:

  • Mbuna African cichlids, characterized by their bright colors and great diversity.
  • Haplochromis African cichlids, characterized by their light colors and adaptability to different water conditions.
  • Labidochromis African cichlids, characterized by their amazing colors and great diversity.

African Cichlid Aquariums in Iraq

In Iraq, where summer temperatures reach 50 °C, electricity outages occur, and tap water is saturated with chlorine, keeping African cichlids can be a challenge. However, you can succeed in breeding these beautiful fish by choosing suitable aquariums with specific water conditions. Aquariums should have features such as:

  1. Sufficient size to accommodate the fish.
  2. An effective filtration system for water purification.
  3. A heating and cooling system to regulate water temperature.

Golden Tip from AQUAVO

Golden Tip from AQUAVO: When choosing African cichlids, consider the aquarium water conditions, temperature, and necessary care to ensure a healthy and thriving life for the fish. You can benefit from AQUAVO's services, which include a wide range of aquarium supplies, with delivery covering 18 governorates in Iraq.

African lake cichlids require hard and relatively alkaline water, which makes them incompatible with soft water fish in the same aquarium. However, you must be careful when buying fish from these markets, as water quality and fish guarantees can vary.

Conclusion

African cichlids are considered among the best ornamental fish for beginners and experts, characterized by stunning colors and great diversity. When keeping these fish in Iraq, consider the aquarium water conditions, temperature, and necessary care to ensure a healthy and thriving life for the fish.
