data.title: Shrimp and Snails in the Aquarium: Copper First, Then Everything Else
data.excerpt: Invertebrates are much more sensitive to copper than fish, and copper does not break down but remains in the substrate for months. What you really need from water, filtration, and hiding places.
data.content:
Before Anything Else: Copper Kills

If you plan to keep shrimp or snails, this is the most important paragraph you will read. Invertebrates are much more sensitive to copper than fish, and copper is found in unexpected places:

  • Fish medications — Many are copper-based and kill shrimp at concentrations that do not harm fish.
  • Snail poisons — Most are copper-based, and shrimp are more sensitive than the targeted snails themselves.
  • Some liquid plant fertilizers.
What's more dangerous is that copper does not break down: it binds to the substrate, rocks, and silicone and slowly leaches out for months. This means a tank treated with copper once may not be suitable for invertebrates afterward at all. The practical rule: always treat fish in a separate tank — this is an added benefit of a quarantine tank: Quarantine.

What They Actually Are, and What They Are Not

BeliefReality
A cleaning crew that eliminates the need for maintenanceThey eat algae and leftover food, but they add to the bioload and do not eliminate the need for water changes.
They tolerate any waterThey are much more sensitive to ammonia and copper than fish.
They don't need foodThey need specialized food if algae become scarce.
They live with any fishMost medium-sized fish will eat small shrimp.

The Water They Need

  • Ammonia and nitrite at zero, without exception. Invertebrates are affected before fish, serving as an early indicator of water deterioration. Reading Water Tests.
  • Sufficient calcium for shells and exoskeletons. Snails and shrimp build shells and exoskeletons, and very soft water results in brittle shells and problems during molting. This is what GH is for — GH and KH Water Hardness.
  • Stability above all else. Sudden changes in temperature or chemistry are more dangerous for them than for fish, so smaller, more frequent water changes are better — Water Change.

The Filter: A Point That Silently Kills the Young

The filter intake can suck in baby shrimp and young snails. The simple solution: a sponge filter, or a sponge cover on the intake of any other filter. Sponge filters are available at AQUAVO in the Filtration and Purification section, and some are specifically made for shrimp and baby fish. Details on types in Choosing a Filter.

Food and Hiding Places

  • Specialized shrimp food is available at AQUAVO in the Fish Food section, and should be offered in very small quantities — excess food pollutes the water quickly.
  • Catapa leaves (Indian almond leaves) break down slowly and provide a surface for shrimp to graze on, and are available in the Water Treatments section.
  • Plenty of hiding places — Shrimp molt and become fragile and weak for hours afterward, needing a place to hide. Driftwood and moss are ideal.

With Which Fish

The honest rule: any fish that can fit a shrimp in its mouth will eat it sooner or later. Small, peaceful fish are a better choice, and medium or large-mouthed fish will not coexist with small shrimp, no matter how calm they seem.

Snails are less vulnerable, but some species will nip at them. And watch the numbers: snails reproduce based on food availability, so overfeeding is what turns a few snails into a population explosion — not the snails themselves.

To calculate your tank's load before adding inhabitants, see How Many Fish Your Aquarium Can Support.

Why the Colony Isn't Growing

Shrimp reproduce on their own under suitable conditions, so if the population remains stable or decreases, the reason is usually one of these:

  • Young are sucked into the filter. The most common silent cause — a sponge on the intake solves the problem.
  • Not enough hiding places. Young require dense plants or moss; a bare tank means complete predation.
  • Molting problems. Shrimp build their shells from water minerals, and water very low in minerals makes molting difficult — one of the most dangerous moments of their lives.
  • Mineral fluctuations. Stability is more important than the number — GH and KH Guide.
  • Fish are eating them. Many fish consider baby shrimp food, even if they coexist with adults.

Do not interfere during molting, and do not remove the shed exoskeleton — it will be reabsorbed.

data.title: Can Aquatic Turtles Be Kept With Ornamental Fish in the Same Aquarium?
data.excerpt: A dream that captivates children and hobbyists, but its reality is dramatic and tragic. Uncovering the mystery of impossible compatibility.
data.content:
Aquatic Turtles + Ornamental Fish = A Guaranteed Disaster!

A dream that captivates every child and hobbyist: an aquarium with colorful turtles and fish swimming together peacefully. But the reality is completely different! Here's the full truth.

Why Doesn't This Mix Work?

  • Turtles are Predators: Even "tame" turtles will chase and eat fish — an instinct that cannot be changed.
  • Massive Waste Production: Turtles produce waste many times greater than any fish of the same size. A standard filter is insufficient.
  • Different Temperature Requirements: Turtles need a dry basking area with temperatures between 30-35°C.
  • Dirty Water: Turtles eat in the water and quickly pollute it — fish cannot tolerate this level of contamination.
  • UVB Lighting: Turtles require UVB rays to synthesize vitamin D3 — this lighting is unsuitable for fish.

The Only Exception

In very large tanks (500+ L) with a powerful sump filter, fast and large fish like Silver Dollars can be kept with small turtles. However, expect some fish losses.

The Better Alternative

Keep the two habitats completely separate! An aquarium for fish and a terrarium/aquaterrarium for turtles.

Golden Rule: Every creature deserves an environment that suits its needs. Forcing them together means suffering for both.

data.seoDescription: Discover why mixing aquatic turtles and ornamental fish in the same aquarium is a recipe for disaster. Learn about the challenges and the best way to house them separately.

data.title: How to Protect Your Fish in Iraq's Summer with 50°C Heat?
data.excerpt: Heat doesn't kill fish directly; it suffocates them: oxygen decreases while the fish's need for it increases simultaneously. An emergency temperature guide and practical methods ranked by effectiveness versus cost.
data.content:
Heat Doesn't Kill Fish Directly — It Suffocates Them

Most people who lose fish during Iraqi summers think the cause is "heat." The real reason is more nuanced, and understanding it completely changes your approach: Heat reduces dissolved oxygen in the water and simultaneously increases the fish's need for it.

Water TemperatureMaximum Dissolved OxygenFish Consumption
20 °CApprox. 9.1 mg/LBaseline
32 °CLowerAround 40–75% Higher
35 °CApprox. 7.0 mg/L — About 23% Lower CeilingMuch Higher

Notice how the two columns move in opposite directions. Supply drops while demand rises, so fish can suffocate even in a well-aerated tank. This is why the first step during a heatwave isn't cooling, but oxygenation.

The sign to watch for: fish gasping at the surface. This isn't "pickiness" or hunger — it's a fish trying to breathe from the oxygen-richest layer. Treat it as an emergency.

Emergency Guide: What to Do at Each Temperature

Most tropical ornamental fish are kept between 24 and 28 °C, and prolonged exposure above 32 °C is dangerous.

TemperatureConditionAction
28–30 °CAlertTurn off the heater, turn off lights during peak hours, increase surface agitation
30–32 °CStressAdd an air pump, use a fan on the surface, reduce feeding by half
32–35 °CDangerAll of the above + gradual cooling + do not feed at all that day
Above 35 °CEmergencyContinuous gradual cooling and constant monitoring; gasping fish means minutes, not hours

Practical Methods, Ranked by Effectiveness vs. Cost

  1. Increase Oxygenation — Always First. Add an extra air pump, or position the filter outlet to agitate the surface. Gas exchange happens entirely at the surface, so agitation there is more critical than deep water movement. Air pumps and airstones are available at AQUAVO.
  2. Fan on the Water Surface. The cheapest effective cooling method: a small fan directed at the surface with the lid raised or replaced with mesh. Cooling occurs through evaporation.
    • You must replace evaporated water promptly, otherwise, the concentration of dissolved substances will rise.
    • The amount of temperature drop depends on humidity, airflow, and surface area — and it's weaker in high-humidity areas. No one can give a fixed number.
  3. Eliminate Heat Sources. Turn off the heater (many forget), turn off lights from noon to evening, and keep the tank away from direct sunlight and windows.
  4. Reduce Feeding. Metabolism is already high, and excess food decomposes, consuming additional oxygen — precisely what you lack.
  5. Frozen Water Bottles — With Caution. Use one sealed bottle, replaced every few hours. Do not place multiple bottles: sudden cooling is a shock in itself and can kill faster than slow heat.

As for chillers, they are a definitive solution for large or valuable tanks, but they are expensive devices that consume electricity — and in Iraq, electricity itself is part of the problem.

Things Not to Do

  • Do not perform large cold water changes at once. Sudden temperature drops are a shock. Cool gradually.
  • Do not rely on ice cubes directly in the water — they melt quickly and alter water chemistry if made from untreated tap water.
  • Do not turn off the filter to reduce heat. You will lose surface agitation and biological filtration simultaneously, which is far more dangerous than gaining a degree.

Heat Plus Power Outages: The Compound Iraqi Problem

This is where the situation becomes more dangerous than the sum of its parts. The power goes out, stopping the filter, air pump, and surface agitation — precisely when the hot water needs them most. Simultaneously, the bacteria inside the filter begin to suffer from the lack of water flow.

The practical order of operations during an outage: manually agitate the water surface with a cup periodically, cover the tank with a light blanket to insulate it from room heat if the room is hotter than the water, and do not feed. Full details in Emergency Tools for Power Outages, and an explanation of respiration and oxygen in Tanks Without Filters.

After the Heatwave: Monitor Ammonia

Heat accelerates metabolism and decomposition, and the resulting ammonia becomes more toxic at higher temperatures because the free ammonia percentage increases with heat and pH. This means the same reading is more dangerous in the summer. Test for ammonia and nitrite after any heatwave or prolonged outage — the mechanism is explained in the Biological Cycle.

If the water becomes cloudy afterward, it's likely a bacterial bloom consuming extra oxygen. The solution isn't frequent water changes — see Diagnosing Cloudy Water. Use the Calculators to estimate your tank volume and evaporated water quantity.

The other side of the same problem occurs in winter, with sudden nighttime cooling rather than heat — see Is a Heater Necessary in Winter. If you must move the tank or fish during peak heat, temperature is the primary constraint — see Transporting Fish and Aquariums.

data.seoDescription: Learn how to save your fish during Iraq's extreme summer heat. Understand the link between temperature, oxygen, and fish stress. Get practical tips and an emergency guide for high temperatures and power outages.

data.title: Large Amazon Sword Plant (Echinodorus bleheri) and How to Propagate It
data.excerpt: The Amazon Sword plant is the king of planted aquariums! Learn how to plant, care for, and propagate it to fill your tank with lush greenery.
data.content:
Introduction to the Amazon Sword Plant

The Amazon Sword plant is one of the most common aquatic plants in ornamental aquariums, growing in the Amazon regions of South America. This plant has large, beautiful leaves and can reach a height of up to 50 cm. The Amazon Sword plant can be grown in aquariums of various sizes, but it prefers large aquariums to grow well.

Growing Conditions for the Amazon Sword Plant

To grow the Amazon Sword plant well, you must provide the following conditions:

  • Bright light: The Amazon Sword plant needs bright light to grow, but the light should not be direct as this can cause leaf burn.
  • Temperature: The water temperature should be between 22-28 °C, which is suitable for the climate in Iraq.
  • Clean water: The water must be clean and at a suitable temperature, and there should be no chemical or biological contaminants.

How to Propagate the Amazon Sword Plant

The Amazon Sword plant can be easily propagated through cuttings and planting. Here are the steps:

  1. Cut the leaves: The leaves should be cut well to obtain healthy cuttings.
  2. Plant the cuttings: The cuttings should be planted in suitable substrate and clean water.
  3. Provide conditions: The appropriate conditions for growth, such as light, temperature, and clean water, must be provided.
A golden tip from AQUAVO: You should choose Amazon Sword plant varieties that suit your tank's conditions.

Challenges of Growing Amazon Sword Plants in Iraq

Growing Amazon Sword plants in Iraq may face some challenges, such as:

  • High temperatures: High summer temperatures can damage the plant.
  • Power outages: Power outages can damage plants and equipment.
  • Tap water: Tap water in Iraq may contain harmful chemicals.

Solutions for the Challenges of Growing Amazon Sword Plants in Iraq

Solutions can be provided for the challenges of growing Amazon Sword plants in Iraq, such as:

  • Using water conditioners: Water conditioners can be used to improve water quality.
  • Using generators: Generators can be used to provide electricity during outages.
  • Choosing suitable plant varieties: Suitable plant varieties for the conditions in Iraq can be chosen.
  • Technical support: AQUAVO store provides technical support for fishkeeping hobbyists.
  • Delivery to 18 governorates: AQUAVO store provides delivery service to 18 governorates in Iraq.

data.title: Cleaning Fish (Scavengers): Which Cleaner for Which Problem?
data.excerpt: No fish eats waste. Otocinclus are not an emergency team—adding them to a new or recently cleaned tank is slow starvation.
data.content:
A Deadly Marketing Myth: No Fish Eats Waste

First, before any selection: No fish eats the waste of other fish. Waste is removed by water changes and biological filtration, not by fish. Fish called "scavengers" in Iraq—like Plecos and Corydoras—only eat growing algae and leftover sinking food.

This leads to a practical point: These fish need their own specialized food, usually sinking wafers, or they will slowly starve in a seemingly clean tank. A perfectly clean tank is the most dangerous tank for an algae eater. See the Feeding Guide.

Which Cleaner for Which Problem

FishWorks OnDoesn't Work On
OtocinclusSoft algae on glass and plant leavesHard algae and waste
CorydorasSifting the substrate and buried excess foodGlass—does not clean it at all
Siamese Algae EaterBlack beard algae and some thread algaeSubstrate and waste

Corydoras, in particular, have different types and specific substrate requirements—Corydoras Types. And for black beard algae specifically, see Black Beard Algae Removal Steps.

Otocinclus: Not an Emergency Team

This point deserves explicit correction, as the common description of Otos as an "emergency team" actually kills them. Otos should be added to a mature tank, not a new tank or one that has undergone a thorough cleaning.

  • Their food is a delicate biofilm that needs time to form on surfaces. A new tank doesn't provide this, so the fish weakens and wastes away within weeks for no apparent reason.
  • The deadly irony: People buy them to solve an algae bloom, so when it succeeds—or when the cause is treated—there's no food left for them. They need alternative food: blanched vegetable slices or algae wafers.
  • They usually arrive stressed. Otos are known for their sensitivity to transport, and many arrive weak to begin with. Quarantine is not a luxury here.
  • A group, not an individual. They live in groups and become lethargic and hidden when alone.
The correct order: Address the cause of the algae first, then decide if you want Otocinclus as a permanent part of the tank—not as a cure. Algae eaters are helpers, not a solution, as explained in the Algae Guide.

The Rule That Precedes Everything

Algae and excess food are symptoms of an imbalance, and fish do not fix the imbalance. Ensure the tank is mature—The Nitrogen Cycle—adjust feeding and lighting, then choose the cleaner based on the task, not the brand name.

And pay attention to the bioload: every cleaner you add is a full fish with its own waste and requirements—How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Hold. If the problem is snails, not algae, the approach is completely different—Aquarium Snail Population Control.
data.seoTitle: Cleaning Fish (Scavengers): Which Cleaner for Which Problem?
data.seoDescription: Learn about "cleaning fish" like Otocinclus, Corydoras, and Siamese Algae Eaters. Understand their roles, dietary needs, and why they aren't a solution for algae or waste.

data.title: Oscar Fish: The Freshwater Giant with a Strong Personality
data.excerpt: The fish that treats you like an aquatic pet dog, bonds with its owner, and dances for them. An icon of challenge and the king of large cichlids.
data.content:
The Oscar: The Freshwater Giant with the Loyalty of a Dog

The Oscar fish is not an ordinary fish—it's an intelligent creature that recognizes its owner, approaches the glass when you get close, and eats directly from your hand. Hobbyists call it the "water dog" due to its strong bond with its keeper. However, it requires special treatment!

Basic Oscar Specifications

  • Size: Up to 35 cm! One of the largest common freshwater fish.
  • Lifespan: Lives 10-15 years with good care.
  • Temperature: 23-28 °C.
  • pH: 6.0-8.0 (very tolerant).
  • Minimum Tank Size: 200 L for a single fish—yes, 200 L!

Proper Feeding

  • Base Diet: High-protein pellets specifically for large cichlids.
  • Variety: Dried shrimp, worms, pieces of fresh fish.
  • Avoid: Red meat (causes digestive issues) and live sick fish.
  • Quantity: What it can eat in 2-3 minutes, twice daily.

Why Hobbyists Love Them?

  • Recognizes its owner and wags its tail upon seeing them (like a dog!).
  • Enjoys playing—moves gravel and decor with its mouth.
  • Each fish has a unique personality and different mood.
  • Very intelligent—can be trained for simple commands.

Important Warnings for Beginners

The Oscar will eat any fish that fits into its mouth. Do not house it with any fish smaller than 15 cm. It requires a very powerful filter because it produces a large amount of waste. A weekly water change of 30-40% is essential.
data.seoTitle: Oscar Fish Guide: Care, Feeding, and Personality | AQUAVO Iraq
data.seoDescription: Learn about the fascinating Oscar fish, known for its intelligence and dog-like personality. Discover essential care tips, feeding requirements, and tank size recommendations for keeping Oscars in Iraq.

data.title: Moving Fish and Tanks: What Really Matters
data.excerpt: The air in the bag is more important than the water. The most costly mistake when moving an entire tank is letting the filter media dry out.
data.content:
Bags and Boxes: What Really Matters

Moving fish is a short but stressful process: small space, limited oxygen, ammonia accumulating without a filter, and changing temperatures. The basic rule defies intuition:

The air in the bag is more important than the water. Fill the bag one-third with water and two-thirds with air. Excess water is not helpful; the air space is what replenishes oxygen throughout the journey.
  • Do not feed for a day before moving — undigested food quickly pollutes the bag water.
  • Double bag and fold the corners, as small fish can get stuck in the corners.
  • Darken the bag with a box or cloth — darkness calms and reduces oxygen consumption.
  • Insulate thermally: a styrofoam box or a lined cardboard box. In the Iraqi summer, a car parked in the sun can be deadly within minutes — Summer Heat.
  • Fish with spines or sharp fins require a stronger bag or a rigid container.

Upon Arrival

Do not open the bag immediately and leave the fish in it for an hour. Opening the bag raises the pH, converting accumulated ammonia into its toxic form — and prolonged dripping inside the bag water increases the damage. The correct method and chemical details are in Acclimating New Fish.

Do not pour the transport water into the tank, and introduce the fish to a quarantine tank if possible — Quarantine.

Moving the Entire Tank

#StepNote
1Do not feed a day before movingReduces pollution during transport
2Save some tank water in clean bucketsFor moving fish in and for refilling part of the tank
3Keep the filter media submerged in tank waterThis is the most important step — dry media means the colony dies
4Transport fish in bags or covered bucketsDo not transport them inside the tank during the move
5Empty the tank completely before moving itA partially filled tank can break from stress on the silicone
6Carry it from the base, not the edgesCarrying from the top rim can break the seals
7Reassemble, then add the fish lastTurn on the filter and heater first
The most costly mistake: letting the filter media dry out during transport. The bacterial colony is lost, the tank effectively becomes uncycled, and ammonia levels will rise after a few days. Keep it submerged at all times. The Nitrogen Cycle.

After Moving: Expect an Unstable Week

  • Test daily for a week — Reading Tests.
  • Feed very sparingly for the first few days.
  • Expect cloudiness from disturbed substrate; it will clear on its own — Diagnosing Cloudy Water.
  • If ammonia rises, treat it as a tank undergoing cycling — Ammonia Spike Emergency Treatment.

Do not add new fish until the tank has been stable for weeks.

Dismantling and Restarting an Established Tank

Moving an established tank is not like moving furniture: you are moving a living system, and its most valuable component is not the glass, but the bacteria.

  1. Filter media, first and last. Place it in a bag filled with water from the tank itself, and do not let it dry out, not even for minutes — drying kills the colony and sends you back to square one.
  2. Retain as much tank water as possible for refilling — it reduces shock, although the bacteria are in the media, not the water.
  3. The substrate holds waste. Disturbing it releases this waste, so expect cloudiness and an ammonia spike after restarting.
  4. Turn on the filter and heater immediately after refilling.
  5. Test daily for the first week — treat the tank as if it is cycling anew — The Nitrogen Cycle.
  6. And feed very sparingly in the first few days.

data.title: White Slime: A True Fungus or Columnaris Bacteria?
data.excerpt: Most of what hobbyists call fungus is actually bacteria that does not respond to any antifungal treatment. How to differentiate by appearance, and why raising the temperature here might accelerate the disease instead of curing it.
data.content:
Most of What Hobbyists Call "Fungus" is Not Fungus

White slime on fish has two completely different causes, and they are constantly confused — and this confusion is costly, because the treatment for one will not work on the other at all.

  • True fungus (from the water mold group) grows on wounds or dead tissue.
  • Columnaris is a bacterium, popularly called "cotton wool disease" although it is not a fungus — and it does not respond to any antifungal treatment.
And here lies the danger: Columnaris is fast, and while antifungal treatments are tried in vain, the bacteria have already progressed. Lost time due to misdiagnosis is what kills, not the difficulty of the treatment.

How to Differentiate Between Them by Appearance

True FungusColumnaris (Bacterial)
AppearanceA 3D cotton-like mass protruding from the bodyA flat patch adhering to the surface
LocationOn a wound or damaged tissueOften without a prior wound — mouth, back, gills
SpeedSlowerFast, can kill within days
TreatmentAntifungalAntibacterial — Antifungal is ineffective

The easiest practical sign: Protruding and dense like cotton = fungus. Flat and adhering without a wound = bacterial. If you see a patch on the back resembling a "saddle" or erosion at the mouth, consider bacterial first.

Both Indicate Something Else Happened First

This is the most important point in the long run: True fungus does not attack healthy fish skin, and Columnaris exploits stress. The appearance of either is a sign of a prior cause:

  • Wounds from sharp decor, fights, or fishing nets.
  • Degraded water — ammonia or nitrite above zero. Read the test kit guide.
  • Temperature fluctuations or consistently high temperatures. Summer temperatures.
  • Overcrowding and chasing — chronic stress. How many fish your aquarium can support.

This is why treating the infection alone gives temporary improvement, and then it returns: the cause remains. The same logic applies to fin rot.

What to Do Practically

  1. Test the water first, before any medication. Symptoms and Diagnosis Guide.
  2. Isolate the affected fish in a treatment tank if possible — it's better for the fish and safer for the rest of the tank and invertebrates. Quarantine guide.
  3. Determine the type by appearance before choosing medication, according to the table above.
  4. Follow the dosage on the package and do not improvise. Methylene blue and bacterial treatment powder are available at AQUAVO in the water treatment section.
  5. Do not raise the temperature automatically. Raising the temperature helps with white spot disease, but it can accelerate Columnaris. Do not transfer protocols from one disease to another. White spot disease.

Limitations of What We Can Say

Final differentiation between these conditions requires microscopic examination, and we will not claim that visual appearance is always sufficient. The table above provides a likelihood, not a certainty — but a correct likelihood is much better than automatically assuming "fungus" for every white slime, an assumption that wastes time in the more dangerous situation.

And do not use human medications under any circumstances: Dangers of human medicine for fish.
data.seoTitle: White Slime on Fish: Fungus vs. Columnaris Bacteria - AQUAVO Guide
data.seoDescription: Learn to distinguish between true fungus and Columnaris bacterial infection on your fish. Understand the causes, symptoms, and correct treatments to save your aquarium inhabitants. AQUAVO Iraq.

data.title: Fish Eye Problems: Protrusion and Cloudiness
data.excerpt: One eye or two? This is the first question and guides the entire investigation: one eye tends to indicate a localized cause, while two suggest water issues or a systemic condition. Protrusion is a symptom, not a disease.
data.content:
One Eye or Two? This is the First Question

Eye problems are among the most obvious issues an aquarium owner notices: an eye bulging outwards, or a white cloudiness covering the surface. The good news is that the eye provides a diagnostic clue that is rarely unclear — the number of affected eyes.

One EyeBoth Eyes
Likely CauseLocalized IssueGeneral or Water-Related Cause
Common CausesCollision with decor, injury from chasing, localized infectionDeteriorating water quality, or systemic condition
First ActionLook for the source of injury in the aquariumTest the water immediately
This is a likelihood, not a diagnosis. Eye protrusion is a symptom, not a disease — the same logic applies to buoyancy problems in bloated or floating fish. The number guides the investigation but doesn't solely determine it.

Bulging Eye (Protrusion)

The eye bulges outwards to varying degrees, from slight to very noticeable. The practical approach:

  1. Test the water first — ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate. This step precedes everything else in the aquarium — reading the test results.
  2. Look for a mechanical cause if it's a single eye: sharp edges on decor, or chasing by tank mates.
  3. Observe the rest of the body. If the protrusion is accompanied by scales sticking out like a pinecone, you are facing a different and more serious condition — refer to the bloating article above immediately.
  4. Improve conditions and observe. Many localized cases improve with clean, stable water and a calm environment without medication.

If treatment is needed, the method — isolation, dosage, and duration — is detailed in proper treatment. We do not provide dosages here.

Cloudy Eye

Cloudiness or whiteness on the surface of the eye. Practically associated causes:

  • Water quality — the most common and the first thing to rule out.
  • Injury or abrasion against a rough surface.
  • Chemical irritation — detergent residue or improperly rinsed treatments.
  • A broader condition where the eye is one of its symptoms.

Do not confuse this with a white spot *on the skin* near the eye: that is a different issue explained in white fungus, and small scattered spots in white spot disease.

A Controversial Point Presented As Is

Epsom salt is often mentioned for reducing eye protrusion. Hobbyist sources repeat it, but evidence for it is weak, and the dosages mentioned are contradictory. Therefore, we do not provide a dosage for it or recommend it as a protocol. We mention it because you will encounter it, and we frankly state that we do not have sufficient basis for a recommendation. Aquarium salt, in general, has its limits and precautions — aquarium salt guide.

Prognosis: What to Expect

  • Improvement is possible if the cause is treated early, especially in localized cases.
  • A severely damaged eye may not return to its original appearance, and the fish may lose vision in it.
  • A fish with one eye can live a normal life in a calm aquarium: eating, moving, and interacting. This is not a situation that warrants a drastic decision.
  • Bilateral eye involvement with other symptoms is more serious, as it indicates a deeper cause — start with the symptom diagnosis guide.

Prevention is the same as prevention for everything else in the aquarium: stable water, decor without sharp edges, and stocking levels that do not cause constant chasing — water changes and how many fish your aquarium can support. And before buying any fish, the eyes are among the first things to check — choosing a healthy fish.
data.seoTitle: Fish Eye Problems: Protrusion and Cloudiness Diagnosis and Treatment
data.seoDescription: Learn to diagnose and treat fish eye problems like protrusion and cloudiness. Understand the causes, symptoms, and effective solutions for a healthy aquarium.

data.title: Why Do Fish Jump Out of the Aquarium? And the Right Lid
data.excerpt: Jumping is a symptom before it's a habit: poor water quality, lack of oxygen, or being chased. And why a completely sealed lid is dangerous for species that breathe atmospheric air.
data.content:
A Jumping Fish Isn't a "Crazy" Fish

Jumping is a natural and ancient behavior: in nature, fish jump to escape predators, to move between bodies of water, or to catch an insect. The behavior itself isn't abnormal — but its repetition inside the aquarium is a sign, often a sign of something you can fix.

Most jumping incidents are discovered late: the fish is found on the floor in the morning. This is why a lid isn't just an aesthetic choice — it's the difference between an incident and survival.

Why Fish Jump in the Aquarium

ReasonAccompanying SignSolution
Poor water qualityGasping, lethargy, or rubbing against surfacesTest immediately — ammonia and nitrite
Lack of oxygenGathering at the surface before jumpingIncrease aeration and surface agitation
Chasing and aggressionTorn fins, hidingReview compatibility and stocking levels
High temperatureExcessive activity followed by lethargyCool down gradually
New, unstable fishOnly during the first few daysDim lighting and quiet
Species' natureWithout any other symptomsA lid — no other solution

Jumping is a symptom before it becomes a habit. If it repeats, start with the water, not the lid — reading water test results then the guide to diagnosing symptoms.

Species That Jump More Than Others

  • Surface-dwelling fish that feed from the surface — their mouths are oriented upwards, and their nature includes leaping.
  • Long, slender, fast species that swim near the surface.
  • Betta fish — they breathe atmospheric air and constantly go to the surface, so the chance of them getting out is higher. An aquarium without a filter explains their aerial respiration.
  • Any new fish during its first few days — acclimating new fish.

The Lid: What to Watch Out For

  1. Cover the gaps, not just the surface. Most incidents happen through the opening for hoses or filters, or a raised corner, not from the middle of the lid.
  2. Do not seal completely. The aquarium needs gas exchange, and some species — like Gouramis — must reach the surface to breathe air. A completely sealed environment is a real danger to them.
  3. Leave a gap between the water and the lid. A water level touching the rim makes it easier for fish to jump out and reduces ventilation.
  4. Consider the temperature. A sealed lid traps heat, which is important in Iraq's summer — summer temperatures.

The balance between coverage and ventilation is the core of the issue: a lid that prevents escape and allows exchange, not a sealed box. Details on exchange in dissolved oxygen and aeration.

If You Find a Fish Outside the Aquarium

Do not assume immediate death if it is still wet and recently fallen. Gently return it to the water and monitor it in a quiet area with dim lighting and good aeration. Chances of survival depend on the duration and gill dryness, and it may survive if the time was short — or it may not survive despite everything, which is possible.

Then, look for the cause: a fish that jumped once may jump again, and the lid addresses the result while examination addresses the cause.
data.seoTitle: Why Fish Jump Out of Aquariums & Choosing the Right Lid

data.title: Tetras, Rasboras, and Danios: Which Schooling Fish to Choose?
data.excerpt: Three families sold as if they were one. The difference between Neon and Cardinal with a single visual check, why not all tetras are peaceful—and which school to choose if you want a larger size.
data.content:
Three Families Sold as If They Were One

Tetras, Rasboras, and Danios are placed in the same small tanks in stores at almost the same price, leading beginners to get three different types with three fish of each type. The result is a stressed tank that doesn't resemble anything in the pictures they saw. The right choice starts with understanding that these are three families, each with its own preferred water parameters and different behavior.

FamilyCommon ExamplesPreferred WaterNote for Purchase Decision
TetraNeon, Cardinal, Black Neon, GlowlightTend towards soft and acidicNot all are peaceful—some are fin nippers
RasboraHarlequin, AmberSoft to mediumUsually the most peaceful and most stable in a community tank
DanioZebra DanioTolerates a wide rangeVery active and fast—disturbs slower species
Practical rule: One large school is better than three small schools. Eight fish of one species give you the natural look and behavior, while three of each species give you three scared groups. Details on numbers in Schooling Fish: Why Six, Not Three.

Neon and Cardinal: Not the Same Fish

This is the most common mix-up, and the difference is not just aesthetic—it affects the price and requirements.

Neon TetraCardinal Tetra
Red StripeCovers only the rear halfExtends the full length of the body
SizeSmallerSlightly larger
TemperatureTolerates relatively cooler temperaturesPrefers warmer temperatures
Price and AvailabilityCheaper and more availableUsually more expensive

The quickest visual check: look at the red stripe. If it reaches the head, it's a Cardinal. For color care and reasons for Neon tetra deaths, refer to the Neon Tetra Care Guide. Cardinals are often mentioned alongside Discus fish as both prefer warmer water.

Not All Tetras Are Peaceful

This is the point that breaks many aquariums. The name "Tetra" does not automatically mean peaceful. Some species are known for fin nipping, especially when kept in small numbers. The fish that pays the price is the one with long fins—Betta and Angelfish.

  • Numbers change behavior. A fin-nipping species in small numbers will direct its activity towards its tank mates; with a sufficient school, it will direct it towards its own kind. The same logic applies to Aggression and Chasing in the Tank.
  • Size at maturity, not at purchase. Adult Angelfish will eat adult Neon tetras—this is not a temperament mismatch, it's a size difference.
  • Long fins attract nipping. Before mixing, consult the Compatibility Guide and Betta Tank Mates.

Water Parameters Matter More Than Preference

Most of these species adapt to a reasonable range of hardness, but stability is more important than the ideal number. Stable hard water is better than fluctuating soft water. Know your water hardness first from the GH and KH Water Hardness Guide, and stabilize readings with a Water Test Kit.

In the hot Iraqi summer, high temperatures are the biggest challenge, not hardness—refer to Protecting Fish in the 50-Degree Iraqi Summer.

And If You Want a Larger School: Rainbowfish

The three families above are all small. But a larger tank can look empty with them, which is where Rainbowfish come in—also schooling, but larger and with a different visual presence.

  • Don't judge them by the store tank. This is the most important practical point: juvenile Rainbowfish look dull and gray, and their true colors only emerge with maturity and in a stable tank. Many overlook them in stores for this reason alone.
  • They need swimming length. They are active fish that constantly traverse the tank, so length is more important than height.
  • Truly schooling. One or two individuals result in a stressed, dull fish—the same logic as Schooling Fish.
  • Males compete display-style, usually harmlessly, and the presence of enough females distributes this activity.

Their larger size means a greater biological load per individual, so calculate accordingly in How Many Fish Can Your Tank Hold, not based on them being "small schooling fish.".

The Correct Purchase Order

  1. Cycle the tank first. Small schools are the first victims of an immature tank—see the Biological Cycle.
  2. Calculate the load before the number. A school of eight has a biological cost—refer to How Many Fish Can Your Tank Hold.
  3. Buy the school all at once if possible, so the group bonds rather than forming a hierarchy over time.
  4. Acclimate slowly—see Acclimating New Fish—and do not skip Quarantine, as small schooling fish usually arrive stressed from transport.

For beginners wanting a less risky start, Danios are among the hardiest options within the Fish That Don't Die Easily. If the goal is a peaceful bottom tank alongside the school, Corydoras are the traditional companions.

data.title: Raising Guppy Fish: The Comprehensive Guide to Care and Breeding
data.excerpt: A breeder's guide to colorful Guppy fish: from proper feeding to breeding and protecting fry.
data.content:
Summary (Guppy Care and Breeding):

Guppy fish are the number one choice for beginners for two reasons: their high tolerance for water conditions and their rapid (livebearing) reproduction without complexity. Guppies need a temperature of 24-28 °C, and it is preferable to place one male for every 3 females in the aquarium to reduce stress. To prevent the parents from eating the fry after birth, a "net breeder box" should be used, or plenty of dense plants should be added for the small fish to hide in.

Why is the Guppy a Favorite in Iraqi Homes?

Guppies are distinguished by the very bright colors of their males, which resemble a dancer's dress. They are surface-dwelling and very active fish, and they get along excellently with small, peaceful fish (Community Fishes) like Neon Tetras and Corydoras.

How Do I Know if a Female Guppy is Pregnant?

The female's belly is noticeably rounded, and a large black spot (Gravid Spot) forms on her lower abdomen near the anal fin. As birth approaches, her belly shape becomes more square-like.

Tips for Guppy Diet

Their mouths are oriented upwards to catch food from the surface. The best option for them is high-quality flakes from trusted brands. It is preferable to gently break them with your fingertips before dropping them in to make them easier to chew, given the small size of the fish.

data.title: How to Choose a Suitable Aquarium for Your Home in Baghdad or the Provinces?
data.excerpt: A step-by-step beginner's guide to buying the ideal aquarium (capacity, type, and glass) and setting it up at home.
data.content:
Summary (Choosing the Ideal Aquarium):

The best aquarium for beginners is one with a capacity between 40 to 80 liters (approximately 60 cm in length). Contrary to popular belief, the larger the aquarium, the easier it is to maintain, as a larger water volume resists sudden temperature changes and toxins, which is crucial, especially with power outages in Iraq.

Why Are Small Aquariums and Glass Bowls a Trap?

Many people in Iraq start by buying a small round bowl and putting a goldfish in it. This leads to the fish dying within days! Small aquariums (under 20 liters) get dirty very quickly and do not have enough space to establish the necessary biological cycle.

Factors for Choosing the Right Aquarium

  • Glass Thickness: Ensure the glass is at least 5 mm thick for medium-sized aquariums to avoid breakage and leaks.
  • Lid: Slows down water evaporation, stabilizing the aquarium's water level and reducing the need for frequent top-offs. This is more important than it seems: only water evaporates, leaving salts and minerals behind, so each uncompensated evaporation gradually increases their concentration. The lid also prevents fish from jumping out of the aquarium.
  • Location in the Home: Keep the aquarium away from direct sunlight (which causes green algae growth) and from cooling vents and air conditioners (which cause sharp fluctuations in water temperature).

When choosing a ready-made aquarium, inspect the quality of the sealant at the corners and ensure it has a level bottom frame, as these are the most common points where leaks begin.

Before deciding on the size, decide on the type: Freshwater vs. Saltwater completely changes the cost and equipment. For budget considerations, check Ornamental Fish Prices, and for choosing where to buy, see The Stores Guide.

data.title: Aquarium Salt: A Medication with Dosage and Duration, Not a Daily Supplement
data.excerpt: Freshwater fish do not need routine salt. The mistake that raises concentration without you realizing, and why disagreements among sources about scaleless fish do not prevent a practical conclusion.
data.content:
Salt is a Medication, Not a Daily Supplement

It is common among hobbyists to believe that adding salt to a freshwater aquarium "strengthens" fish and prevents diseases. This is not true as a general rule: freshwater fish do not need salt routinely, and their natural environment is freshwater.

Salt is a therapeutic tool for specific conditions and for a limited duration. The difference between a "medication" and a "supplement" is not just semantics — medication has a dosage, duration, and reason, while a supplement is added without thought. Treating it as a supplement is the source of most harm.

The Deadly Mistake: Salt Does Not Evaporate

Water evaporates, but salt remains. If you replace evaporated water with fresh water, the concentration stays the same — but if you "replenish" salt with every top-off, you are raising the concentration each time without realizing it, until it reaches a harmful level.

The rule: Salt only leaves the aquarium through water changes. Add salt only to the amount of new water being replaced, not to the entire tank again. In the Iraqi summer, where evaporation is high, this mistake accumulates much faster.

A Controversial Point Presented As Is

It is often said that scaleless fish — such as catfish, corydoras, and loaches — cannot tolerate salt at all. The truth is that sources do indeed differ:

StanceArgument
Against UseSpecialists consider it a medication not to be used with scaleless fish, pointing to osmotic imbalance.
With Cautious UseLong-experienced breeders consider the generalization exaggerated, and a study on corydoras recorded the survival of the entire group at a low concentration.

We will not settle an unsettled dispute. However, the practical conclusion does not require a definitive answer: with scaleless species specifically, caution is the reasonable approach — a lower dose, shorter duration, and close monitoring, or avoiding it altogether if an alternative exists.

What Salt Does Not Do

  • It does not cure everything. It is used for specific conditions and is not a universal cure for any symptom.
  • It is not our standard treatment for white spot. The protocol we stand behind — gradually raising the temperature with a dedicated medication and strong aeration — is detailed in White Spot. We do not publish a therapeutic salt dosage because dosages vary between sources and species.
  • It is not suitable for planted aquariums. Plants are generally sensitive to salt at therapeutic concentrations.
  • It does not compensate for water quality. If ammonia is high, the problem is the water, not a disease — read the test kit guide first.

If You Decide to Use It

  1. For a specific reason and limited duration, not permanently.
  2. In a separate tank if possible — treat one fish instead of exposing the entire aquarium. A quarantine tank is perfect for this: Quarantine New Fish.
  3. Dissolve it in water before adding, and do not pour it directly on fish or substrate.
  4. Add it gradually, not all at once.
  5. Remove it with water changes after the period ends, do not wait for it to dissipate.

Note: AQUAVO does not sell aquarium salt; this article is purely educational and does not direct you to purchase anything.

data.title: Driftwood in the Aquarium: How to Boil and Treat Yellowing Water
data.excerpt: Driftwood adds natural beauty but yellows the water! Learn how to treat it by boiling and soaking before adding it to your tank.
data.content:
Introduction to Driftwood in the Aquarium

Driftwood is a popular aesthetic element in aquariums, adding a touch of nature and beauty to the aquatic environment. However, driftwood can cause problems in the tank, such as yellowing water, if not properly treated. In this article, we will discuss how to boil driftwood and treat yellowing water, focusing on the specific conditions in Iraq.

Why Should Driftwood Be Boiled?

Driftwood should be boiled for several reasons:

  • Killing germs and bacteria: Driftwood can harbor germs and bacteria, which can cause diseases in fish.
  • Removing chemicals: Driftwood may contain chemicals such as lead and arsenic, which can harm fish.
  • Preventing yellowing water: Driftwood can cause yellowing water if not properly treated.

How to Boil Driftwood

The ideal method for boiling driftwood is to immerse it in boiling water at 100 °C for 2-3 hours. This can be done using a large pot or a kettle. After boiling, the driftwood should be left to dry completely before being added to the aquarium.

A Golden Tip from AQUAVO

A golden tip from AQUAVO: Always use driftwood from reliable sources, and always boil it before adding it to your aquarium.

Treating Yellowing Water

Yellowing water is a common problem in aquariums and can be caused by driftwood if it is not properly treated. Yellowing water can be treated with activated carbon along with periodic water changes. However, it is important to use these chemicals with caution, as they can harm fish if used in large quantities.

Specific Conditions in Iraq

In Iraq, summer temperatures can reach 50 °C, which can increase the risk of yellowing water. Additionally, tap water in Iraq may be mixed with chlorine, which can harm fish. AQUAVO store can provide solutions to these problems, such as our water purification products and ensuring the quality of the products we offer.

Conclusion

Driftwood can be a wonderful aesthetic element in aquariums, but it can cause problems if not properly treated. By boiling driftwood and treating yellowing water, you can create a healthy and beautiful aquatic environment for your fish.

data.title: Discus Fish: The Queen of Freshwater Aquariums and How to Care for Her
data.excerpt: Beautiful and intimidating to care for! Get to know the most challenging and stunning ornamental fish, known as the water butterfly.
data.content:
Discus: The Queen of Aquariums and the Most Beautiful Freshwater Fish

Their stunning disc shape and incredible colors have earned them the nickname "Queen of Aquariums." However, caring for Discus is not for beginners — it requires patience and knowledge. Are you ready?

What Makes Discus Special

  • Fabulous Colors: Red, blue, orange, pearl, and dozens of color mutations.
  • Calm and Regal Behavior: They swim slowly and gracefully like water butterflies.
  • Social Fish: They must be kept in a group (5+ fish) to feel secure.
  • Recognize Their Owner: They come to the glass when they see you and eat from your hand.

Basic Care Requirements

  • Aquarium: 250 L minimum for a small group (5 fish).
  • Temperature: 28-30°C (higher than most tropical fish!).
  • pH: 6.0-6.5 (slightly acidic — soft water).
  • Water Changes: 30-50% every two weeks (very important).
  • Food: Bloodworms + specialized Discus pellets + minced turkey heart.

Common Mistakes with Discus

  1. Keeping them in cold water (below 27°C) — they get sick immediately.
  2. Keeping a single fish — it becomes stressed and refuses to eat.
  3. Mixing them with aggressive or fast fish that steal their food.
  4. Not paying attention to water quality — Discus are very sensitive to nitrates.

Compatible Fish for Discus

Neon Tetra, Cardinal Tetra, Rummy Nose Tetra, Sterbai Corydoras, and Amano Shrimp. They all prefer the same temperature and pH and live peacefully with Discus.

AQUAVO Tip: If you are a beginner, start with easier fish for a year, then move on to Discus. You'll thank us later!

data.title: Aquatic Plant Fertilization: When They Need It and When They Don't
data.excerpt: Algae benefit from excess nutrients, so balance is the goal, not the maximum. Where do plants get their food from, and why plants attached to wood don't benefit from substrate fertilizer.
data.content:
Plants Eat, and Water Alone Isn't Enough

An aquatic plant needs three things combined: lighting, nutrients, and carbon dioxide. A deficiency in any one of these will halt the utilization of the other two — this explains why increasing only the lighting doesn't grow plants, but rather grows algae.

The most important rule on this topic: Algae benefit from excess nutrients. Lighting stronger than the plant's consumption capacity, or more nutrients than it needs, goes to the algae. Balance is the goal, not the maximum. Algae Guide.

Where Plants Get Their Food From

SourceFeedsNote
Fish wastePrimarily nitrates and phosphatesSufficient on its own for many low-demand aquariums
Nutrient-rich substrate / root tabsRooted plantsPlaced under the substrate during setup
Liquid fertilizerPlants that absorb through leavesFor Anubias and Java Fern attached to wood
Root tabsHeavy-feeding plantsPlaced directly near the roots

An important practical note: Plants attached to wood and rocks — Anubias and Java Fern — absorb from the water column, not the substrate. Applying substrate fertilizer to them is not very effective.

Do You Even Need Fertilizer?

Not always, and here's an honest answer, not a dodge:

  • An aquarium with fish, moderate lighting, and low-demand plants: Fish waste is often sufficient. Start without fertilizer.
  • An aquarium with strong lighting or fast-growing plants: Consumption exceeds what the fish produce, so fertilizer becomes necessary.
  • An aquarium with almost no fish: No natural nutrient source — it will require fertilization.

AQUAVO offers a root fertilizer for planted tank substrates, a precision dosing syringe, and aquascape substrate, all within the substrate and decor section.

The Golden Rule: Reduce, Don't Increase

  1. Start with less than the recommended dose on the packaging, and observe for two weeks.
  2. Change only one thing at a time. If you increase fertilizer and lighting together and then algae appear, you won't know the cause.
  3. Lighting first. Set the lighting duration to 6–8 hours before touching any fertilizer — Lighting Guide.
  4. Regular water changes reset the balance. Excess is removed and buildup is prevented — Water Change.

Caution: Fertilizer and Invertebrates

Some liquid fertilizers contain copper among the trace elements, and copper is toxic to shrimp and snails at concentrations that do not harm fish. If your aquarium contains invertebrates, read the ingredients before purchasing and choose one that is stated to be safe for them. Details in Shrimp and Snails.

And If Plant Symptoms Appear

Yellowing, holes, and melting are not always a fertilizer deficiency — it could be an adaptation phase or a lighting problem. Diagnose it before adding anything: Aquatic Plant Problems. And choosing the right species from the start reduces the need for fertilization: Best Low-Tech Aquarium Plants for Beginners.

data.title: The Difference Between a Sump and an External Filter for Large Aquariums
data.excerpt: Your aquarium is large and you're undecided between a sump and an external filter? A detailed comparison of pros and cons to choose the most suitable for your tank size.
data.content:
Introduction

In the world of aquariums, sumps and external filters are among the most important components that ensure the health and well-being of fish. However, there is a significant difference between these two components, which depends on how each one works and its purpose. In this article, we will provide you with a comprehensive overview of the difference between sumps and external filters in large aquariums, and discuss how to choose the best for your needs.

What is a Sump?

A sump is a water filtration system used to improve water quality in large aquariums. A sump works by removing impurities and waste from the water, which helps maintain fish health and the diversity of the aquatic environment. A sump is usually installed below the aquarium and connected to it via pipes to achieve continuous water circulation.

Benefits of a Sump

  • Improves water quality in large aquariums
  • Removes impurities and waste from the water
  • Helps maintain fish health and the diversity of the aquatic environment

What is an External Filter?

An external filter is a device used to purify water and improve environmental conditions in aquariums. An external filter works by removing impurities and waste from the water, in addition to adding chemicals that help improve water quality.

Benefits of an External Filter

  • Purifies water and improves environmental conditions
  • Removes impurities and waste from the water
  • Works to add chemicals that help improve water quality

The Difference Between a Sump and an External Filter

The main difference between a sump and an external filter is that a sump is used to improve water quality in large aquariums, while an external filter is used to purify water and improve environmental conditions. Additionally, a sump is installed below the aquarium, while an external filter can be installed anywhere in the tank.

Golden tip from AQUAVO: When choosing a sump or an external filter, you must consider the size of the aquarium and the number of fish in it. You should also choose a device that suits your needs and works effectively under the environmental conditions in Iraq, such as extreme heat and water pollution.

Using Sumps and External Filters in Iraq

In Iraq, the use of sumps and external filters is essential to ensure the health and well-being of fish. Due to the extreme heat in the summer, which can reach 50 °C, you must consider using a device capable of withstanding these conditions.

Tips for Use in Iraq

  1. Choose a device that suits your needs and works effectively under the environmental conditions in Iraq
  2. Ensure that the device can withstand the extreme heat in the summer
  3. Choose a device capable of effectively removing impurities and waste from the water

In conclusion to this article, we hope to provide you with a comprehensive overview of the difference between sumps and external filters in large aquariums. We also hope to help you choose the best for your needs. data.title: Fish Symptom Diagnosis Guide: Start with Water, Not Medication
data.excerpt: Most sudden illnesses in beginners are not diseases but water poisoning that presents the same symptoms. A table of symptom → most likely cause → first step, and when a situation is an emergency.
data.content:
Start with Water, Not Medication

Most sudden "illnesses" in beginner aquariums are not diseases. Water poisoning presents symptoms that are exactly like a disease, but medication will not help – it only adds stress to an already poisoned fish.

The rule before any diagnosis: test for ammonia and nitrite first. If either is above zero, that is your problem until proven otherwise, no matter how similar the symptoms appear to a disease. Reading water tests.

Table: Symptom → First Possibility

What you seeMost Likely CauseFirst Step
Gasping at the surface, rapid breathing, clear waterLow oxygen or high nitriteIncrease aeration immediately, then test
White spots like salt grainsWhite spot diseaseGradual temperature increase + specific medication
Torn fins or white edgesFin rot, often after stress or poor water qualityImprove water quality before any medication
Rubbing body on gravel and decorEarly parasite or chemical irritationTest water, and watch for spots
Red gills or bodyAmmonia burns or untreated chlorineTest, and check water treatment
Lethargy at the bottom and clamped finsGeneral stress: temperature, water, or bullying from tank matesReview temperature, test results, and compatibility
Floating upside down or difficulty balancingDigestive/bloating issue, common in round-bodied fishTwo-day fast and reduce floating food
Refusing food with no other symptomsWater or temperature issue, or a new fish that hasn't acclimatedTest water, and allow time

Three Common Diagnostic Mistakes

  • Treating the symptom instead of the cause. Fin rot is often a result of poor water quality; medication treats the infection, but the problem returns because the cause remains. Details in Fin Rot Treatment Guide.
  • Confusing suffocation with disease. Gasping at the surface in clear water is usually due to low oxygen or nitrite, not parasites. Dissolved Oxygen and Aeration.
  • Preventive medication. Giving medication without a diagnosis stresses the fish and harms beneficial bacteria in the filter.

When It's an Emergency

Act immediately, then test, if you see:

  • More than one fish gasping at the surface at the same time.
  • Sudden death of more than one fish within hours.
  • Ammonia or nitrite above zero on any reading.

The first action in these cases is the same: increase aeration and change a portion of the water with treated water of the same temperature, then diagnose. The full protocol is in Emergency Treatment for Sudden Ammonia Spikes.

Prevention That Eliminates the Need for Diagnosis

  • Quarantine for every new fish – most diseases enter the aquarium this way. Quarantine.
  • Stable temperature – fluctuations weaken immunity more than any specific number.
  • Regular water changes instead of waiting for a problem. Water Changes.
  • Stocking density within the aquarium's capacity – overcrowding causes chronic stress. How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Hold.
  • Do not use human medications or guess dosages. Dangers of Human Medicine for Fish.

Honest note: this table ranks possibilities, it does not provide a definitive diagnosis. Many symptoms share common causes, which is why testing is the deciding factor, not just visual appearance.

And the Eyes? A Question That Precedes the Table

The table above does not cover the eyes, which are among the fastest things an aquarist notices because they are visible. The first question is not "what is the disease?" but: one eye or two?

  • One – suggests a localized cause: rubbing against decor, a bite, or injury after transport.
  • Two – suggests a more general cause affecting the whole fish, and the first thing to check is the water.

This is a suggestion, not a diagnosis, like the rest of the table – details in Fish Eye Problems.

data.title: The Correct Treatment: Quarantine Tank, Dosage, and Duration
data.excerpt: Most treatment failures are not due to the medication itself. Five common mistakes can undermine any correct treatment—the first being dosing based on the stated tank volume rather than the actual volume, and the last being activated carbon that removes the medication.
data.content:
Most Treatment Failures Are Not Due to the Medication

A tank where "all medications have been tried without success" has likely never had any of them administered correctly. The right medication with an estimated dose, or for half the required duration, or in a tank with active carbon that removes it, or for a fish whose real cause is ammonia poisoning, not a microbe—all these end with the same result and are perceived as medication failure.

Two rules before anything else. First: Start with water, not medication. Second: The product's instructions and a veterinarian's guidance take precedence over any general advice—including what is in this article; this is a framework, not a substitute for the instructions of the product you have. A significant percentage of what appears to be illness is ammonia or nitrite poisoning presenting with similar symptoms, and treating it with an antibiotic will only worsen it—see the symptoms diagnosis guide and reading test results.

The Treatment Tank: Why Separate

Treating the main aquarium is usually a bad option. A simple treatment tank is better for practical reasons:

IssueIn the Main TankIn a Treatment Tank
Medication AmountLarge volume = higher cost and greater errorSmall, calculated volume
Beneficial BacteriaMany medications harm themThe main filter remains safe
Shrimp and InvertebratesDamaged or killedCompletely outside the exposure
Fish ObservationDifficult amidst decorClear and direct
  • No substrate or porous decor. Gravel and wood absorb medication, making the concentration unknown. A bare bottom with a simple hiding place made of non-porous material.
  • An air-driven sponge filter, preferably one that has been run previously in the main tank to carry beneficial bacteria—see which filter suits your tank.
  • Heater and aeration. Many medications reduce dissolved oxygen, making aeration even more critical—see air pumps.
  • Same equipment, different purposes. A quarantine tank and a treatment tank have similar equipment but different functions: Quarantine is for observation of a new fish that appears healthy, for a set period and without presumptive medication; treatment is an intervention for a fish showing signs of illness. Preventive treatment for every new arrival is not quarantine—it is exposure without cause. Details in the quarantine guide.

The Five Mistakes That Undermine Any Medication

  1. Dosing based on the stated tank volume, not the actual volume. A "100 L" tank with substrate, decor, and water not filled to the brim holds significantly less water. Calculate the actual volume—see calculating tank capacity in liters. Insufficient dosage does not kill the pathogen and may train it; excessive dosage can kill the fish.
  2. Stopping treatment when symptoms disappear. The disappearance of visible signs does not mean the cycle is over. The clearest example is white spot disease, where the stage sensitive to medication is not the stage you see—see white spot disease. Complete the prescribed duration.
  3. Ignoring what the instructions say about activated carbon. Carbon absorbs dissolved substances from the water, and many medication instructions request its removal during treatment for this reason. However, this is not an absolute rule for every product—some do not require it. Read the instructions and follow them; do not assume. If removal is requested, replacing it after the treatment course is a common way to remove residues—see activated carbon.
  4. Mixing two medications without proven compatibility. Do not combine two products unless the instructions for one explicitly mention compatibility; the absence of a warning is not permission. Mixing can double the stress and may produce an unexpected effect from either product, and switching every two days means you haven't given either one a chance. Use one medication, complete the full course, then evaluate.
  5. Ignoring sensitive species. Scaleless fish and shrimp have different rules—see the loaches guide and shrimp and snails guide. Read the product instructions before any dosage.

During and After Treatment

  • Perform water changes before the next dose as per the instructions—this prevents uncalculated accumulation.
  • Monitor breathing. Sudden gasping after a dose is a sign of stress or oxygen deficiency, not improvement.
  • Do not overfeed—a sick fish eats less, and excess food spoils the water in a small tank quickly.
  • After completion: use activated carbon to remove residues, then perform a water change, then gently return the fish to the main aquarium—see acclimation.
We will not publish dosages or compound names: availability, formulation, and concentration vary between markets and products, and publishing a single number that works for one product but not another is harmful rather than helpful. The instructions accompanying the product are the reference, and if a veterinarian specializing in fish is available, they are the correct authority. Never use human medications—see dangers of human medications for fish.

For specific conditions: external parasites, internal parasites, fungal infections, fin rot.

Water Changes During the Treatment Cycle

A recurring question: Should I change the water while treating? The answer depends on the instructions, but the general rules are clear:

  • The instructions are paramount. Many products specify a certain percentage of water change before each subsequent dose; follow what they say, not what you are accustomed to.
  • Water changes remove part of the medication—which is why recalculation is needed afterward if the instructions require it. Do not add a full dose to water that has not been fully changed.
  • Do not stop water changes for fear of diluting the medication. A sick fish in deteriorating water will not improve, no matter how correct the treatment is.
  • After the cycle is complete: perform a water change, then use activated carbon to remove residues if the instructions requested its removal during treatment.

The water change method itself is detailed in the aquarium water change guide.

data.title: Where to Place Your Aquarium and What to Consider: Weight, Leveling, and Safety
data.excerpt: Water alone weighs one kilogram per liter. A single grain of gravel under the base is enough to create a pressure point that can crack glass, and a full aquarium should never be moved.
data.content:
An Aquarium is Much Heavier Than It Looks

This is a point often overlooked until damage occurs. Water alone weighs approximately one kilogram per liter, to which the weight of the glass, substrate, and rocks is added. This means a medium-sized aquarium, once filled, becomes a static load of tens of kilograms concentrated on a small area.

ComponentWeight Contribution
WaterLargest — approximately one kilogram per liter
GlassIncreases rapidly with size and thickness
Substrate and RocksHeavier than water for the same volume
First, calculate your aquarium's actual capacity — Calculate Capacity in Liters — then estimate the total weight before deciding on a location or stand. A table that holds a television does not necessarily mean it can support an aquarium.

Leveling is Not Just an Aesthetic Detail

A glass aquarium distributes pressure along its edges. If the surface is uneven, or if there is a grain of gravel or a protrusion under the aquarium's base, the pressure concentrates at a single point instead of spreading out — this is the most common reason for aquariums cracking without an apparent cause.

  1. Check for levelness with a water level in both directions before filling, not after.
  2. Ensure a perfectly clean surface under the base — a single grain of sand can become a pressure point.
  3. Never move a filled aquarium, not even partially. The weight warps and stresses the frame beyond its design limits. Empty completely before any move — Transporting Fish and Aquariums.
  4. Pay attention to the type of flooring. Soft or unstable surfaces can shift under a constant load over time.
And the limits of what we can say: estimating the aquarium's weight is a simple calculation, but can this specific location bear this load is an open question that depends on the building itself — the type of ceiling, floor, and the location within the room. We cannot answer it from here, and one should not assume safety just because the floor looks solid. For large aquariums, or placement on an upper floor or wooden floor, the right person to consult is a building contractor who can inspect the site.

Where to Place It: Four Considerations

  • Away from direct sunlight. Sunlight raises the temperature and fuels algae growth uncontrollably — and in the Iraqi summer, the heat alone is enough to be dangerous. Details in the Lighting Guide and Summer Heat Protection.
  • Away from vibrations and impacts. A wall with a door that slams shut, or a surface near a source of vibration, keeps fish in a constant state of alertness. And tapping on the glass is not a harmless game.
  • Away from the kitchen and aerosol sprays. Cooking fumes, insect sprays, and air fresheners enter the water through the surface — Airborne Toxins.
  • Near electricity and a drain. Weekly water changes become a burden if the aquarium is far from a water source, and a burden leads to postponing changes — Water Change Guide.

Electricity and Water in the Same Place

An aquarium is an electrical appliance that runs non-stop next to tens of liters of water. Safety rules here are not optional, the most important being the drip loop: ensure the cord of each device drops to a point lower than the outlet before rising to it, so any water running down the cord drips off at that point instead of reaching the electricity.

Full details in Electrical Safety Around the Aquarium, and an outage plan in Emergency Aquarium Tools.

Before You Fill It

One sequence saves you many problems: choose the location, secure the stand and ensure it is level, place the empty aquarium, check the levelness again, then begin filling. Any adjustment after filling requires complete emptying.

This stage precedes everything else in Setting Up Your First Aquarium, and influences the choice of size from the beginning — How to Choose an Aquarium Tank.

Signs of Early Leaks

Aquariums rarely explode suddenly; they usually give signals first. What to watch for:

  • Moisture or white salt-like residue on the edge of the base or the table underneath.
  • Bubbles or separation within the silicone seal at the corners — the seal should be continuous and fully attached.
  • A drop in water level faster than normal evaporation, especially if the aquarium is covered.
  • Any crack in the glass, no matter how superficial — do not ignore it or wait.

The decorative top silicone is different from the structural silicone between the panels; repairing the latter is a delicate job requiring complete emptying, drying, and full removal of the old sealant, and many prefer replacement. If you notice any of these signs, empty the aquarium before moving it — Transporting Fish and Aquariums — and do not move it while it contains water.

data.title: Sudden Ammonia Spike: Do This Now, In This Order
data.excerpt: Ten articles on this site link here in emergencies. These six steps are prioritized—and why cleaning the filter now turns a problem into a disaster.
data.content:
Do This Now, Then Read the Rest

If your ammonia reading is above zero and fish are gasping or lethargic, start with these steps in this order. The order is intentional.

#ActionWhy This Order
1Stop Feeding CompletelyFastest and cheapest action: stops new ammonia production immediately
2Increase AerationAmmonia burns gills, and a stressed fish needs more oxygen, not less
3Perform a Partial Water Change with treated water of the same temperatureDilution is the only quick way to actually lower the concentration
4Add a Water Conditioner that Binds AmmoniaTemporarily converts it to a less harmful form until the bacteria catch up
5Find the CauseWithout this, it will return within days
6Retest After a Few HoursOne reading is a snapshot; two readings show a trend
Do not clean the filter, do not change its media, and do not rinse it in tap water—not today, and not this week. The bacteria that process ammonia live there, and cleaning the filter during an ammonia crisis turns a problem into a disaster.

Why the Number Alone Isn't Enough

Ammonia exists in two forms, and the ratio between them is determined by temperature and pH. The toxic form increases in proportion as either rises. Therefore:

  • The same ammonia reading is much more dangerous in a warm, alkaline tank than in a cool, acidic one.
  • And in Iraq's summer, both factors combine: high temperature and lower oxygen—the fish take a double hit. Summer Heat.

Do not attempt to lower the pH to reduce toxicity; pH fluctuations are an additional stress on an already compromised fish. The full table of the relationship is in the Biological Cycle.

Where Did It Come From? Look Here

An ammonia spike is the result of a cause. Review what has changed in the past few days:

  • Overfeeding—the number one cause by a wide margin. Feeding Guide.
  • A dead fish hidden behind decor or under the substrate—search thoroughly and count your fish.
  • Rinsing the filter in tap water or replacing all the media. Treating Tap Water for Fish.
  • A prolonged power outage that stopped water flow over the bacteria. Emergency Tools.
  • New fish that suddenly increased the bioload. How Many Fish Can Your Tank Handle.
  • Medication that harmed the beneficial bacteria.
  • A new tank that hasn't completed its cycle—this is not a crisis but a normal stage.

A New Tank: The Different Situation

If your tank is cycling, an ammonia spike is expected, and the goal is different: keep the concentration low enough for fish safety without halting colony establishment. Smaller, more frequent water changes and patience. Large, frequent changes slow down cycling.

And if the tank is fishless, there's no need to intervene—let it complete.

Signs of Fish Poisoning

  • Gasping at the surface and rapid breathing.
  • Red gills or bloody streaks on fins.
  • Lethargy, staying at the bottom, refusing food.
  • Rubbing the body against surfaces.

Note: High nitrite presents nearly identical symptoms; the difference is revealed by testing, not observation. Refer to the Symptom Diagnosis Guide and Reading Water Tests. AQUAVO offers test strips and liquid test kits for ammonia and nitrite, and water conditioners, in the Testing & Monitoring and Water Treatment sections.

After the Crisis Ends

Do not immediately return to the old routine. Reintroduce food gradually, test daily for a few days, and review the root cause—the water change schedule, the number of fish, or the amount of food. A recurring crisis is not an accident but an unbalanced system.

Chronic ammonia poisoning precedes many symptoms that are misdiagnosed as independent diseases—including bloating and buoyancy problems, detailed in Bloated or Floating Fish. Most of these spikes are due to the same recurring mistakes in Beginner Mistakes.

data.title: Distinguishing Male from Female: Reliable Signs and Knowledge Limits
data.excerpt: Incorrect sex ratios lead to constant chasing and unplanned breeding. Signs vary by species, and situations where visual determination is impossible.
data.content:
Why Knowing Male from Female Matters

The question might seem like mere curiosity, but it's entirely practical — incorrect sex ratios cause real problems:

  • Constant Chasing. In livebearers like guppies and mollies, males chase females relentlessly. One male with one female means an exhausted female.
  • Unplanned Breeding. Livebearers give birth to live fry without any intervention from you, leading to a sudden increase in bioload.
  • Aggression Between Males in territorial species.
The practical rule for livebearers: two or three females per male. This distributes the chasing instead of concentrating it on one female.

Signs by Species

SpeciesMaleFemale
GuppySmaller, bright colors, large tail fin, and pointed anal finLarger, duller, full belly, fan-shaped anal fin
Molly and PlatyPointed, stick-like anal finBroad, triangular anal fin
BettaLong fins, stronger colors, builds bubble nestsShorter fins, and often a vertical line when ready to breed
CorydorasThinner and smallerClearly wider from above, especially when carrying eggs
GoldfishSmall white spots on gills and fins during breeding seasonMore rounded from the side

The clearest and easiest sign in livebearers is the shape of the anal fin — the fin under the belly. A pointed, stick-like fin means male, and a broad, fan-shaped fin means female. This is more reliable than color or size.

When You Can't Be Sure — And That's Normal

We won't give you a definitive method for every species because it doesn't exist:

  • Fry do not show differences before maturity, and most fish sold are juveniles.
  • Many species — most tetras, rasboras, and danios — have very subtle and unreliable visual differences.
  • Hybrid strains have altered colors and fins, obscuring traditional markers.

If a species cannot be visually distinguished, the practical solution is simple: buy a group and deal with the outcome. This also aligns with the needs of schooling fish for adequate numbers — Schooling Fish and Their Minimum Numbers.

If Fry Are Born Unplanned

Livebearers breed in a regular aquarium without any preparation. Usually, most fry are eaten, which is a natural balance that doesn't require intervention. But if you want to save them:

  • Dense hiding places — plants or moss at the surface are enough for some to survive.
  • Breeder box or hatchery for the female near birth, and return her to the tank immediately afterward, as confinement is stressful. Breeder boxes and hatcheries are available at AQUAVO in the Isolation and Breeding section.
  • Monitor the bioload — fry grow. Twenty fry today means a crowded tank in a few months. How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Support.
  • Food for fry appropriately sized for their mouths, available in the Fish Food section.

And remember that any increase in numbers raises ammonia before the bacteria can catch up — The Biological Cycle.
