data.title: The Impact of Placing an Aquarium in Bedrooms (Feng Shui and Sound Effects)
data.excerpt: Is it healthy to place an aquarium in the bedroom? Learn about its effect on sleep and Feng Shui, and when it is suitable and when it is not.
data.content:
Introduction

Today, we will discuss an important topic related to installing an aquarium in homes, especially in bedrooms. This topic concerns all fish enthusiasts in Iraq, as an aquarium can add an aesthetic touch and tranquility to the room. However, there are some points we must consider when choosing a location for the aquarium.

The Impact of an Aquarium's Placement on Sleep

Sleep is an essential part of our daily lives, and placing an aquarium in bedrooms can affect sleep quality. Some studies have shown that placing an aquarium in bedrooms can:

  • Reduce stress and anxiety levels
  • Increase relaxation and psychological comfort
  • Help improve sleep quality

However, we must consider that placing an aquarium in bedrooms may lead to some problems, such as:

  • Noise disturbance
  • Temperature fluctuations
  • Excessive humidity

The Impact of Sound on Sleep

Sound is one of the factors that can affect sleep quality. The sound of fish and the filter can be annoying if an appropriate location for the aquarium is not chosen. In Iraq, where temperatures can reach 50 °C in the summer, the filter's sound may become louder due to increased water circulation speed.

Therefore, we must choose a suitable location for the aquarium so that its sound does not disturb sleep. We can achieve this by:

  1. Placing the aquarium in a corner of the room
  2. Using a silent filter
  3. Providing sufficient distance between the aquarium and the bed

A Golden Tip from AQUAVO

A golden tip from AQUAVO: When choosing an aquarium, we must consider the room size and sleep pattern. We can choose a small aquarium and a silent filter to avoid disturbance.

Using an Aquarium in Bedrooms in Iraq

In Iraq, placing an aquarium in bedrooms can be challenging due to the difficult conditions. Temperatures can reach 50 °C in the summer, which may lead to increased water circulation speed and a louder filter sound.

Therefore, we must choose an aquarium suitable for Iraqi conditions. We can do this by:

  • Choosing a sealed aquarium
  • Using a high-efficiency filter
  • Providing a backup power source to handle power outages

At AQUAVO, we offer a wide range of high-quality aquariums and water filters that can meet your needs in Iraq. We also have delivery service to 18 governorates in Iraq.

Conclusion

Placing an aquarium in bedrooms can have a positive impact on sleep and psychological comfort, but we must consider some points when choosing a location for the aquarium. In Iraq, placing an aquarium in bedrooms can be challenging due to the difficult conditions, but we can achieve this by choosing a suitable aquarium and a silent filter.

data.title: Your Readings Are High: Adjust the Water or Choose Fish That Suit It?
data.excerpt: Stable water that isn't ideal is better than fluctuating ideal water. When is choosing smarter than adjusting, and when does mixing demineralized water actually make sense.
data.content:
The Decision That Precedes Any Adjustment

You tested your water and the readings are high — high pH, or high GH and KH. The natural question is: How do I lower them? But the correct question precedes it: Do you actually need to lower them?

And before anything else, know your actual numbers instead of assuming them. Tap water varies from region to region and season to season, and it's incorrect to assume a number for any city or country. Testing with strips or a test kit is the only valid source — reading the test and explaining the numbers themselves in the GH, KH, and TDS Guide.

The practical answer for most situations: Stable water that isn't ideal is better than fluctuating ideal water. Fish adapt to a wide range of hardness and acidity, but they do not adapt to constant change. Chasing an "ideal" number results in fluctuation, and fluctuation is what kills.

Your Path Based on Your Readings

Your SituationMost Suitable Option
High and stable readings, and you are still choosing your fishChoose species that suit this water — the easiest and most successful
High readings and you have adapted, healthy fishDon't change anything — stable fish don't need saving
You want a species that specifically requires soft water (e.g., for breeding)A calculated adjustment by mixing demineralized water — not with quick chemical additives
The readings are already fluctuatingAddress the cause of the fluctuation first before any adjustment

Why Choosing is Better Than Adjusting

  • Adjustment is a permanent commitment. Every water change resets the tank to the starting point, forcing you to repeat the treatment each time, with the same precision, forever. Any time you forget means a sudden jump.
  • Quick pH reducers cause swings. KH is what resists acidity changes, and attempting to lower pH with high KH water ends with the number bouncing back up and then dropping again — which is worse than a stable high reading.
  • Locally available fish are often adapted to the local water if they were bred locally, making them a better fit than you might expect.
  • Many species truly tolerate a wide range, not just by courtesy — see Fish That Don't Die Easily.

Species That Handle Harder Water Well

If your readings are high, these families are generally described as being comfortable in hard or medium-hard water:

  • Livebearers — Mollies, Platies, Guppies, and Swordtails, and among the most suitable for harder water — Livebearer Fish.
  • African Cichlids — Associated with harsh, alkaline lake environments — African Cichlid Species.
  • Danios and hardy schooling species — Choosing Small Schooling Fish.
  • Conversely, species like Discus and Cardinal Tetras prefer softer water, making them a more difficult choice for hard water.

Plants also vary: many low-maintenance species handle a wide range without issues — Best Low-Tech Aquarium Plants for Beginners.

When Mixing Demineralized Water Makes Sense

Mixing RO water with tap water is a true dilution method, but it suits specific situations, not general use:

  1. A specific goal — breeding a species that requires soft water, or a specific sensitive species. Not just "because the numbers are high."
  2. A consistent and measured ratio each time, because the goal is stability, not reaching a number.
  3. Remineralization when needed — RO water alone is poor in minerals and lacks the ability to resist acidity changes, which is a danger in itself.
  4. Ongoing cost and effort — The background on RO Water vs. Tap Water for Aquariums.
And the limits of what we can say: We do not publish mixing recipes or target numbers. The ratio depends on your water readings and the species you keep, and the correct number for one tank might be wrong for another. The only general rule: Change slowly, measure, and stabilize.

And If You Decide to Adjust Despite All This

  • Very slowly. Sudden changes in hardness or acidity are a shock — and worse than the number you're trying to escape.
  • Adjust in a bucket, not in the tank. Prepare the replacement water and measure it before adding it.
  • Monitor KH. Its collapse means losing the ability to resist acidity changes, which is the gateway to swings.
  • And watch out for wood and rocks. Some slowly raise hardness, and some lower acidity — Testing Aquarium Rocks and Wood and Driftwood Preparation.

And always start by treating tap water before any other calculation — How to Treat Tap Water for Fish in Iraq.

data.title: Acclimating New Fish: Why Opening the Bag Increases Risk
data.excerpt: The sealed bag protects the fish chemically. Opening it raises the pH, converting existing ammonia into its toxic form. Practical methods and the debate between drip acclimation and rapid transfer.
data.content:
The Unnoticed Danger: Opening the Bag Increases Ammonia Toxicity

This is the most crucial piece of information, contrary to what most people believe. A fish inside a sealed bag releases ammonia. Simultaneously, carbon dioxide accumulates in the bag, lowering the pH. A low pH converts ammonia into a much less toxic form.

This means the sealed bag was chemically protecting the fish. When you open it:

  • Carbon dioxide escapes into the air.
  • The pH begins to rise.
  • The same amount of ammonia present then gradually converts to its toxic form.
The practical result: Every extra minute the bag is open increases the toxicity of the ammonia within it. Slow drip acclimation for an hour inside the bag water could be worse than rapid transfer, especially if the fish spent a long time in the bag before reaching you. The mechanism of how pH affects ammonia is explained in the Biological Cycle.

The Practical Method

StepExecutionReason
1. Float the bag sealed15–20 minutesTemperature equalization, and the bag remains sealed, keeping the pH low
2. Open and transferUsing a net or cup, without the bag waterReduces exposure time after pH rise
3. Discard bag waterOutside the aquarium completelyCarries ammonia and possibly pathogens
4. Dim lightingFor hours after transferReduces stress during the initial hours
5. Do not feedFor the first 24 hoursStressed fish do not eat; uneaten food decomposes and pollutes

If the chemical difference is indeed significant—store water being completely different from your home water—then drip acclimation remains beneficial. However, do it after transferring the fish to a clean container without the bag water, not inside the bag itself.

A Point of Contention, Stated Clearly

There is a genuine disagreement among experts: some prefer slow drip acclimation to minimize chemical shock, while others—especially for fish shipped over long distances—prefer floating for temperature equalization followed by direct transfer to minimize ammonia exposure. We will not settle an unsettled debate, but the balance shifts based on your situation: The longer the fish spent in the bag before arrival, the greater the risk from ammonia exposure, making speed preferable.

Common Mistakes

  • Pouring the bag water into the aquarium. The most common and easiest mistake to avoid.
  • Drip acclimating for an hour or more inside the open bag—for the chemical reason stated above.
  • Introducing the fish directly into the main aquarium without quarantine. Details in the Quarantine Guide for New Fish.
  • Adding multiple fish at once—this suddenly increases the bioload before the bacteria can establish. See How Many Fish Your Aquarium Can Support.
  • Turning on bright lighting immediately after transfer.

After Transfer

Monitor for the first 48 hours: rapid breathing, staying at the bottom or surface, refusing food after the first day, or scratching the body on surfaces. Test for ammonia and nitrite after two days—any new fish adds to the bioload, and if readings rise, follow the procedure in Emergency Treatment for Ammonia Spikes. Test strips and ammonia test kits are available at AQUAVO under Testing and Monitoring.

data.title: Betta Fish: Can They Live in a Small Water Glass? (The Truth Revealed)
data.excerpt: The common myth we believed to be true for many years. Learn about the real needs of Thai fighting fish.
data.content:
Direct Summary for Anyone Keeping Betta Fish:

No, absolutely not! Confining betta fish to small glasses (or vases) is torture. Although they can breathe from the surface air, the fish quickly poisons itself with its own waste accumulating in the small water volume, becomes depressed, and withers. Every betta fish needs an aquarium of at least 10 liters (preferably 20 liters), equipped with a quiet sponge filter and a heater to set the temperature precisely at 26 °C.

The Secret Behind the "Mud Puddle" Myth

Some say: "In nature, these fish live in shallow, small mud puddles, so they don't need space!". This is a commercial lie. Betta fish live in mud puddles, but these extend for kilometers through rice fields in Asia, connected to each other. They suffer drought during difficult times, but not a 250 ml glass!

How to Create a Luxurious Home for Your Betta Fish!

  • Choose a soft substrate (sand or fine gravel) because their fins are delicate and silky.
  • Add soft live plants or dried Indian almond leaves (sold as Catappa leaves at AQUAVO) which release organic acidic compounds that kill microbes and give it the feel of its natural environment.
  • Provide a (small cave) for it to rest inside, as it is a fish that loves privacy.

Beyond these discussions lies a deeper question about the fish's perception itself — Can Fish See and Recognize Their Owners?. On the other hand, the aquarium also has an effect on its owner: Aquarium Keeping for Stress Relief and Mental Health and Aquarium in the Bedroom: Feng Shui and Sound Effects.

data.title: What Fish Are Compatible with Betta Fish?
data.excerpt: Can other fish be kept with Betta fish? Yes! But with conditions. Here is a list of compatible and incompatible fish with Betta fish.
data.content:
Introduction

If you are an ornamental fish enthusiast in Iraq, you have likely considered adding Betta fish to your aquarium. However, choosing suitable tank mates for Betta fish can be a challenge, especially given the hot environmental conditions in Iraq, where temperatures can reach 50 °C in the summer. In this article, we will provide you with the answer to this question, focusing on the needs and environmental requirements of Betta fish.

Betta Fish: Requirements and Nature

Betta fish are solitary fish that prefer to live alone in an aquarium. However, Betta fish can be kept with other fish, provided that suitable tank mates are chosen. You must consider the size, nature, and environmental requirements of Betta fish when selecting tank mates.

  • Size: Tank mates should be smaller than Betta fish to avoid detection and fighting.
  • Nature: Tank mates should be calm and passive to avoid disturbing or affecting the Betta fish.
  • Environmental Requirements: Tank mates must be able to adapt to the same environmental requirements as Betta fish, such as temperature and pH.

Best Tank Mates for Betta Fish

After considering the requirements and nature of Betta fish, we can recommend some fish that can be kept with Betta fish.

  1. Platy fish: These fish are small and peaceful, making them among the best tank mates for Betta fish.
  2. Neon Tetras: These fish are small and fast, making them among the best tank mates for Betta fish, provided a sufficiently large aquarium is available.
  3. Corydoras Catfish: These fish are peaceful and passive, making them among the best tank mates for Betta fish, provided a sufficiently large aquarium is available.

Golden Tip from AQUAVO

If you are looking for suitable tank mates for Betta fish, do not forget to consider the environmental conditions in Iraq, such as heat and humidity. Choose aquarium companions based on the size of the aquarium, the temperature, and the fish's temperament, not just what is available at the time of purchase.

Conclusion

Choosing tank mates for Betta fish is a decision that depends on the aquarium size, temperature, and the fish's temperament itself, not on what is available at the time of purchase. After any addition, monitor the aquarium for the first few days: frequent chasing or torn fins are an indication that the combination is not working, not that it needs more time. Be prepared to separate the fish if necessary — some individual Bettas will not accept company, no matter how successful the choice of tank mate, and this is an individual behavior that cannot be corrected by changing tank mates.

data.title: Building Professional 3D Backgrounds for Aquariums
data.excerpt: A 3D background transforms your aquarium into a work of art! A practical guide to building a professional 3D background with simple, readily available materials.
data.content:
Introduction to Building 3D Backgrounds

Building 3D backgrounds in an aquarium is an art that requires care and attention to detail, especially in a country like Iraq where temperatures can reach 50 °C in the summer, affecting life conditions inside the tank. Therefore, materials capable of withstanding these harsh conditions must be chosen. The only criteria that matter when selecting materials are that they are inert and non-toxic in water: chemically untreated polystyrene foam, waterproof cement free of additives, and epoxy paint intended for aquatic use.

Choosing the Right Materials

To start building a 3D background, you must choose the appropriate materials. These materials include:

  • Sand: Fine sand suitable for the type of fish in the aquarium should be chosen.
  • Rocks: Natural or artificial rocks can be used to create stunning landscapes.
  • Artificial Plants: Artificial plants offer diverse, high-quality options and are a good alternative to live plants, which can be difficult to care for in Iraq's conditions.

Designing the Background

After selecting the materials, the background must be designed to be compatible with the aquarium size and the nature of the fish. The following factors should be considered:

  1. Aquarium Size: The design must be proportional to the aquarium's size, so the tank doesn't appear crowded or empty.
  2. Nature of the Fish: Materials and colors should be chosen to suit the behavior and nature of the fish.
  3. Coordination: There should be good coordination between the different materials to create a cohesive and aesthetic look.
A golden tip from AQUAVO: When building a 3D background, we must consider providing enough space for the fish to move and swim freely. Fluctuations in the electrical current in Iraq should also be considered to avoid harming the fish.

Installing the Background

After designing the background, it must be installed precisely in the aquarium. High-quality adhesives should be used to ensure the background's stability and prevent erosion over time. If using live plants, treat tap water for chlorine before adding it, as chlorine harms both plants and beneficial bacteria.

Conclusion

Building 3D backgrounds in an aquarium is a process that requires patience and attention to detail. With the right material selection and precise design, a beautiful and ideal environment can be created for your fish. Don't forget that AQUAVO is your trusted partner on this journey, providing everything you need to create the perfect aquarium, with warranties and delivery throughout Iraq. Feel free to leverage our expertise to achieve your dreams of building an aquarium that suits your tastes and interests.

data.title: Tank Mates: Who Lives With Whom? (Compatibility Guide) 🤝
data.excerpt: Can you put a Betta with Guppies? Or Angelfish with Neons? Learn how to choose peaceful tank mates.
data.content:
The Big Mouth Rule — The Golden Rule

"If it fits in another fish's mouth, it will be eaten." This simple rule saves you from significant losses. However, compatibility isn't just about size — behavior, temperature, and pH are all important factors.

Key Compatibility Factors

  • Size: Do not put very small fish with large ones. Rule: The size difference should not exceed 3x.
  • Temperament: Peaceful fish (Guppies, Mollies) do not coexist with aggressive ones (African Cichlids).
  • Swimming Zones: Distribute fish among the surface, mid-water, and bottom levels to reduce conflict.
  • Temperature: Goldfish (cold water 18-22°C) do not live with tropical fish (25-28°C).
  • pH Level: African Cichlids (pH 7.8-8.5) are not suitable for Tetras (pH 6-7).

Absolutely Forbidden Pairs ❌

  • Betta + Male Guppy: Bettas dislike long, colorful fins and will attack them aggressively.
  • Goldfish + Neon Tetra: Small Tetras are a snack for large Goldfish.
  • African Cichlid + Any Peaceful Fish: African Cichlids are territorial and highly aggressive.
  • Oscar + Any Smaller Fish: Oscars eat anything that fits in their mouth.
  • Flowerhorn + Anything: It's best kept alone — its aggression is limitless.

Ideal Friends Living in Peace ✅

  • Molly + Platy + Guppy + Swordtail: The peaceful livebearer family — a party of colors!
  • Neon Tetra + Corydoras + Guppy: An ideal community for a planted aquarium.
  • Discus + Neon Tetra + Ram Cichlid: Fantastic color coordination and royal tranquility.
  • Angelfish + Congo Tetra + Corydoras: An elegant Amazonian aquarium.
  • Female Betta + Nerite Snail + Amano Shrimp: A peaceful nano aquarium.

Quick Compatibility Chart

Before adding any new fish, ask yourself 3 questions:

  1. Is its size suitable for the existing fish?
  2. Does it require the same temperature and pH?
  3. Is its temperament compatible (peaceful with peaceful)?

If you answer "yes" to all three, you're on the right track! If you're unsure, contact the AQUAVO team via WhatsApp, and we'll help you for free.

The biggest source of incompatibility is cichlids, as the name groups two completely different sets of fish based on water parameters and behavior — the difference between American and African cichlids and types of African cichlids. Some species are unsuitable for any tank mates, like pufferfish, and some setups go beyond fish entirely, like turtles with fish.

data.title: Aggression and Chasing in the Aquarium: Causes and Solutions
data.excerpt: Chasing is a functional, not personal, behavior. A useful paradox: schooling fish become aggressive in small numbers, not large ones—and breaking sightlines is more effective than increasing liters.
data.content:
Chasing Isn't Personal

A fish doesn't "hate" its neighbor. Aggression in the aquarium is a functional behavior with specific causes, most of which can be fixed by changing conditions, not by removing the "evil" fish.

PatternMost Likely CauseSolution
Constant chasing of one individualTerritoriality, or unbalanced sex ratioBreak sightlines, adjust ratio
Chasing between males of the same speciesTerritorial competitionOne male, or more space and hiding places
Nipping at long finsSpecies-specific behaviorSeparate species—not fixed by space
Sudden aggression in a calm tankBreeding, deteriorating water, or overcrowdingTest the water first
Chasing within a small schoolBelow minimum numbersIncrease school size
A useful paradox: Schooling fish become more aggressive in small numbers, not large ones. A school distributes interactions; three individuals mean one receives all the pressure. Increasing the number often calms the tank. Schooling Fish.

Three Tools to Reduce Aggression

  1. Break sightlines. The most important of these: plants, driftwood, and rocks that obstruct direct vision across the tank. Two fish that don't constantly see each other fight less—this is more effective than just increasing liters.
  2. Multiple hiding places and exits. A hiding place with a single entrance is a trap; give the chased fish an escape route.
  3. Distribute food in multiple spots—feeding time is the most stressful moment.

When the Problem is a Wrong Choice, Not Conditions

Some combinations don't work, no matter how much you improve the conditions:

  • A naturally territorial fish in a small tank—some cichlids need space that the average home aquarium doesn't provide.
  • Greatly varying sizes—what fits in the mouth gets eaten, without aggression in the first place. Angelfish.
  • Fin nippers with long-finned fish—species behavior doesn't change.
  • Betta with similar-looking species—Betta Compatibility.

Prevention before purchase is more useful than any solution afterward: Fish Compatibility.

Test the Water Before Blaming the Fish

Sudden aggression in a previously stable tank is often a symptom, not a cause. Overcrowding and deteriorating water increase stress and manifest as aggressive behavior.

  • Test for ammonia and nitrite—Reading Your Test Kit.
  • Review the stocking level against tank capacity—How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Hold.
  • Check the temperature: High temperatures increase metabolism, activity, and stress simultaneously.

Injuries After Fights

A wound is an open door for infection, first appearing as fuzz or erosion. Prioritize improving water quality over immediate medication—White Fuzz and Fin Rot Treatment. If the chased fish constantly hides and refuses to eat, separation is sometimes the only honest solution.

The most common case where temperament is blamed instead of behavior is fin nipping in Barbs. On the other end of the spectrum are species with structural, not situational, aggression like the Flowerhorn.

data.seoDescription: Learn why fish chase each other in aquariums, the causes of aggression, and effective solutions like breaking sightlines and managing stocking levels. Prevent conflicts with proper tank mate selection.

data.title: Snail Reproduction in the Aquarium: The Real Cause and Control
data.excerpt: A population explosion is an indicator of overfeeding, not of malicious snails. And why copper-based snail killers kill shrimp first and remain in the substrate for months.
data.content:
Snails Don't Reproduce Out of Nowhere

Common complaint: "One snail entered, and the tank is now full." The real reason isn't the snail itself — it's overfeeding. Snail populations follow the amount of available food: more food means more snails, and a lack of food will naturally limit their numbers.

This population explosion is a useful diagnostic indicator: If snails are reproducing rapidly, you are likely overfeeding. Address the cause, and their numbers will decrease on their own. Feeding Guide.

Are They Actually Harmful?

BeliefReality
They eat plantsMost common species graze on algae and dead tissue; healthy plants are rarely eaten
They pollute the tankThey add bioload like any organism, but they also break down detritus
A sign of a dirty tankSpecifically a sign of overfeeding
They must be eliminatedA moderate number is actually beneficial as a cleanup crew

Controlling Numbers — In Order

  1. Reduce feeding. The first and by far the most effective measure.
  2. Remove uneaten food after feeding, especially vegetables.
  3. Manual removal. Place a piece of boiled vegetable in the tank overnight, and remove it in the morning with the snails attached. Repeat for several days.
  4. Gravel vacuuming removes eggs and young along with waste — Aquarium Cleaning.
  5. Inspect new plants before adding them; eggs can be attached to the leaves.

Important Warning: Snail Killers

Most "snail killer" products are copper-based. This means:

  • They kill shrimp before snails — shrimp are more sensitive to copper than the target snails themselves.
  • Copper does not break down: it binds to substrate and silicone and leaches out for months, potentially making the tank unsuitable for invertebrates long-term.
  • Sudden mass die-off of snails will cause a severe ammonia spike — dozens of decaying bodies at once.

Details in Shrimp and Snails. The takeaway: reducing food is safer and more effective than any product.

Snail-Eating Fish: A Solution with Conditions

Some fish eat snails, but adding them is a permanent decision, not a temporary fix:

  • They will remain in your tank after the snails are gone and require their own space and care.
  • They may eat desirable shrimp and snails, not just the excess population.
  • And they add to the bioload — How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Handle.

Do not introduce a living creature for a single function and then neglect it. If the problem is overfeeding, the solution is less food.

Beneficial Snails

A moderate population grazes on algae on the glass and decor and breaks down leftover food. Some species sift through the substrate, preventing the formation of anaerobic pockets. Their high sensitivity to water degradation makes them an early indicator — if your snails start dying or their shells erode, test your water and hardness before your fish are affected. GH and KH Water Hardness.

And before you rely on a snail-eating fish, understand its long-term cost — Loaches Before You Buy.
data.seoTitle: Snail Reproduction in Aquarium: Causes, Control, and Dangers of Snail Killers
data.seoDescription: Learn why snails overpopulate aquariums (it's overfeeding!), how to control them naturally, and the serious risks of copper-based snail killers, especially for shrimp.

data.title: Current and Water Movement: An Independent Factor, Not a Filter Byproduct
data.excerpt: Surface agitation is more important than deep water current, as gas exchange occurs there. Learn how to detect dead zones where waste silently accumulates.
data.content:
Current is an Independent Factor, Not a Filter Byproduct

Most hobbyists choose a filter and then accept whatever current it produces. However, water movement is an environmental factor in itself: it determines where oxygen reaches, where waste settles, which fish are comfortable, and which are exhausted.

A clear indicator of its importance: two aquariums with the same volume, the same fish, and the same filter can behave completely differently if one directs the output towards the surface and the other towards the side glass.
Current LevelSuitable ForSign of a Problem
CalmBetta, Gourami, long-finned speciesStagnation and persistent waste spots on the substrate
ModerateMost community tanks—
StrongActive swimmersFish constantly hiding or struggling to maintain position

The Surface is More Important Than Depth

Gas exchange occurs at the water surface. Oxygen enters and carbon dioxide exits from there, not from the depths of the aquarium. Therefore, surface agitation is practically more important than the current strength within the water.

  • A completely still surface means poor exchange, which is first noticeable at night when plants stop producing oxygen and consume it.
  • An oily film on the surface is a sign of surface stagnation, indicating that exchange is partially blocked.
  • And in the Iraqi summer, the issue becomes critical: warmer water holds less oxygen, so the same current that is sufficient in winter may not be enough — see Summer Heat and When an Air Pump is Necessary.

Dead Zones: The Problem You Don't Notice

Current is rarely distributed evenly. Corners and spots behind decor form where flow doesn't reach, allowing waste and leftover food to accumulate and decompose locally.

  1. How to detect them: Turn off feeding for a day and observe where suspended particles settle. The place where they gather and don't move is a dead zone.
  2. Why they matter: They are a silent source of ammonia and localized algae growth — see Ammonia Spike Emergency Treatment and The Algae War Guide.
  3. The solution isn't always a stronger filter. Often, redirecting the output at a different angle or moving a piece of decor is sufficient — see Hardscape: Rock Arrangement for Visual Depth.
  4. And siphoning remains essential, regardless of good current — see How to Clean Your Aquarium Properly.

When Current is Too Much

Fish don't "exercise" in strong currents; they get exhausted. Chronic stress weakens immunity like any other pressure.

  • A fish constantly swimming in place against the current to maintain its position.
  • Constant hiding behind decor on one side of the aquarium.
  • Fins folded against the body most of the time.
  • Difficulty eating — food is swept away before they can catch it, which harms slower fish like Discus and Gourami.

The practical solution is to break the current, not eliminate it: direct the output towards the glass or surface, or use plants and driftwood as barriers to create calm areas the fish can move between. An aquarium with varied intensity zones is better than one with uniform intensity.

Plants also offer a dual benefit here: they break the current and consume nutrients — see Best Low-Tech Aquarium Plants for Beginners. When choosing a filter, consider the current, not just the filtration — see Which Filter is Right for Your Aquarium and How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Support.

The Oily Film on the Surface

A thin film covers the water surface, breaking its reflection and appearing as a static, greasy layer. It's not dangerous in itself, but it hinders gas exchange at the surface — which is precisely where it happens.

  • Its source is proteins and fats from food and organic debris, accumulating where there is no movement.
  • The root solution is surface agitation — slightly angle the filter output upwards, or add aeration.
  • Quick removal: Gently skim the surface with a paper towel, repeating as needed.
  • Review feeding amounts, as recurring film indicates organic overload — see Aquarium Fish Feeding Guide.
data.seoTitle: Water Current and Movement in Aquariums: Beyond Filter Output
data.seoDescription: Understand why water current is a critical independent factor for gas exchange, waste removal, and fish health in your aquarium. Learn to identify and fix dead zones and excessive current.

data.title: Traveling and Leaving Your Aquarium: Starvation is Better Than Foul Water
data.excerpt: Most aquariums lost during travel are not due to starvation but overfeeding before departure. Plan according to your absence duration, and preparation starts two days prior, not one hour before.
data.content:
Fish Can Tolerate Hunger Better Than Foul Water

The first concern for a traveler is: Who will feed the fish? The truth is, this should be your last concern. A healthy adult fish can go for days without food with no significant harm—but it cannot tolerate days with deteriorating water.

Most aquariums lost during travel did not die of starvation. They died because someone overfed before the trip or left it to a relative to "feed them every day," causing the excess food to decompose and raise ammonia levels unnoticed. Overfeeding is far more dangerous than fasting.

According to the Duration of Absence

DurationFeedingPreparation
Two to three daysNothing — do not feed at allWater change before travel, nothing else
One weekNothing for healthy adult fishWater change, cleaning, testing, reduce lighting
More than one weekSomeone feeds once every two or three days with pre-portioned amountsAll of the above + written instructions

Small fish and fry are an exception: they need frequent feeding and cannot be left unattended. The same applies to sick fish or those undergoing treatment.

Two Days Before Travel, Not One Hour

  1. Change a portion of the water and siphon the substrate — start your absence with the lowest possible nitrates. Water Change Guide.
  2. Test for ammonia and nitrite. If the aquarium is already unstable, traveling will reveal it, not hide it. Reading Test Results.
  3. Clean the filter a week before, not immediately before traveling. Cleaning temporarily disrupts the bacterial colony, and you want that to happen while you are present.
  4. Reduce lighting hours or turn it off — less light means less algae in your absence.
  5. Check the water level: Evaporation during your absence concentrates everything dissolved, and evaporation is high during Iraqi summers. Keep the level full.
  6. Check the heater and filter — a malfunction that appears during your absence is the worst possible timing. Heater Guide.

If You Leave Someone to Feed

This is the most dangerous point in practice, and the solution is not more trust but reducing what can go wrong:

  • Pre-portion the doses into small bags or containers — one for each feeding. Never leave the entire container.
  • Write the instructions in one clear sentence: "One bag every three days, and nothing else."
  • Explicitly ask them not to add anything — no water, no medication, no "cleaning."
  • Tell them frankly: If you forget, do not compensate with a double dose.

The Iraqi Context: Absence and Power Outages

Here, the risks multiply: a long power outage during your absence means a stopped filter and fluctuating temperatures with no one to intervene. There is no complete solution, but there is damage mitigation:

  • Do not add fish for weeks before your trip — the aquarium needs stability, not a new load. Quarantine New Fish.
  • Reduce the bioload before a long absence: less food means less ammonia means a larger safety margin.
  • Leave the lid partially open for better gas exchange if the weather is hot — Protecting Fish in Iraqi Summer (50 Degrees).
  • Explain to anyone checking on the house what to do during a long outage: agitate the water surface with a cup, and do not feed. Emergency Aquarium Tools for Power Outages.

After Returning

Do not compensate for the fasting with a large meal. Start with a small amount, test ammonia and nitrite before anything else, and change some water if readings are high or the absence was long.

Automatic Feeders: When They Help and When They Harm

An automatic feeder solves the problem of long absences but introduces a new risk: a malfunction that empties the entire quantity at once, which is worse than starvation.

  • Test it for a week before traveling while you are present, and monitor the actual quantity per meal.
  • Set it to dispense less than you think. Adult fish tolerate underfeeding easily and do not tolerate foul water — this remains the principle of this entire article.
  • Humidity can clump the food and clog the dispenser; place it away from surface vapor.
  • For short absences, you don't need it at all.

data.seoDescription: Learn how to prepare your aquarium for your absence. Discover feeding schedules, essential preparations, and how to mitigate risks like power outages and overfeeding to ensure your fish survive.

data.title: Best Low-Tech Aquatic Plants for Beginners (No CO2 Needed)
data.excerpt: You don't need an expensive CO2 system to plant your aquarium! Here are the best easy aquatic plants that grow without carbon dioxide.
data.content:
Introduction

When it comes to creating an aquatic paradise at home, choosing the right plants is crucial. Especially in Iraq, where the climate is characterized by extreme heat during summer and frequent power outages, which increases the challenges of caring for aquatic plants. Therefore, low-maintenance plants — such as Anubias, Microsorum, and Vallisneria — are the most suitable choice for beginners: they grow under medium lighting and without carbon dioxide injection.

Low-Tech Aquatic Plants

Low-tech aquatic plants are a great choice for beginners because they do not require additional equipment such as carbon dioxide pumps or complex filtration systems. Some common aquatic plants that do not require carbon dioxide include:

  • Anubias: An attractive aquatic plant that grows slowly and can thrive in low-light conditions.
  • Java Fern: A hardy aquatic plant that can tolerate high temperatures and grows well in shallow water.
  • Crinum: A beautiful aquatic plant that grows quickly and can thrive in low-light conditions.

Aquatic Plant Challenges in Iraq

In Iraq, aquatic plants face challenges such as extreme summer heat, which can reach 50 °C, and frequent power outages, which can affect the performance of aquarium equipment. Tap water also needs treatment for chlorine before use, as chlorine is harmful to plants and beneficial bacteria.

Golden tip from AQUAVO: Use treated water for growing aquatic plants, and choose plants capable of withstanding harsh conditions.

How to Choose the Right Aquatic Plants

When choosing aquatic plants, you should consider several factors, such as:

  1. The lighting level in your aquarium.
  2. The temperature in your aquarium.
  3. The level of care you can provide for the plants.

data.title: Stunning Aquascaping on a Budget: Secrets Revealed 🎨
data.excerpt: You don't need to spend a fortune to have a magazine-worthy aquarium. Here's how to design a masterpiece at the lowest cost.
data.content:
Aquascaping Isn't Just for the Wealthy!

Many believe that designing a stunning aquascape requires a huge budget. The truth is, you can create an aquatic masterpiece for under $50 if you know the right secrets. Here's AQUAVO's comprehensive guide!

Step 1: Choosing the Right Aquarium

You don't need a massive tank. A 40-60 L aquarium is ideal for beginners and inexpensive. Look for regular glass tanks instead of Ultra Clear to save 50% of the cost.

Step 2: Free Rocks and Wood

  • Rocks: Collect them from nature! Volcanic and limestone rocks are found in the Iraqi environment. Just wash them thoroughly and boil them for 20 minutes.
  • Wood: Dried tree branches make excellent driftwood after boiling and soaking for a week.
  • Warning: Avoid rocks that fizz with vinegar (they contain calcium that raises pH).

Step 3: Inexpensive, Fast-Growing Plants

  • Java Moss: Grows without substrate, CO2, or strong lighting — tie it to rocks.
  • Anubias Nana: A nearly indestructible plant — tie it to wood.
  • Vallisneria: A tall background plant that grows like grass — fills the tank quickly.
  • Elodea: Very cheap and excellent for water purification.

Step 4: Principles of Visual Design

  1. Rule of Thirds: Don't place the main element in the center — position it on one-third of the tank.
  2. Height Gradient: Short plants in front, medium in the middle, tall in the back.
  3. Single Focal Point: A large rock or distinctive piece of wood should be the center of attraction.
  4. Negative Space: Don't fill every centimeter — empty space creates beauty.

Step 5: Cost-Effective Lighting

You don't need expensive professional lighting. A 6500K white LED bulb from any electronics store is sufficient for easy plants. Run it for only 8 hours a day (use an inexpensive timer).

AQUAVO Tip: Start with only 3-4 types of plants. Too many plants at the beginning can be overwhelming. Let them grow and fill the spaces naturally over two months.

Installing a Carbon Dioxide System

data.title: Schooling Fish: Why Six, Not Three?
data.excerpt: A school is a safety mechanism, not just decoration. A schooling fish kept alone lives in constant alertness, weakening its immunity. Buying three instead of six is not a saving, but a loss of the three.
data.content:
A Schooling Fish Alone is Not a Happy Fish

Schooling species evolved to live in groups, and the group is not an aesthetic luxury — it is a safety mechanism. A fish within a school knows that danger is distributed, so it behaves naturally: swimming in the middle, eating with confidence, and showing its colors.

The same species alone or in pairs lives in a state of constant alert: hiding, losing color, eating hesitantly, and sometimes becoming aggressive towards others. This chronic stress weakens the immune system, leading to frequent illnesses for no apparent reason.

This means buying three tetras instead of six is not a saving. It often ends with the loss of the three, because chronic stress opens the door to everything — starting with white spot: white spot.

The Practical Minimum

TypeCommon ExamplesReasonable Minimum Number
True SchoolingNeon Tetra, Rasbora, DanioSix or more, preferably more
Social Bottom DwellersCorydorasSix or more of the same species
Flexible Group DwellersGuppy, Molly, PlatyA small group, considering the female-to-male ratio
Solitary or TerritorialBetta, some CichlidsOne, or a pair under specific conditions

Important note: six of one species, not six mixed. Two fish of one species and three of another do not form a school — each remains alone in a crowded tank.

The Seemingly Logical Mistake

Beginners want variety, so they buy two of each species. The result is a tank with visual diversity and zero comfort: each species is below its minimum number, and the bioload is high as if it were a full school.

The better alternative: one or two species in sufficient numbers. A tank with eight neons and six corydoras is visually more beautiful and biologically healthier than a tank with twelve species in pairs of each.

And Here the Number Collides with the Bioload

A school of six means a higher bioload than two fish. This is why the decision about schooling cannot be made in isolation from the tank size and filtration strength:

  • Calculate based on the full school from the beginning, not on what you will buy today.
  • Add the school in small, spaced-out batches to allow the bacteria to catch up — the nitrogen cycle.
  • If the tank cannot support six of a species, then that species is not suitable for this tank. Choose a smaller species instead of reducing the number — how many fish can your tank support.

Swimming Space, Not Just Liters

Active schooling fish swim horizontally constantly, so the length of the tank matters more than its height. A long, low tank is better for an active school than a tall, narrow one with the same liters — and it has a second advantage: a larger surface area means better gas exchange. Dissolved Oxygen and Aeration.

Signs of an Incomplete School

  • Constant hiding among plants and decor, with only brief appearances at feeding time.
  • Dull colors compared to what you saw in the store.
  • Chasing within the same species — behavior that appears in small numbers and calms down with sufficient numbers.
  • Frequent illnesses despite a clean water test. Refer to the symptom diagnosis guide first to rule out water issues.

If you discover your school is incomplete, the solution is to gradually add more individuals of the same species — provided the tank can support the full number.

data.title: RO Water vs. Tap Water in Aquariums: Which is Better?

Introduction to the World of Aquariums in Iraq

In our country, Iraq, where summer temperatures reach 50 °C, power outages are frequent, and tap water is highly chlorinated, choosing the right water for aquariums becomes a real challenge. This makes selecting the correct water for fish and aquatic plants extremely important.

What is RO Water?

RO water, or Reverse Osmosis Treated Freshwater, is water treated with an advanced technology to remove impurities and contaminants. This technology works to remove ions and inorganic compounds, resulting in pure water with a balanced pH.

What is Tap Water?

Tap water is water that has been frozen and then thawed; it is natural water with a low impurity level. However, tap water may contain some impurities or ions that can affect the chemical balance of aquariums.

The Difference Between RO Water and Tap Water

The main difference between RO water and tap water lies in the degree of purity and chemical balance. RO water is purer and has a controlled pH, making it safer for fish and aquatic plants.

  • High Purity: RO water is treated to remove impurities and contaminants, making it purer.
  • Chemical Balance: RO water has a balanced pH, contributing to the health of fish and aquatic plants.
  • Controllability: The purity and chemical balance of RO water can be controlled, making it ideal for aquariums.
RO water is almost devoid of minerals, which is why it is not used alone: it is mixed with treated tap water or remineralization salts are added, otherwise the water becomes unstable in pH.

Using RO Water in Aquariums

Using RO water in aquariums ensures a healthy aquatic environment and thriving fish and aquatic plants. You can use RO water in all types of aquariums, whether they are for beginners or advanced aquarists.

  1. Choosing the Right Water: Choose RO water to ensure a healthy aquatic environment.
  2. Temperature Control: Use temperature control devices to ensure stable temperatures.
  3. Provide Good Ventilation: Use ventilation devices to ensure adequate oxygen supply.

data.title: Breeding as a Decision: Livebearer or Egg-Layer, and Do You Really Want It?
data.excerpt: The question precedes the method: where will the offspring go? The difference between livebearers and egg-layers, and four different schools within egg-layers that completely change preparation.
data.content:
Breeding is a Decision, Not a Reward

Most discussions about breeding start with "How do I make them reproduce?" The correct question precedes that: Do you actually want fry? Because the result isn't ten cute little fish — it's dozens of mouths in a tank with a limited capacity, and subsequent decisions about where they will go.

Practical rule: Do not start breeding before you know where the offspring will go. A grow-out tank, a buyer, or an aquarist friend. Without this answer, successful breeding turns into an overstocking problem — how many fish your tank can handle.

Two Strategies Govern Everything

Freshwater fish reproduce in two ways, and the difference between them dictates every subsequent practical step.

LivebearerEgg-Layer
OffspringSwimming fry, ready to goEggs that need hatching
Happens without planning?Yes — oftenNo, requires prepared conditions
ExamplesMolly, Platy, Guppy, SwordtailTetra, Cichlid, Gourami, Corydoras
First ChallengeManaging the numbersAchieving hatching in the first place

Livebearers are explained in detail in Livebearing Fish and Managing Numbers and The Guppy Guide. Egg-layers, however, are not a single category.

Egg-Layers: Four Different Schools

  • Scatter spawners. They scatter eggs among plants and forget them, and many eat them immediately afterward. Protection here involves dense plants or separating the parents after spawning. Most small schooling fish are of this type.
  • Surface spawners. They clean a leaf or a rock and lay eggs on it, then the pair guards it. The Angelfish is a well-known example, where the peaceful pair turns into an aggressive guardian.
  • Mouthbrooders. They carry the eggs in their mouths until hatching — common among African Cichlids. The female stops eating during this period.
  • Bubble nest builders. The male builds a bubble nest at the surface and guards it. This is a behavior of Gouramis and Bettas, and is directly related to their aerial respiration method.

Knowing which school your species belongs to completely changes the preparation: dense plants are useless for mouthbrooders, and a flat rock means nothing to a scatter spawner.

What Actually Stimulates Breeding

Breeding is not a button to be pressed. It is a response to environmental cues that tell the fish that conditions are suitable for raising a generation:

  1. Dietary conditioning. A varied, high-quality diet for a period before attempting — Feeding Guide.
  2. Larger than usual water changes. In many species, this is interpreted as a seasonal signal — Water Changes.
  3. Stable water and temperature above all else. A fluctuating tank does not breed, and if it does, the eggs will be infertile.
  4. The presence of a compatible pair. This assumes sexing the fish — How to Sex Aquarium Fish.
A neglected note: Many fish will breed on their own when their conditions are already excellent. So if your tank is stable and your feeding is regular and nothing has bred, the reason is likely the absence of a compatible pair, not a lack of "stimulation."

The Unspoken Side

Breeding changes the tank's behavior. The guarding pair will chase away anything that approaches, and a peaceful community tank becomes stressful for weeks — Aggression and Chasing in the Aquarium and Compatibility Guide.

And after hatching, a completely different phase begins with its own requirements: Raising Fish Fry. Before introducing any new fish with the intention of breeding, pass them through Quarantine.

data.title: Aquatic Plant Problems: Yellowing, Holes, and Melting — Read the Leaf
data.excerpt: A single diagnostic key separates most symptoms: Are old or new leaves affected? And a correction of a common confusion — submerged plants are not watered.
data.content:
Read the Leaf: Old or New?

Aquatic plant symptoms look similar — yellowing, holes, melting — but there is one diagnostic key that separates most of them: which leaves are affected first.

Some nutrients can be transported internally by the plant, which it draws from older leaves to build new ones. Some cannot be transported. The result:

Affected LeavesMeansExample
Old firstDeficiency of a mobile element — the plant breaks it down to feed new growthNitrogen, Potassium, Magnesium
New firstDeficiency of an immobile element — it cannot be drawn from old leavesIron

Symptom Chart

What You SeeMost LikelyFirst Step
Yellowing between veins with veins remaining green, on new leavesIron deficiencyFertilizer containing iron, and check lighting
Small pinprick holes, and yellow edges, on old leavesPotassium deficiencyAll-around fertilizer
Old leaves yellow, become translucent, then meltNitrogen deficiencyOften a tank with few fish or excessive water changes
Widespread melting a few days after purchaseNatural transition from emersed to submerged growthDo nothing — wait for new growth
Rhizome buried and plant rottingPlanting error, not nutrient deficiencyLift the rhizome and tie it to wood or rock
Algae covering leavesExcess light or nutrientsAlgae Guide

Melting After Purchase: Normal, Not Failure

Most plants are grown in nurseries out of water with emersed leaves. When submerged, those leaves melt because they are not adapted to underwater life, and the plant grows new leaves of a different shape. This is a transition, not death — and discarding the plant at this stage is a common mistake.

The rule: Judge by new growth. If the new leaves are healthy, the plant is fine no matter how much the old ones melt. If symptoms continue on new growth after it has stabilized, then look for an actual deficiency.

Important Correction: Aquatic Plants Are Not "Watered"

A confusion between houseplants and aquatic plants is widespread in Arabic content, leading to tank problems being attributed to "overwatering" or "underwatering." Submerged plants live in water permanently, and watering has no meaning for them. The real causes of root rot are:

  • Burying the rhizome for Anubias and Java Fern — the number one cause by far. These plants are tied to a surface, not buried.
  • Compacted substrate with no water movement, creating anaerobic pockets at the roots.
  • Leftover dead tissue rots and spreads rot to surrounding areas.
  • Deteriorated water itself — Reading Water Tests.

Practical Treatment

  1. Trim dead tissue with clean scissors. A melting leaf will not recover, and its presence pollutes and consumes oxygen.
  2. Lift the rhizome if it is buried, and tie it with thread or aquascape glue to wood or rock.
  3. Improve water movement around stagnant areas — Choosing a Filter.
  4. Stabilize lighting to 6–8 hours before changing anything else — Lighting Guide.
  5. Change one factor and wait two weeks. Plants respond slowly, and changing everything at once prevents you from knowing what worked.

Details on fertilizing and when you actually need it are in Aquatic Plant Fertilization, and choosing tolerant types in Low-Tech Aquarium Plants for Beginners.

Limits of Visual Diagnosis

Symptoms overlap: a deficiency of two elements together creates a complex picture, and poor lighting mimics nutrient deficiency because the plant cannot consume them. The chart above suggests, but does not confirm. The safest rule is to start with lighting and consistency, as they are free, before adding substances to the water.

data.title: Goldfish: Five Mistakes to Avoid Before You Buy
data.excerpt: Goldfish are not small or tropical fish: they grow to 25-30 cm, require cold water and a 110 L tank with stronger filtration than tropical fish—making them one of the worst choices for a hot summer.
data.content:
The First Mistake Happens Before Purchase: Tank Size

Goldfish are not small fish. Common and Comet goldfish reach 25–30 cm at maturity, sometimes longer. The common image of a small fish in a round bowl has no relation to the actual animal.

Common BeliefReality
Lives in a round bowlA round bowl has a small surface area = less oxygen, and cannot accommodate a filter
Stays small25–30 cm for single-tailed varieties
A 20 L tank is enoughStart with 110 L for a single fish; larger varieties need more
Tropical fishA coldwater fish: 18–24 °C

Note on "stunted growth": A goldfish in a small tank does not remain healthy and small—its external body growth slows while its internal organs continue to develop, which is why its lifespan is short in small bowls.

The Second Mistake: Treating Them as Tropical Fish

Goldfish are coldwater fish. Their comfortable range is 18–24 °C, and they are active and eat well at much lower temperatures than tetras or bettas require. So, do not place them in a tropical tank at 26–28 °C just because a heater is present.

Here is an important point for Iraq: Goldfish are one of the worst choices for the Iraqi summer. They are inherently coldwater fish and produce a lot of waste, requiring more oxygen than other fish—while hot water holds less oxygen. Both factors work against you. If you are in a hot area without stable cooling, choose a calm tropical species instead.

The complete mechanism of temperature and oxygen is discussed in Protecting Fish from Summer Heat.

The Third Mistake: An Undersized Filter

Goldfish produce significantly more waste than any ornamental fish of the same size. Their bodies are full, meaning they eat and excrete more. This results in a higher than usual biological filtration load.

This flips the common advice on its head: Goldfish require stronger filtration than small tropical fish, not weaker. See the Filter Selection Guide for choosing the type and capacity.

The Fourth Mistake: Skipping the Cycling Process

Because they produce a lot of waste, goldfish in an uncycled tank will raise ammonia levels faster than other fish. Most cases of "died within a week" are ammonia poisoning, not disease.

Cycle the tank before purchasing, and test ammonia and nitrite weekly afterward—refer to The Nitrogen Cycle Explained. For immediate action if readings rise, see Emergency Treatment for Ammonia Spikes.

The Fifth Mistake: Overfeeding

Goldfish always appear hungry and beg at the glass; this is natural behavior, not hunger. Overfeeding causes two problems simultaneously: water pollution and digestive issues, including buoyancy problems common in round-bodied varieties.

  • One or two small feedings daily, finished within two minutes.
  • Soak pellets for a few seconds before feeding to reduce air swallowed with floating food.
  • A weekly fasting day is a common and beneficial practice for round-bodied fish.

Conclusion

Goldfish are not the easy beginner fish their reputation suggests: they grow very large, pollute heavily, and require cold water, a larger-than-expected tank, and stronger filtration. If you can provide these conditions, they are wonderful, long-lived fish. If your tank is small or your room is hot without cooling, the honest choice is a different species—see 5 Hardy Fish for Beginners, and use the Calculators to determine your tank size.

data.title: Can Fish See or Recognize Us? Shocking Scientific Facts

Introduction

Have you ever wondered about the ability of fish to see and recognize humans? This question sparks the curiosity of many fish enthusiasts in Iraq, where keeping fish is a popular and enjoyable hobby for many. In this article, we will explore shocking scientific facts about the ability of fish to see and recognize humans, and discuss some tips for caring for your fish at home.

How Do Fish See?

Fish have eyes capable of seeing light and color, but the structure of their eyes differs from that of human eyes. Fish can see movement and vibrations, but they do not have the ability to see stationary objects clearly. This means that fish can see a person moving in front of them, but they do not recognize them individually.

Factors Affecting Fish Vision

  • Light: Light plays an important role in fish vision, as they can see light and color.
  • Movement: Fish can see movement and vibrations, which help stimulate their behavior.
  • Color: Fish have the ability to see colors, but they do not possess the same level of color discrimination as humans.

How Do Fish Recognize People?

Fish cannot recognize people individually, but they can adapt to their environment and develop specific behaviors towards people they have interacted with. For example, if you feed your fish at a specific time each day, the fish will learn to expect food at that time.

data.title: Aquarium Cleanliness and Your Safety: Simple Precautions
data.excerpt: The hobby is safe and problems are uncommon, but one rule is worth knowing: never put a broken skin into the water. If an infection appears that doesn't improve, tell your doctor you have an aquarium.
data.content:
The Hobby Is Safe — With One Precaution Worth Knowing

Almost everything on this site talks about fish safety. This article is about your safety. This is because maintaining an aquarium requires you to constantly put your hands in the water — for siphoning, cleaning glass, planting, or catching fish. This creates a daily point of contact between your skin and a warm aquatic environment.

The balanced takeaway: Fishkeeping is a safe hobby, and associated health problems are uncommon. However, a simple and free precaution exists, and knowing it can be helpful if something happens — because a doctor might not ask about the aquarium if you don't mention it.

The Golden Rule: Never Put Broken Skin in Water

This is the most important point in the entire article. Warm water contains natural microorganisms, and intact skin is an effective barrier against them. Problems begin when that barrier is compromised.

  • A cut, scratch, or crack on your hand? Cover it with a waterproof bandage, use a long glove that covers your forearm, or postpone the task.
  • Wash your hands with soap and water after any contact with the aquarium — before eating and before touching your face.
  • Be mindful of scratches during the work itself. The edges of decor, rocks, and glass can easily cause cuts while you are focused on other tasks.
  • Never siphon water with your mouth. Start the flow by submerging and lifting or using a manual pump. This is a common habit with no justification.

What Might Happen, and What It Looks Like

It is medically known that handling aquarium water can transmit — through a wound — a slow-developing skin infection known by names such as "fish tank granuloma." It is uncommon, but it has a practical characteristic worth knowing:

CharacteristicGeneral Description
LocationUsually the hand or forearm — the area of contact
AppearanceA localized nodule or lesion that develops slowly
SpeedSlow to appear and slow to respond to standard treatment
Why It MattersThe slow response is what makes mentioning the aquarium to your doctor important
This is the limit of what we can say: This article does not diagnose or prescribe treatment. We do not mention human medications or dosages. The only thing we state with confidence: If you develop a skin infection that does not improve as usual while you are handling an aquarium, tell your doctor you have a fish tank. This information alone may save them a lot of time, and it is all we can offer.

Practical Precautions Without Overdoing It

  1. Dedicate tools for the aquarium — a bucket, sponge, and siphon that are used only for the aquarium.
  2. Use a long glove for extended work or if you have any wounds.
  3. Do not wash aquarium equipment in the kitchen sink where food is prepared; use another location and wash it afterward.
  4. Wash your hands after every interaction — the simplest and most effective measure.
  5. If you have a health condition that affects your immune system, ask your doctor about additional precautions suitable for your situation. This is a personal medical question we cannot answer here.

Children and the Aquarium

An aquarium is an excellent educational experience for a child. The same precautions apply and no more: washed hands after touching, not putting hands with wounds into the water, and supervision when handling water or electrical equipment. For the electrical aspect specifically, refer to Aquarium Electrical Safety.

The Opposite Direction Also Matters

Just as aquarium water warrants precautions from you, you are also a source of risk to the aquarium: hand creams, soaps, perfumes, and detergent residues enter the water directly from your hands. Rinse your hands with clean water before putting them in if they have any product on them — and Airborne Toxins explains the other pathway.

And never give your fish human medication — the reversed direction of this article is explained in Dangers of Human Medicine for Fish. For routine aquarium cleaning, refer to How to Clean an Aquarium Properly and Aquarium Water Change Guide.

data.title: 5 Common Mistakes Beginners Make That Cost Them Their First Fish
data.excerpt: Before you buy any fish, read this! Avoid these mistakes and save your money and the lives of your pets.
data.content:
Why Do Beginner Fish Die?

Losing your first fish is rarely due to the fish itself being weak. More often, the aquarium wasn't ready to receive them: the water wasn't cycled, the bioload was too high for the filter's capacity, or a proper care routine hadn't been established. The five mistakes below are the most frequent for beginners, and all are avoidable before buying your first fish — not after.

Mistake 1: Immediately Adding Fish to a New Aquarium

This is the number one killer. A new aquarium lacks the beneficial bacteria needed to process fish waste. The result? Ammonia poisoning within 3-5 days.

Solution: Run the aquarium empty for at least two weeks, adding a starter bacteria product. This is called "cycling the aquarium" (Cycling).

Mistake 2: Overfeeding Fish

Excess food that isn't eaten by the fish decomposes at the bottom, turning into toxic ammonia, clouding the water, and causing algae growth.

Solution: Feed your fish only once or twice a day. The appropriate amount is what the fish can consume within 2-3 minutes. Anything remaining should be removed.

Mistake 3: Not Performing Regular Water Changes

Even with the best filter, nitrates accumulate over time. Without regular water changes, the fish's immune system gradually weakens until they become sick.

Solution: Change 20-25% of the water every week. Do not change more than 50% at once — sudden changes can cause shock.

Mistake 4: An Aquarium That Is Too Small for the Number of Fish

A 20-liter tank with 15 cm of fish = disaster. Overstocking increases waste, reduces oxygen, and causes aggression among fish.

Solution: The general rule is: 1 liter per centimeter of fish length. A 5 cm fish needs at least 5 liters.

Mistake 5: Washing the Filter with Tap Water

The chlorine in tap water instantly kills the beneficial bacteria in the filter. After washing, the aquarium is left without biological protection, as if it were new.

Solution: Wash the filter sponge only with old tank water. Squeeze it gently and do not over-clean it.

AQUAVO Tip: If you are a complete beginner, start with 3-5 hardy fish like Zebra Danios or Platies. Learn with them first before buying sensitive fish.

data.title: Comprehensive Guide to Aquarium Substrates and Decor: Choosing the Ideal Surfaces for Your Tank's Beauty and Balance
data.excerpt: Discover the key criteria for selecting aquarium substrate and decor to create a healthy and attractive environment for fish and plants, with practical tips for installation and maintenance in our comprehensive guide.
data.content:
When building a successful aquarium, it's not just about choosing fish or plants; it also requires selecting suitable substrate and decor that ensure a healthy ecological balance and visual appeal. In this guide, we will cover the most important considerations for choosing substrate and decor, along with practical instructions for their installation and maintenance.

The Importance of Substrate in the Aquarium

Substrate is not just a material that covers the bottom of the aquarium; it is an essential part of the ecosystem. It affects:

  • pH Balance – Some substrates maintain a stable pH level, which is crucial for many species.
  • Chemical Buffering – Prevents the buildup of ammonia and nitrates.
  • Microbial Stability – Provides an environment for beneficial microbes that break down waste.
  • Visual Appeal – Adds depth and variety to the landscape.

Most Common Types of Substrate

  1. White Mud (or Dry Mud) – Ideal for species that require a soft substrate, such as bottom-dwelling fish.
  2. Small Gravel (Beige or Gray) – Adds a natural texture and is preferred for species that like to swim over a hard surface.
  3. Wood-Coated Mud – Adds a natural flavor and promotes algae growth.
  4. Fluorine-Mixed Mud – Used for species that require a moist substrate, such as Japanese species.

Choosing Decor: How to Add Beauty and Functionality?

Decor is not limited to aesthetic elements; it plays an important role in providing suitable spaces for swimming, hiding, and plant growth. When choosing decor, consider:

  • Size and Placement – It should be appropriate for the tank size and fish species.
  • Safe Materials – Avoid materials that may contaminate the water or harm fish.
  • Compatibility with Plants – Some plants need specific surfaces to grow on.
  • Light Control – Position decor in areas that receive appropriate light for algae.

Preferred Decor Types for Different Species

  1. Rock Formations – Ideal for species that like to jump and swim near the surface.
  2. Large Stone Pieces – Provide hiding places for small species.
  3. Driftwood Pieces – Used for species that need diving spaces.
  4. Algae-Coated Wood Pieces – Promote algae growth and add a natural look.

Steps for Installing Substrate and Decor

To ensure successful installation, follow these steps:

  1. Pre-Cleaning – Wash the substrate and decor with warm water to reduce dust.
  2. Garden Preparation – Place a thin layer of mud or gravel at the bottom of the aquarium to secure the decor.
  3. Even Distribution – Arrange the decor evenly to avoid water pooling.
  4. Chemical Balance Control – Add pH control components according to the substrate type.
  5. Maintenance Check – Regularly monitor the substrate and decor to identify any changes or contamination.

For more details on choosing substrate and how to maintain it, or about suitable decor for different species, you can visit our specialized pages.

Substrate and Decor Maintenance: Practical Tips

Substrate and decor require continuous care to maintain the health of the aquarium:

  • Regular Cleaning – Use a small brush to remove accumulated dirt.
  • Regular Water Changes – Reduces waste buildup on the substrate surface.
  • Chemical Monitoring – Test pH and nitrate levels regularly.
  • Replace Substrate When Needed – If you notice a change in color or odor, you may need to replace it.
  • Dealing with Excess Algae – Use algae removal tools or add plants that compete with algae.

Conclusion

Choosing the right substrate and decor is not just an aesthetic step; it is the foundation for building a healthy and balanced environment for fish and plants. By following these guidelines, you will be able to create an aquarium that overflows with beauty and ensures the well-being of your aquatic animals.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

  • What is the best type of substrate for bottom-dwelling species? White mud or dark mud mixed with gravel is preferred to provide a soft and suitable surface for bottom-dwelling species.
  • How do I choose the right decor for small species? It is preferable to choose small-sized pieces with ample hiding spaces, such as small rocks or driftwood pieces.
  • Can the same substrate be used for Japanese species? It is recommended to use fluorine-mixed substrate or substrate specifically for Japanese species to ensure pH balance and contain necessary elements.
  • How often do I need to clean the substrate? It is advisable to clean the substrate periodically every 4-6 weeks, or when you notice waste accumulation or a change in color.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best type of substrate for bottom-dwelling species?

White mud or dark mud mixed with gravel is preferred to provide a soft and suitable surface for bottom-dwelling species.

How do I choose the right decor for small species?

Choosing small-sized pieces with ample hiding spaces, such as small rocks or driftwood pieces.

Can the same substrate be used for Japanese species?

It is recommended to use fluorine-mixed substrate or substrate specifically for Japanese species to ensure pH balance and contain necessary elements.

How often do I need to clean the substrate?

It is advisable to clean the substrate periodically every 4-6 weeks, or when you notice waste accumulation or a change in color.

data.title: Comprehensive Guide to Filtration and Purification in Aquariums
data.excerpt: A comprehensive guide explaining the basics of filtration and purification in aquariums, with explanations of filter types, how to choose them, and effective maintenance to ensure clean and healthy water.
data.content:
One of the most important elements affecting the health of any aquarium is the filtration and purification system. The filter ensures the removal of harmful substances, maintains the chemical balance of the water, and provides a stable environment for aquatic life. In this article, we will review together what a filter is, the different types, how to choose the most suitable one for your tank, in addition to a maintenance guide that helps you maintain the filter's performance in the long term.

What is a Filter?

Filter Definition

A filter is a device through which water passes through materials designed to remove impurities and waste, whether suspended particles, chemicals, or microorganisms. The filter contributes to improving water quality and reduces the need for large water changes.

Types of Filters

  • Mechanical – Uses materials like cloth or media to trap suspended particles.
  • Biological – Relies on microbes living on surfaces to break down organic matter.
  • Chemical – Uses carbon materials or chemical treatments to absorb ammonia and nitrates.
  • RO Filter (Reverse Osmosis) – Removes most ions and contaminants from water.
  • UV Filter – Uses ultraviolet light to kill germs and microbes.

Importance of Filtration in Aquariums

Filtration is not limited to removing impurities only; it plays a pivotal role in:

  • Maintaining a stable pH level.
  • Reducing the concentration of ammonia and nitrates.
  • Protecting the biological system from waste accumulation.
  • Improving water clarity.

Choosing the Right Filter

When choosing a filter, several factors must be considered to ensure its compatibility with the tank size and its needs:

  • Tank Size – The larger the tank, the higher the filter's flow rate needs to be.
  • Water Flow Rate – The flow rate should exceed 4–5 times the tank volume per hour.
  • Water Type – Local water may require an additional chemical filter.
  • Filter Maintenance – Choose a filter that is easy to clean and replace.

To help choose a filter, you can visit the Mechanical Filter or Biological Filter page on our website.

Filter Maintenance

Filter maintenance is the primary factor in maintaining its efficiency. Here are basic maintenance steps:

  1. Turn off the filter and drain the water.
  2. Clean the mechanical filter media with running water.
  3. Replace carbon or media materials according to the manufacturer's recommendations.
  4. Check the filter pressure to ensure proper flow.
  5. Restart the filter and ensure there are no leaks.

Adhering to a regular maintenance schedule (every 2–4 weeks) ensures the filter's continued performance.

Advanced Filtration Technologies

RO Filter

Used to precipitate harmful agents from water, it is preferred for tanks requiring high-purity water.

UV Filter

Combats germs and bacteria, and is an important addition to biological filtration.

Carbon Filter

Removes unwanted odors and chemicals, and is often used with mechanical filters.

Tips to Reduce Common Problems

  • Monitor filter pressure regularly.
  • Avoid overloading the tank with more than 80% of its water capacity.
  • Use filter media compatible with the filter type.
  • Replace filter media in a timely manner.

By following these tips, you will ensure that the filtration system remains effective and maintains water quality in your aquarium.

Conclusion

Filtration and purification are the fundamental pillars of any successful aquarium. Choosing the right filter, maintaining it regularly, and applying advanced filtration techniques ensure clean and healthy water. Your investment in a reliable filtration system is an investment in the sustainability of the aquatic environment within your tank.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between a mechanical and biological filter?

A mechanical filter removes suspended particles, while a biological filter removes organic matter using microbes.

How often should the filter be cleaned?

It is recommended to clean the mechanical filter every 2–4 weeks, while the carbon filter is replaced according to the manufacturer's recommendations.

Can a UV filter be used with a biological filter?

Yes, combining them is considered a powerful addition to reduce germs and improve water quality.

What is the importance of the filter's water flow rate?

The flow rate should exceed the tank volume by 4–5 times per hour to ensure excess waste removal.
