data.title: How to Deal with Summer Heat in Aquariums? Seasonal Tips for Home Aquarists
data.excerpt: Learn the best ways to deal with summer heat in aquariums, from cooling and ventilation to choosing the right equipment and maintaining fish health.
data.content:
Summer heat is one of the most significant challenges faced by aquarium owners, especially in regions with high ambient temperatures. Elevated water temperature negatively affects oxygen levels, the overall environment, and fish health. Therefore, it is essential to implement effective measures to regulate temperature and maintain a stable environment.

1. Understanding the Impact of Heat on Aquariums

Temperature is influenced not only by the external air temperature but also by internal factors such as light intensity, aquarium size, and fish species. When the temperature rises above 30 °C, oxygen in the water can decrease, causing health stress for fish. Thus, regular temperature monitoring is crucial.

2. Reducing Heat Sources Inside Aquariums

One of the most important steps is to minimize any heat sources within the aquarium. Avoid placing aquariums in direct sunlight or near heat sources like air conditioners or electronic devices. It is also preferable to position the aquarium in a cooled or shaded area, using special covers to prevent water heating.

Tools for Temperature Control

  • Air Fans: Placed near the aquarium to cool the surrounding air, thereby reducing water temperature.
  • Cooling Condensers: Installed on the cooling line of the filtration system to cool the water before it returns to the aquarium.
  • Air Cooling Condensers: Can be installed in the aquarium room to cool the ambient air.

3. Improving Ventilation and Increasing Oxygen

Good ventilation is essential for maintaining oxygen levels in the water. Use aerators or air pumps to increase airflow. It is also recommended to place your aquarium in a location that allows for natural air circulation.

Ventilation Tools

  • Air Pumps: Installed in your aquarium to circulate air across the water surface.
  • Air Fans: Placed in the room to cool the ambient air.
  • Air Cooling Condensers: Installed in the aquarium room.

4. Regular Water Changes

Periodic water changes help remove oils and pollutants that may accumulate as temperatures rise. It is advisable to change 10–15% of the water weekly, using water conditioners to reduce chlorine and harmful substances.

Temperature Considerations During Water Changes

  • Ensure the new water is at the same temperature as the tank water or slightly cooler to avoid thermal shock.
  • Use water conditioners that maintain pH and temperature balance.
  • Perform water changes in the early morning or evening to minimize interaction with high ambient temperatures.

5. Using a Mechanical Cooling System

In cases of extreme heat, you may need a mechanical cooling system. It is preferable to use cooling condensers specifically designed for aquatic systems, which are installed on the cooling line of the filtration system. These condensers reduce water temperature before it returns to the aquarium.

Cooling System Components

  • Cooling Condenser: Installed on the cooling line.
  • Cooling Fan: Mounted on the condenser to cool the air.
  • Water Pump: Maintains water flow through the condenser.

6. Continuous Temperature Monitoring

Ensure a thermometer is installed in the aquarium. A digital thermometer with temperature indicators is preferred, allowing for quick action when the temperature rises.

Temperature Monitoring Tools

  • Digital Thermometer: Accurately displays the water temperature.
  • LED Temperature Indicators: Visually show temperature levels.
  • Monitoring Apps: Connect to smart devices for remote monitoring.

7. Additional Tips for Maintaining Fish Health

  1. Avoid overfeeding fish during periods of high temperatures.
  2. Use aquarium lids to reduce water evaporation.
  3. Add aquatic plants that help improve water quality.
  4. Ensure filters are cleaned regularly to prevent pollutant buildup.
  5. Make sure aquariums are not exposed to sudden temperature fluctuations.

Conclusion

Managing summer heat in aquariums requires a combination of prevention, cooling, ventilation, and regular water changes. By using appropriate control tools and careful monitoring, you can ensure a stable and healthy environment for your fish, even during high temperatures.

Useful Internal Links

  • Temperature Management
  • Filtration and Purification
  • Water Treatment
  • Fish Food
  • Decor and Equipment
  • Ventilation and Oxygen
  • Testing and Monitoring

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the optimal temperature for aquariums in summer?

The optimal temperature ranges between 24 °C and 28 °C. If the temperature rises above 30 °C, additional cooling measures should be taken.

How can water temperature in the aquarium be reduced?

Use cooling condensers on the cooling line, place the aquarium in a cooled area, or add air fans for surrounding ventilation.

What is the importance of ventilation in aquariums?

Ventilation maintains oxygen levels in the water and reduces carbon dioxide buildup, ensuring fish health.

Can an air conditioner be used to cool the aquarium?

An air conditioner can help cool the ambient air but does not directly cool the water. It is preferable to use cooling condensers specifically designed for aquatic systems.

data.title: Treating Tap Water for Fish: Chlorine vs. Chloramine, and the Practical Difference
data.excerpt: Proper treatment depends on the type of disinfectant in your municipal water supply. Letting water sit in the sun works for one but not the other. A simple test can give you the answer for your specific source.
data.content:
The Bottom Line

Tap water is disinfected, and the disinfectant that protects us also kills fish gills and beneficial bacteria in the filter. Never add tap water to your aquarium before treating it – neither for regular water changes nor for rinsing filter media.

The correct treatment depends on one thing: Does your water supply use free chlorine or chloramine? Because the treatment differs, and the old-fashioned method works for one but absolutely not for the other.

Free ChlorineChloramine
Evaporates with aeration?Yes, within 24–48 hoursNo — it's stable and practically does not evaporate
Does a regular dechlorinator suffice?YesIt breaks the bond and leaves ammonia in the water
What is requiredA simple water conditionerA conditioner that states it neutralizes chloramine and ammonia

Honest Point: We Don't Know What Your Water Supply Uses

It's widely claimed in Arabic content that Iraqi water treatment plants have switched to chloramine. We haven't found a reliable source to confirm this for all governorates, and we won't state it as fact because the difference is practical, not theoretical: if you assume chloramine when you actually have free chlorine, you've spent money unnecessarily. If you assume the opposite, you've left ammonia in your tank.

The only sure way: Ask your local water authority, or – which is easier – test for ammonia immediately after a water change. If ammonia appears in clean, treated water, your supply is likely using chloramine, and your current conditioner isn't handling it.

This practical test gives you an answer about your specific source, instead of making a generalization about an entire country. Test strips and ammonia test kits are available at AQUAVO in the Testing & Monitoring section.

The "Leave it in the Sun" Method — When It Works and When It Doesn't

Leaving water exposed for a day or two does indeed dissipate free chlorine, and aeration speeds this up. However:

  • It does not work for chloramine, no matter how long you leave it.
  • It does not remove heavy metals that may leach from old pipes.
  • It's impractical during Iraqi summers: exposed water heats up and evaporates, leading you to add hot water to an already heat-stressed tank.

So, it's an old method that works in only one scenario, while a water conditioner is faster and more reliable in all cases.

Practical Usage

  1. Treat the water before adding it, not after. Adding tap water to the tank and then adding the conditioner means the fish and bacteria are exposed to chlorine, even if only for a few minutes.
  2. Dose based on the volume of water being added, not the total tank volume – unless the product instructions state otherwise.
  3. Bring the temperature of the new water close to the tank's temperature before adding it. Temperature shock is a stressor in itself.
  4. Rinse your filter media in tank water, never under the tap – chlorine kills beneficial bacteria, which is the most common reason for a stable tank crashing.

Water conditioners and dechlorinators are available at AQUAVO in the Water Treatment section.

Why This Matters More Than It Seems

Chlorine doesn't just harm fish; it devastates the biological filtration. The bacteria that convert ammonia live on the surfaces of the filter and substrate. Rinsing them with tap water effectively resets your tank to a 'new tank' state without you realizing it – then ammonia levels spike days later, even though nothing outwardly changed.

The full process is explained in the Biological Cycle, and if readings do spike, the immediate action for sudden ammonia spikes is detailed there. To calculate the amount of water needing treatment, use the Calculators.

data.title: Aquatic Plant Trimming and Propagation: Method by Type
data.excerpt: A plant left untrimmed shades itself and dies from the bottom. A table of methods for each type, and why leaving cuttings in water raises ammonia.
data.content:
Trimming is Not Just for Aesthetics — It Keeps Plants Alive

An aquatic plant left untrimmed shades itself: the upper leaves block light from the lower ones, causing the lower leaves to yellow and rot, then decompose and increase the load on the water. The result is a plant that "dies from the bottom" even though its top looks excellent.

Trimming has a second benefit: a trimmed plant grows bushier. Cutting the tip temporarily stops vertical growth and stimulates lateral branching, giving you a better shape and a healthier plant simultaneously.

Method by Plant Type

TypeExamplesPropagation and Trimming
StemElodea, HygrophilaCut the tip and plant it in the substrate — it becomes an independent plant
RhizomeAnubias, Java FernDivide the rhizomes with a clean knife, do not bury them, and tie them to wood or stone
RosetteAmazon SwordProduces side shoots; separate them after they have formed roots
RunnerVallisneriaSpreads runners under the substrate; separate the new plant after it has established
MossJava MossDivide the clump and attach it to a new surface

A note specifically on Java Fern: it produces small plantlets on the edges of older leaves. Do not remove them too early — wait until they have formed small roots before separating.

Practical Rules

  1. Clean, sharp scissors. Dull tools crush tissues instead of cutting them, causing the edges to rot.
  2. Remove cuttings immediately. Floating leaves decompose and raise ammonia. This is the most commonly forgotten step.
  3. Do not trim more than a third of the plant at once. Trimming is stressful, and overdoing it will halt growth.
  4. Do not trim a plant that is already melting — if it is transitioning from emersed growth, wait for new growth. Aquatic Plant Problems.
  5. Inspect after major trimming — cut tissues and leaked materials may temporarily cloud the water.

Trimming and Algae

An old, damaged leaf is fertile ground for algae: its growth is slow, so algae attach to it faster than it can resist. Removing damaged leaves is a preventative measure against algae, not just for aesthetics — Algae Guide.

After heavy trimming, nutrient consumption temporarily decreases because the plant mass has been reduced. This may lead to a surplus that feeds algae. Reduce fertilization for a week after any major trimming — Plant Fertilization.

Propagation Saves You Money

Most beginner plants propagate themselves without special equipment: a stem cutting that you plant becomes a full plant within weeks. This is the cheapest way to fill your aquarium, and also the most reliable, as the resulting plant is already adapted to your tank's water — unlike a new plant that requires a transition period.

Start with low-demand species — Low-Demand Plants — and get your lighting right before expanding: Lighting Guide. For attaching to wood and rock, AQUAVO offers threads, nets, and aquascape glue in the substrate and decor section.

data.title: How to Arrange Aquarium Rocks (Hardscape) to Create Great Visual Depth
data.excerpt: Rock arrangement is an art with rules! Learn Hardscape techniques to create stunning visual depth that makes your aquarium look three times larger.
data.content:
Introduction to Aquarium Rock Arrangement

Aquarium rock arrangement, known as hardscape, is an art that requires imagination and aesthetics. It is one of the most important elements in aquarium design, aiming to create a beautiful and interesting natural environment. In Iraq, where summer temperatures can reach 50 °C, fish keepers must choose suitable rocks that can withstand harsh conditions.

Choosing the Right Rocks

When selecting rocks, fish keepers in Iraq should consider several factors, including:

  • Rock type: Non-dissolving rocks, such as granite or sandstone, should be chosen.
  • Rock size: Rocks of an appropriate size for the aquarium should be selected.
  • Rock shape: Rocks with varied shapes should be chosen to achieve a three-dimensional effect.

Before introducing any rock to the aquarium, ensure it is chemically inert: place a few drops of vinegar on it. If it reacts and releases bubbles, it is calcareous and will raise hardness and alkalinity over time.

Aquarium Rock Arrangement Methods

There are several methods for arranging aquarium rocks, including:

  1. Gradual method: Rocks are arranged in a gradient extending from bottom to top.
  2. Circular method: Rocks are arranged in a circle around a central point.
  3. Branching method: Rocks are arranged in a branching pattern extending from a central point.

In each case, fish keepers should ensure that the rocks are evenly distributed in the aquarium to achieve a three-dimensional effect.

Golden tip from AQUAVO: Fish keepers in Iraq must ensure the aquarium has an effective water purification system to prevent the buildup of harmful chemicals, and treat tap water for chlorine before use.

Treating Rocks Before Arrangement

Before arranging the rocks, fish keepers in Iraq must treat them to prevent the spread of bacteria and fungi. Treatment materials such as chlorine or formaldehyde can be used. After treatment, the rocks must be washed thoroughly before being arranged in the aquarium.

Using Aquarium Rocks in Iraq

In Iraq, where there are issues with water and electricity supply, fish keepers must ensure that the aquarium is designed to withstand harsh conditions. Aquarium rocks can be used to achieve this, as they can help provide a stable environment for the fish.

By using aquarium rocks correctly, hobbyists in Iraq can create a stunning aquarium that adds beauty and elegance to the home. With AQUAVO offering product delivery services to 18 governorates in Iraq, all hobbyists can access the best products and services to design their dream aquarium.

If you want to apply these principles in a specific style, Iwagumi is the clearest school that relies solely on stones. For implementation on a lower budget, see Decor on a Limited Budget, and for full depth behind the glass, consider DIY 3D Backgrounds.

Composition Rules: Where to Place the Main Piece

Three simple rules explain why one arrangement looks better than another:

  • Do not place the main piece exactly in the center. The literal center divides the scene into two equal halves and looks static; shifting it off-center creates movement.
  • One focal point. Two pieces competing for attention cancel each other out—one leads, and the rest support.
  • Odd numbers. Three or five rocks look more natural than two or four, as even numbers tend towards symmetry, and symmetry looks artificial.

Apply these to the slope and depth explained above, and see a full application in Iwagumi.

data.title: Is a Heater Necessary for Ornamental Fish in Winter in Iraq?
data.excerpt: Iraq's winter is harsh on your fish! Is a heater truly necessary? Learn about ideal temperatures and when a heater becomes essential.
data.content:
The Importance of a Heater for Ornamental Fish in Iraq

In Iraq, where summer temperatures can reach 50 °C, a heater might seem unnecessary in winter. However, it can play a significant role in maintaining the health of ornamental fish, especially if the species requires a specific temperature.

Fish Species That Do Not Need a Heater in Winter

  • Coldwater fish species, such as guppies and neons.
  • Fish that can adapt to different temperatures, such as platies and kuhli loaches.

The Need for a Heater in Winter

In some cases, a heater may be necessary for ornamental fish during winter in Iraq, especially if:

  1. The water temperature drops below 15 °C.
  2. The fish species requires a specific temperature to remain healthy.
  3. There is a need to promote fish growth or stimulate breeding.
A golden tip from AQUAVO: Ornamental fish keepers in Iraq should consider the type of fish they wish to keep, the ideal water temperature for these fish, and ensure they have the necessary equipment to maintain that ideal temperature.

The Impact of a Heater on Ornamental Fish Health

Ornamental fish keepers in Iraq should understand that a heater can have a positive impact on their fish's health, especially if used correctly. However, they should also be aware that a heater can increase energy consumption, thus raising electricity costs.

How to Choose the Right Heater for Ornamental Fish

When choosing the right heater for ornamental fish, fish keepers should consider several factors, including:

  • Aquarium size.
  • Fish species.
  • Ideal water temperature.
  • Energy consumption.

A practical rule for selecting heater wattage is approximately 1 watt per liter in a moderately temperate room, increasing the wattage if the room is cold or the aquarium is near a window.

data.title: Electrical Safety Around the Aquarium: Drip Loops and Basic Rules
data.excerpt: Water and equipment running 24 hours a day. A drip loop is a free measure that prevents the most dangerous path, and one non-negotiable rule before putting your hand in the water.
data.content:
Water and Electricity in One Place

The aquarium combines water and electrical equipment running 24 hours a day: filter, heater, pump, lighting. This is completely safe under simple conditions — and a real risk without them, to both fish and humans.

The first and non-negotiable rule: disconnect the electricity from all devices before putting your hand in the water. No exceptions, no "just quickly," no "I'm just adjusting the decor." Most household electrocution accidents around aquariums start with the phrase "I'll be done in a minute."

The Drip Loop: Simplest and Most Important Measure

Let the cord of each device descend to below the level of the outlet and then rise back up to it, forming a U-shaped curve.

Without a Drip LoopWith a Drip Loop
Water dripping on the cord slides towards the outletWater collects at the bottom of the curve and drips onto the floor

This is a completely free measure, takes a second to set up, and prevents the most common dangerous path. Apply it to every cord without exception.

Operating Rules

  • Do not operate the heater outside of water, nor pull it out while it is running — thermal shock can crack the glass casing, and a crack inside the water is a double danger.
  • Turn off the heater before changing the water if the water level will drop below it, and turn it back on after refilling.
  • Do not run a filter dry — many pumps are cooled by the water passing through them.
  • Periodically inspect cords for cracks or wear, especially near water entry points.
  • Do not use a wet or exposed extension cord, and keep outlets above the aquarium level if possible.

Power Outages and Restorations

The sudden return of power can turn on all devices at once. Two practical points in Iraq:

  • A heater that remained on with a lowered water level during an outage may be partially exposed, then overheat and experience thermal shock when the water returns.
  • A filter that stopped for hours needs attention before restarting — stagnant media may have degraded. The full procedure is in Emergency Tools for Power Outages.

Signs of an Electrical Problem

  • A slight tingling sensation when touching the water — immediately shut off everything at the breaker, and unplug devices one by one to identify the source. Do not ignore mild tingling.
  • Fish congregating in one corner for no apparent reason with a healthy water test — a weak electrical leak is a possibility worth investigating.
  • A burning smell or abnormal heat from a device or outlet.
  • A breaker tripping when a specific device is turned on — do not reset it before identifying the cause.

Limitations of Our Advice

Home electrical wiring and protection specifications vary from house to house, and we will not describe electrical modifications for you to perform yourself. Our advice is limited to aquarium-related matters: a drip loop for every cord, disconnecting power before inserting your hand, periodic cord inspection, and consulting a qualified electrician for any doubts about the wiring itself. If you notice any tingling, this is not a fish issue — shut everything down and seek professional help.

data.title: Cleaning the Aquarium Without Killing Bacteria: What to Clean, When, and How
data.excerpt: A visually clean aquarium is not a biologically healthy one. A schedule of what to clean and when, four rules, and signs that you've cleaned too much.
data.content:
Incorrect Cleaning Kills More Than It Cleans

The most common beginner's disaster: emptying the entire aquarium, moving the fish to a container, and scrubbing everything until it shines — followed by the fish dying within days, even though the aquarium is "clean".

The reason is that a visually clean aquarium is not a biologically healthy aquarium. The bacteria that process ammonia live on surfaces: sponges, gravel, and decor. Washing them means destroying the processing system, returning the aquarium to the state of a new tank without you noticing. The biological cycle.

What to Clean and When

ItemFrequencyMethod
Gravel vacuuming + water changeWeeklySiphon, and new water treated to the same temperature
Inner glassWeekly or as neededMagnet or dedicated sponge, no soap
Filter mediaOnly when flow weakensLight rinse with removed tank water
Decor and driftwoodRarelyScrub with tank water, do not remove and wash completely
Outer glassAs neededSpray onto cloth, not onto the aquarium

Do not clean the filter in the same session as a large water change. Each of them slightly disrupts the balance, and combining them on the same day doubles the effect. Space them out by days.

The Four Rules

  1. No soap, detergents, or bleach. Absolutely none, not even "a very small amount and rinse well." Detergent residue is lethal.
  2. Use tank water to rinse media, not tap water. Chlorine kills the bacterial colony — treating tap water.
  3. Do not replace all media at once. Replace a portion and leave the rest for two weeks to allow the new media to colonize.
  4. Disconnect power before putting your hand in. Electrical safety around the aquarium.

Why Specifically the Siphon

Waste and leftover food accumulate between the gravel pieces, not on the surface. Sucking water from the top takes relatively clean water and leaves the source in place. The siphon sucks up water and waste together, performing two functions in one operation.

In planted tanks, reduce siphoning near the roots to avoid uprooting plants or sucking up the nutrient-rich substrate. Siphons and gravel vacuums are available at AQUAVO in the Maintenance and Cleaning section.

Signs You've Cleaned Too Much

  • Ammonia or nitrite spike one or two days after cleaning — reading the test.
  • Cloudy white haze after cleaning — bacterial bloom, and its treatment is not more cleaning. Diagnosing cloudiness.
  • Lethargic or gasping fish immediately after the session.

If this happens: stop cleaning, reduce feeding, increase aeration, and monitor. Emergency treatment for ammonia spikes.

Conclusion

The goal of cleaning is to remove the excess — extra food, waste, and accumulated nitrates — not to eliminate the microorganisms that run the aquarium. Less intervention and more regularity is better than a comprehensive cleaning campaign every two months. Details on water changes are in the water change guide.

Your Hygiene During Cleaning

All of the above concerns aquarium cleanliness. However, cleaning is the moment your hand touches the aquarium water the most, and it deserves a simple precaution in the opposite direction: cover any wounds on your hand before inserting it, wash your hands after finishing, and never siphon water with your mouth.

Details — and why it's important to tell your doctor if you have an aquarium if a skin infection doesn't improve — are in Aquarium Hygiene and Your Safety.

data.title: Angelfish: A Peaceful-Looking Cichlid
data.excerpt: Sold at the size of a coin, they grow up to 15 cm long and 20 cm tall. They are cichlids that become territorial when mature. Learn why tank height matters more than length for them.
data.content:
A Cichlid with a Peaceful Appearance

Angelfish are often sold as calm ornamental fish. The truth is, they are from the cichlid family — which explains any surprises a beginner might encounter later: territoriality upon reaching maturity, aggression during breeding, and chasing smaller fish.

They are magnificent fish but not strictly for beginners. The reason isn't their care difficulty, but rather what they transform into after a few months.

Size and Tank: The First Mistake

Reality
Size at PurchaseOften the size of a coin
Adult SizeReaches 15 cm in length, up to 20 cm in height with fins
What Matters in a TankHeight before length — their body is laterally compressed, and their fins are long vertically
Short TankUnsuitable, regardless of its volume
This is almost the only fish where tank height is a crucial factor. A wide but short tank forces adult angelfish into an unnatural posture, a consideration that doesn't apply to most other fish — see Choosing the Right Aquarium Tank.

Tank Mates

  • Do not keep them with very small fish. The classic Neon Tetra with Angelfish is a bad idea: adult angelfish eat anything that fits in their mouth, and Neons are exactly that size.
  • Do not keep them with fin nippers — some barb species constantly nip their long fins.
  • Angelfish with Angelfish: A group of juveniles will coexist, then upon reaching maturity, a pair will form and chase away the rest. This is natural behavior, not a defect, but it means the tank must accommodate the outcome.
  • Best option: Calm, medium-sized fish that are neither too small to be eaten nor fin-nippers.

General compatibility principles are in Fish Compatibility, and stocking limits are in How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Hold.

Water and Temperature

Angelfish are from South America and prefer relatively warm water with gentle flow. Practical points:

  • Gentle flow. Their long fins make swimming in strong currents strenuous — aim the filter outlet at the glass to break up the flow. Choosing a Filter.
  • Stable temperature is more important than an ideal number. Fluctuations are what invite disease.
  • Tank height means a taller water column and a relatively smaller surface area, so pay attention to ventilation. Dissolved Oxygen.
  • Ammonia and nitrite should be zero in any established tank. Reading Water Tests.

Long Fins: A Practical Weakness

The long fins of angelfish make them more susceptible to two things: tears from sharp decor or fin-nipping tank mates, and fin rot after any tear if the water quality is poor. Choose decor with smooth edges, and address water quality before resorting to medication for any fin damage — see Fin Rot Treatment and White Fuzzy Growth on Fish.

Limitations of What We Can Say

We won't give you a definitive compatibility chart with specific names: angelfish behavior varies between individuals and between juvenile and adult stages, and between spacious and cramped tanks. The honest rule is more accurate than any list: plan for the territorial adult fish, not the calm juvenile you bought — and most angelfish problems start from forgetting this.

data.title: Gourami: A Fish That Breathes Air, and What That Means Practically
data.excerpt: The labyrinth organ gives them a safety margin during power outages and summer heat — but it also means a completely sealed aquarium lid is dangerous for them.
data.content:
A Fish That Breathes Air

Gouramis belong to the Anabantoidei group, along with Bettas. Both possess a labyrinth organ: a structure within the head lined with blood vessels that allows them to draw oxygen directly from the air.

This explains their first behavior that worries beginners: their frequent trips to the surface to take a breath. This is completely normal and not a sign of suffocation.

This leads to an important practical requirement: do not seal the aquarium completely airtight. Gouramis must be able to reach the surface, and for some species, aerial respiration is mandatory, not optional. Leave an air gap between the water and the lid, and only cover the gaps — see Jumping and the Correct Lid.

Note: This ability means they tolerate low dissolved oxygen levels, but it absolutely does not mean they tolerate ammonia. No fish tolerates ammonia. Learn more about the mechanism in Dissolved Oxygen and Aeration and Aquariums Without Filters.

Why They Suit Iraqi Conditions

The ability to breathe air makes Gouramis less affected by situations that would kill other fish: power outages that stop the filter and pump, and summer heat that reduces dissolved oxygen.

However, this is a safety margin, not immunity. Filters remain essential for biological filtration — and ammonia will rise in the same way if the filter stops. See Emergency Aquarium Tools and Protecting Fish in the Iraqi Summer (50 Degrees).

Behavior: What Surprises Beginners

BehaviorExplanation
Frequent trips to the surfaceNormal breathing via the labyrinth organ — don't worry
Aggression between malesTerritorial; increases in cramped tanks or those lacking hiding places
Bubbles on the surfaceA bubble nest built by the male — normal reproductive behavior
Chasing a specific fishOften territorial or due to an unbalanced sex ratio
Long, thread-like finsSensory organs used to explore their surroundings — not a deformity

Learn how to distinguish males from females and adjust ratios in How to Sex Aquarium Fish.

Suitable Aquarium Setup

  • Calm surface. This is the most crucial point specifically for Gouramis: strong surface currents disturb fish that constantly ascend to breathe. Direct the filter outlet downwards or onto the glass. See Choosing the Right Filter.
  • Plants and floating surfaces provide a sense of security and reduce aggression.
  • Hiding places and broken lines of sight — decor that breaks up sightlines reduces territoriality more effectively than just increasing space.
  • Sufficient surface area — because the surface is not just for gas exchange but also for direct breathing.

Tank Mates

  • Peaceful, medium-sized fish that do not nip at long, thread-like fins.
  • Avoid fin-nippers and overly active fish that keep the surface agitated.
  • Males in a small tank are a recipe for constant chasing — either keep one male or a spacious tank with plenty of hiding places.
  • With Bettas: Both are territorial anabantoids, and keeping them together is risky. See Betta Compatible Tank Mates.

The stocking limit, as always, should be determined by testing, not guesswork — see How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Hold.

data.title: Importing Ornamental Fish to the Middle East: Where Do Store Fish Originate?
data.excerpt: Ever wondered where the fish in Iraqi stores come from? An exciting journey tracing the path of fish from global farms to your aquarium.
data.content:
Introduction

When choosing ornamental fish for homes in the Middle East, many people find themselves asking about the origin of these fish. In Iraq, where summer temperatures range between 40 and 50 °C, power outages are frequent, and the water supplied to homes is often chlorinated, selecting suitable fish becomes a real challenge.

Sources of Ornamental Fish

Ornamental fish come to the Middle East from various countries, but they can be divided into three main categories:

  • Locally Farmed Fish: These fish are raised in local farms, which reduces transportation costs and ensures the availability of certain species.
  • Fish Imported from Asia: Most ornamental fish come to the Middle East from countries like Indonesia and the Philippines, where they are raised in large quantities and marketed worldwide.
  • Fish Imported from Europe and America: Some types of ornamental fish are imported from countries like Germany and the United States, where they are raised in a more specialized manner and marketed to a specific audience.

Challenges of Importing Ornamental Fish

Importing ornamental fish to the Middle East faces several challenges, including:

  1. Difficult Transportation Conditions: Long-distance transport can stress fish and increase the risk of disease.
  2. Temperature Differences: High temperatures in the Middle East can affect fish health, especially if they are not properly prepared.
  3. Water Quality: The quality of tap water can affect fish health, especially if the water contains chlorine or other chemicals.
Regardless of the fish's origin, quarantine it in a separate tank for two weeks before introducing it to the main aquarium. This step alone prevents most disease transmissions to the rest of the fish.

Conclusion

In summary, ornamental fish are imported to the Middle East from various countries, but most of them come from Asia.

data.title: Quarantining New Fish: Why Weeks, Not Days
data.excerpt: Most diseases enter the aquarium with a seemingly healthy fish, because parasites have hidden stages. A simple quarantine tank, a reasonable duration, and practical steps if you don't have one.
data.content:
Most Diseases Enter Your Aquarium With a New Fish

A stable aquarium doesn't get sick out of nowhere. Parasites and pathogenic bacteria need a carrier, and the most common carrier is a new fish that appears completely healthy — because most diseases have a latency period after which they appear.

Quarantine is a simple separate tank where you place the new fish before introducing it to the main aquarium. Its cost is much lower than treating an entire aquarium, and the difference is that it protects your old fish, which are usually your most expensive and oldest.

Why Weeks, Not Days

Take white spot disease as an example. The parasite spends part of its cycle inside the fish's skin where it cannot be seen and medication cannot reach it, part inside a cyst on the gravel, and part swimming freely looking for a host. Therefore:

  • A fish that looks clean today might be carrying the hidden stage.
  • The quarantine period must cover at least one full cycle for the disease to appear if it is present.

The stages are explained in detail in White Spot.

The common duration is between two and four weeks. We haven't found a single definitive source, so consider it a range: two weeks is a reasonable minimum, and four is safer — especially if your main aquarium contains expensive or old fish.

The Quarantine Tank: Simpler Than You Imagine

ItemRequiredWhy
AquariumSmall, no gravelA bare bottom is easier to clean and doesn't hide parasite stages
FilterSponge filterGentle, and you can run it in your main aquarium beforehand to colonize it with bacteria
HeaterYesStable temperature is crucial for a stressed fish
Hiding placeTube or potReduces stress, and stress itself opens the door to disease
LightingDimCalmer for the new fish

The most important practical detail: run the sponge filter inside your main aquarium for weeks before you need it. This way, it will be colonized with bacteria and ready immediately, and you won't have to set up a quarantine tank from scratch when needed. For small aquariums and breeder boxes, see the isolation and breeding section at AQUAVO.

The Procedure Step-by-Step

  1. Do not pour the store water into your aquarium. This is the most important and easiest step. Transfer the fish with a net or a clean cup, and leave the bag water out.
  2. Acclimate the fish gradually to the temperature and chemistry of the quarantine tank: float the bag to equalize the temperature, then add a little of the tank water to the bag in portions before transferring.
  3. Observe daily: white spots, torn fins, rapid breathing, rubbing against surfaces, refusal to eat.
  4. Do not treat preventatively without illness. Treating without cause stresses the fish and breeds resistance. Quarantine is for observation first.
  5. If a disease appears, treat it inside the quarantine tank — this is its second benefit: you treat one fish in a small tank instead of a whole aquarium.
  6. Transfer it to the main aquarium after the period has passed without symptoms.

And If You Don't Have a Quarantine Tank?

The minimum acceptable: do not transfer store water at all, introduce the new fish in small numbers at once instead of successive batches, and monitor the aquarium closely for two weeks, and test for ammonia and nitrite, as any additional fish immediately increases the bioload.

Note that adding new fish increases the load on the filtration — if your aquarium is already at the limit of its capacity, the addition alone can cause an ammonia spike without any disease. See How Many Fish Your Aquarium Can Handle and the Biological Cycle.

The need for quarantine begins even before the store: most ornamental fish go through a long chain of transport before they arrive — Where Do Store Fish Come From. This is why who you buy from matters, especially with online sales — Fake Stores.

Quarantine Does Not Compensate for a Bad Choice

Quarantine catches what appears within weeks, but it doesn't fix a fish that was already exhausted when you bought it. The cheapest treatment is a fish you didn't buy.

  • Look at the whole system, not just the fish: the store tank and its neighbors say more about it than it does itself.
  • Ask to see it eat before you pay.
  • And if you buy it, quarantine is still mandatory — a good choice reduces the probability, it doesn't eliminate it.

And what to look for exactly: Choosing a Healthy Fish Before Purchase.

data.title: Aquarium Without a Filter: Which Fish Can Actually Tolerate It, and Under What Conditions?
data.excerpt: No fish can live without a filter and without oxygen. This guide distinguishes between the device and biological filtration, explaining which fish can actually tolerate low oxygen and under what conditions—and why goldfish and neons are the worst choices.
data.content:
The Short Answer

No fish can live "without a filter and without oxygen." What exists is something else entirely: fish that can tolerate low dissolved oxygen in the water because they breathe atmospheric air directly, and aquariums that run without a filter device because the biological filtration has moved elsewhere—not because it has disappeared.

This difference is the whole story. And the two most common answers to this question—goldfish and neon tetras—are precisely the worst choices you could make.

Three Things People Confuse

The PhraseIts Real Meaning
"Without a filter"Without a device. Biological filtration is bacteria that live on surfaces—gravel, decor, wood, plant leaves—and work whether you have a filter or not.
"Without oxygen"Without an air pump. Gas exchange happens at the water's surface, and surface movement accelerates it.
"Without maintenance"Completely wrong. An aquarium without a filter requires more water changes, not less. The filter's job isn't eliminated; it's transferred to you.

If you want to understand why bacteria are the foundation, not the device, read The Biological Cycle in an Aquarium first. Without it, the rest of this article will be of no use to you.

Fish That Actually Tolerate Low Oxygen

The Anabantoidei suborder has a respiratory organ called the labyrinth organ—a structure lined with blood vessels inside the head that allows them to draw oxygen directly from the atmospheric air. This is why you see them come to the surface to take a breath. Studies link this organ to their ability to survive in oxygen-poor waters.

  • Betta (Betta splendens)—It breathes atmospheric air optionally, meaning it benefits from both: gills and surface air.
  • Blue Gourami (Trichopodus trichopterus)—Its aerial respiration is mandatory, meaning it must reach the surface. Do not cover the aquarium tightly for it.
Note the important difference: These fish tolerate low oxygen. They do not tolerate ammonia. No fish on earth tolerates ammonia.

Why Goldfish and Neons Are Wrong

The FishThe Problem
GoldfishThey produce far more waste than any fish of the same size, and their bodies are full, so they eat and excrete more. They require stronger filtration and a larger water volume, not less. The myth of the "goldfish in a bowl" worked in the past because they changed the water every day.
Neon TetraThey require a fully mature and stable aquarium, and ammonia and nitrite must be zero—even a short spike harms them. They are sensitive to fluctuations in pH and hardness. They are among the most sensitive fish to instability, not the least.

When an Aquarium Without a Filter Device Works

It works, under conditions. All of them reduce the load on the water or increase its treatment capacity:

  1. A large water volume relative to the number of fish. More water dilutes ammonia and stabilizes temperature.
  2. A very small number of fish. This is the most important condition and the one most often broken.
  3. Many surfaces for bacteria. Gravel, driftwood, rock, porous decor—every surface hosts a part of the biological filtration.
  4. Live plants if possible. They consume nitrates, provide hiding places for fish, and help stabilize the aquarium.
  5. Surface movement. Even without a pump, an exposed, non-stagnant surface is much better than a closed, still surface. And in the hot Iraqi summer, warmer water dissolves less oxygen, making the surface even more important.
  6. Frequent, small water changes. This is the true replacement for the filter.

The Deciding Number, Not Opinion

We will not give you a "liters per fish" ratio because it's not precise: it changes with size, plants, temperature, and amount of food. The only things that determine if your filterless aquarium is successful are two readings:

  • Ammonia—must be zero.
  • Nitrite—must be zero.

Test them at least weekly. Any number above zero means the number of fish exceeds the aquarium's capacity, and the solution is an immediate water change and reduced feeding. Test strips and ammonia/nitrite test kits are available at AQUAVO. If the reading is indeed high, see Emergency Treatment for Ammonia Spikes.

What If the Power Goes Out?

This is a different question than "aquarium without a filter," and more urgent in Iraq. A cycled aquarium with a running filter doesn't collapse in seconds: the real danger is that the bacteria inside the filter start to die when water and oxygen stop flowing over them, so when you restart the filter after a long time, you are effectively pumping foul water into the aquarium.

The practical rule: for short outages, leave the filter in place. For long outages, rinse the filter media with aquarium water before restarting it, reduce feeding, and monitor ammonia. Details and tools are in Emergency Tools for Power Outages.

Conclusion

If you want an aquarium that can withstand Iraqi power outage conditions, the honest answer is not "choose a fish that lives without a filter." The answer is: Betta or Gourami, in small numbers, in a relatively large tank, with plenty of surfaces for bacteria, regular water changes, and weekly ammonia and nitrite testing. To accurately calculate your tank size, use the calculators, and for specific details on Betta keeping, read The Truth About Betta Fish and Bowls.

data.title: Air Toxins: How Insect Sprays Can Kill Your Aquarium in Hours
data.excerpt: The air pump draws room air and pumps it directly into the water. This explains sudden mass die-offs with a perfectly normal water test—and prevention is simpler than you think.
data.content:
Your Aquarium Breathes Room Air

Hobbyists focus on water quality and forget that the aquarium is open to the room in two ways: the water surface and the air pump. The pump specifically draws room air and pumps it directly into the water—meaning anything volatile in the room enters the tank via the fastest possible route.

This explains cases of "the tank was excellent and suddenly all the fish died" without any change in the test results. The water was indeed fine—the problem entered through the air.

Most Common Sources in Iraqi Homes

SourceDanger LevelAction
Insecticide SprayHighest—Originally designed to kill invertebratesTurn off the air pump, cover the aquarium, and spray in another room
Incense, Air Fresheners, and SpraysMedium to High with frequent useGood ventilation, stay away from the aquarium room
Cigarette SmokeCumulativeDo not smoke in the aquarium room
Paints, Solvents, and ThinnersHigh during painting and dryingMove the aquarium or completely seal off the room
Cleaners and Bleach with FumesMediumDo not clean the aquarium glass with any cleaner
Hand Cream and Alcohol-Based SanitizerDirectly via handsWash your hands with water only before putting them in the tank

The Most Dangerous Situation: Spraying Pesticides

Insecticides are designed to kill arthropods, and shrimp and snails are aquatic arthropods and mollusks—making them ideal targets. Fish are also affected, and quickly.

If spraying is unavoidable:

  1. Turn off the air pump well before spraying—this is the most crucial step, as it prevents direct pumping.
  2. Cover the aquarium with a lid or plastic to reduce surface contact.
  3. Turn off the filter with an exposed outlet if it vigorously agitates the surface, for a short period only.
  4. Ventilate the room well after spraying before restarting equipment.
  5. Do not keep equipment off for too long. One or two hours is acceptable; extended periods create an oxygen problem larger than the original issue—see Dissolved Oxygen and Aeration.

Invertebrates are always the most sensitive and the first to be affected: see Aquarium Shrimp and Snails Guide.

Hands: The Forgotten Source

Soap, hand cream, and alcohol-based sanitizers enter the water directly with your hands. The rule: wash your hands with water only before putting them in, or use tools instead of your hands. After using alcohol-based sanitizer, wait until it is completely dry.

How to Know if Air is the Cause

The distinguishing sign: sudden, widespread symptoms with a normal water test. If ammonia and nitrite are zero, and the temperature is stable, yet fish are gasping or dying within hours, consider what happened in the room over the past day, not what happened in the water.

  • Test first to rule out water issues—see Reading Your Water Test.
  • Review other possibilities—see Fish Disease Symptoms and Diagnosis Guide.
  • The emergency procedure is the same: a relatively large water change with treated water at the same temperature, and activated carbon in the filter to absorb what can be absorbed, along with strong aeration.

Prevention

  • Do not spray anything in the aquarium room, even if it's "far away" from the tank.
  • Place the air pump where the air is clean, and do not place it near sources of fumes.
  • Partially cover the aquarium—this reduces contact and also reduces evaporation.
  • Warn household members: this is a risk that no one knows about unless explicitly told.

data.title: Reading Aquarium Water Tests: What Each Number Means
data.excerpt: Two numbers must always be zero, and one is read by trend, not value. And why an ammonia reading alone, without pH and temperature, can completely mislead you.
data.content:
Five Numbers, Each Telling You Something Different

Testing is not a monthly ritual to do and forget. Each number answers a different question, and most importantly, two of them must always be zero, with no discussion.

MeasurementAnswersRequired ReadingIf Deviates
AmmoniaIs the biological filtration working?ZeroEmergency — Immediate water change
NitriteIs the second stage working?ZeroEmergency — Fish are suffocating
NitrateIs the water change schedule sufficient?Stable between changesIncrease changes or reduce bioload
pHHow toxic is the existing ammonia?Stable rather than a specific numberInvestigate the cause of fluctuation
KHIs the pH protected from crashing?Sufficient to stabilizeCheck hardness

Ammonia: The Number Alone Isn't Enough

This is the point that completely changes how you read your tests. Ammonia exists in two forms: a toxic form and a much less toxic form, and the ratio between them is determined by pH and temperature.

This means the same ammonia reading on the test kit can be almost tolerable in a cold, acidic tank, and an emergency in a warm, alkaline tank. So never read ammonia alone — read it with pH and temperature. The full chart is in The Nitrogen Cycle Explained.

And if ammonia reads above zero, the immediate action is in Emergency Treatment for Ammonia Spikes.

Nitrite: Suffocation in Clear Water

Nitrite prevents blood from carrying oxygen. The fish will gasp and stay at the surface even though the water is clear and aeration is working — this deceives many, leading them to look for a non-existent aeration problem. Any nitrite reading above zero should be treated as an emergency.

Nitrate: Read the Trend, Not the Number

Nitrate is the end product of the cycle, and the filter doesn't remove it — water changes do. We won't give you a numerical ceiling because the commonly cited numbers lack a reliable primary source, but the practical rule is clearer than any number:

  • Stable between changes = Your schedule is adequate.
  • Climbing week after week = Output is less than production. Increase water changes or reduce feeding and fish count.

Implementation is in the Water Change Guide, and stocking limits are in How Many Fish Your Aquarium Can Handle.

When to Test

  • New Tank: Every other day until readings stabilize — this is how you know where you are in the cycling process.
  • Established Tank: Weekly before a water change, as this is the peak of the weekly cycle.
  • After Any Change: New fish, medication, filter cleaning, a long power outage, or a heatwave.
  • For Any Strange Behavior before assuming illness — most sudden "illnesses" are water poisoning.

Mistakes That Render Testing Meaningless

  • Testing immediately after a water change. You'll be reading the new water, not your tank. Test beforehand.
  • Expired test strips or strips stored in heat — and the Iraqi summer is harsh on reagents. Store them in a cool, dry place.
  • Reading colors under yellow lighting — read in daylight.
  • Not keeping records. A single reading tells you the status; a series of readings tells you the trend, which is the most important.

9-in-1 test strips and liquid ammonia and nitrite test kits are available at AQUAVO in the Testing & Monitoring section.

And if your tap water readings are difficult to adjust, the next question is the source of the water itself — RO Water vs. Tap Water. And note that activated carbon removes substances from the water and affects what you read, so know when it's in the filter and when to remove it.

How Often to Actually Test

Daily testing isn't necessary in a stable tank, and random testing every few months reveals nothing in time. Frequency follows the tank's condition, not the calendar:

ConditionReasonable FrequencyMost Important
New cycling tankDaily or every other dayAmmonia and Nitrite
After adding fishEvery other day for a weekAmmonia
Stable tankOnce a week or every two weeksNitrate indicates change sufficiency
When any symptom appearsImmediately and before any medicationAll

A single reading is less useful than a trend: one number doesn't tell you if the situation is improving or worsening. Simply record the readings and compare them to the previous week — this reveals decline before it becomes a crisis.

data.title: Using Activated Carbon in the Aquarium: When to Add and When to Remove?
data.excerpt: Activated carbon is a double-edged sword! Learn when to add it to your filter and when to remove it immediately to avoid harm to your fish.
data.content:
Introduction

The aquarium is one of the most beautiful and stunning decorations in Iraqi homes, but it requires special care to ensure the health and well-being of the fish. One of the essential components in an aquarium's filtration system is activated carbon, which plays an important role in removing impurities and unpleasant odors. In this article, we will discuss the use of activated carbon in the aquarium, when to add it, and when to remove it.

What is Activated Carbon?

Activated carbon is a type of charcoal that has been chemically treated to increase its surface area, allowing it to absorb pollutants and unpleasant odors. Activated carbon is used in many applications, including water filtration and air drying.

How Does Activated Carbon Work in an Aquarium?

When activated carbon is added to an aquarium's filtration system, it absorbs pollutants and unpleasant odors from the water, helping to maintain water quality and health. Activated carbon can absorb:

  • Ammonia and nitrite, which can be harmful to fish
  • Unpleasant odors, which can affect water quality
  • Organic pollutants, which can affect fish health

When Should Activated Carbon Be Added to the Aquarium?

Activated carbon should be added to the aquarium in the following situations:

  1. When ammonia or nitrite levels are high
  2. When unpleasant odors are present in the water
  3. After a water change of 25% or more
  4. When pollutants or unpleasant odors appear in the water

A Golden Tip from AQUAVO

We recommend using activated carbon from trusted brands, such as the activated carbon available at AQUAVO. Additionally, you should follow the manufacturer's instructions to ensure effective use of activated carbon.

When Should Activated Carbon Be Removed from the Aquarium?

Activated carbon should be removed from the aquarium in the following situations:

  1. When ammonia or nitrite levels have decreased to safe levels
  2. When unpleasant odors have disappeared from the water
  3. After the activated carbon has been completely consumed

Using Activated Carbon Under Iraqi Conditions

In Iraq, temperatures can be very high in the summer, increasing the risk of water contamination. Additionally, power outages can cause the filtration system to stop, increasing the risk of water contamination. In these situations, activated carbon can play an important role in maintaining water quality and health.

Activated carbon removes chlorine, medication residues, and odors, but it does not treat ammonia and loses its effectiveness within weeks, requiring periodic replacement. Activated carbon can absorb excess chlorine, contributing to the health of the fish.

Conclusion

Activated carbon is an essential component of an aquarium's filtration system and can play an important role in maintaining water quality and health. Activated carbon should be added to the aquarium when ammonia or nitrite levels are high, or when unpleasant odors are present in the water. Activated carbon should be removed from the aquarium when ammonia or nitrite levels have decreased to safe levels, or when unpleasant odors have disappeared from the water.

data.title: Loaches (Clown and Kuhli): Before You Buy
data.excerpt: A fish sold finger-sized that grows to many times its size and lives for years. Being scaleless changes the medication protocol for your entire tank.
data.content:
A Fish Sold Finger-Sized That Grows to Forearm Length

Loaches are a beloved bottom-dwelling family, with the most common species in the market being the Clown Loach and the Kuhli Loach. The difference between them isn't a minor detail—it's the difference between a fish suitable for a small tank and one that shouldn't be introduced at all.

Clown LoachKuhli Loach
Adult SizeVery Large—many times the size soldSmall and slender, resembling a worm
Expected LifespanVery long—a commitment of yearsRelatively shorter
Suitable TankLarge tanks only, not a beginner optionSuitable for moderate-sized tanks
BehaviorSocial, requires a groupSocial and hides during the day
The most common mistake: buying a small clown loach for a small tank, assuming it's a quiet bottom dweller. It is indeed quiet, but it grows large and lives a long time. Buy based on adult size, not shelf size—and calculate the load based on how many fish your tank can support.

Scaleless: The Most Important Point Before Any Medication

Loaches are described as scaleless or having very fine scales, which makes their skin more exposed to dissolved substances in the water. Practically, this means medications and salt require extra caution with them.

  • Full dosage is not a safe assumption. Many medication instructions include a special note for scaleless fish. Read the instructions before treating a tank with loaches.
  • Salt is a truly controversial matter, and sources differ on it. This is presented as is in the Aquarium Salt Guide rather than being definitively settled without evidence.
  • Absolutely no human medications—see Dangers of Human Medicine for Fish.
  • Loaches clearly show white spot disease and are considered sensitive species—refer to White Spot Disease.

The Substrate Isn't Just Decorative

Loaches search for food using sensitive barbels that they run over the substrate. Coarse or sharp gravel will injure these barbels over time, causing them to erode and become inflamed.

  1. Soft substrate—sand or fine, rounded gravel. This is the same requirement as for Corydoras. Refer to substrate options in Soil and Substrate Secrets.
  2. Real hiding places. Loaches are nocturnal and need caves and driftwood—ensure what you add is safe by Testing Aquarium Rocks and Wood.
  3. A group, not an individual. A solitary loach will constantly hide and become inactive—see Schooling Fish: Minimum Numbers.

Loaches and Snails: Expect Less Than You're Told

Loaches are often recommended as a solution for snail overpopulation, and this is only partially true. Some loach species do eat snails, but this treats the symptom, not the cause. A population explosion of snails is fundamentally an indicator of overfeeding. If the excess food remains, the problem will return.

Worse yet: introducing a large, long-lived fish to solve a temporary problem creates a permanent commitment. Full details in Snail Overpopulation: The Real Cause and How to Control It, and adjust feeding in the Fish Feeding Guide.

Before You Buy: Three Questions

  • Does my tank accommodate the adult size, not the size sold?
  • Is my substrate soft enough for their barbels?
  • Am I prepared to adjust the medication protocol because the tank now contains a scaleless fish?

If the answer to any of these is no, it's best to postpone the purchase. Always start new additions with Quarantine, as loaches usually arrive stressed and may carry parasites without visible symptoms.

Introduction to the World of Aquascaping

Aquascaping is the art of designing a beautiful aquarium by combining natural elements like rocks, plants, and water to create a breathtaking landscape that resembles a living work of art. Choosing Rocks

To create an Iwagumi aquascape, rocks must be chosen carefully. Rocks should be compatible with each other in shape and color, and they must be strong enough to withstand water pressure. Various types of rocks can be used, such as basalt rocks or sandstone rocks. Rocks must be thoroughly cleaned before being placed in the aquarium to avoid any contamination.

Arranging Rocks

After selecting the rocks, they should be arranged freely in the aquarium. The rocks should be arranged in a way that creates movement and harmony in the design. Rules such as the rule of thirds or the rule of balance can be used to create a harmonious landscape. Sufficient space should be left between the rocks to allow fish and plants to move freely.

Choose fish based on your actual aquarium water parameters (pH and GH), as water characteristics vary between cities and supply sources.

data.title: 5 Ornamental Fish That Don't Die Quickly (Toughest Fish for Beginners)
data.excerpt: A list of hardy fish species that can tolerate beginner mistakes and unstable water conditions.
data.content:
Fish That Don't Die Easily — The Smart Choice for Beginners

Instead of crying over expensive fish that died due to a simple mistake, start with fish that hobbyists call "tanks" — hardy fish that tolerate beginner mistakes and give you a chance to learn!

1. Zebra Danio — The Absolute Toughest 🏆

  • Why: Tolerates temperatures from 18° to 28°C, pH from 6 to 8, and even sudden changes.
  • Size: Only 4-5 cm.
  • Behavior: Peaceful and active, swim in schools (buy 6+ to see them at their best).
  • Price: Very cheap and available everywhere.

2. Platy — Cheerful and Easy Colors 🌈

  • Why: Tolerates various water conditions and rarely gets sick.
  • Size: 5-6 cm.
  • Bonus: Livebearer fish — you'll be surprised by colorful fry every month!
  • Compatibility: Completely peaceful — lives with everyone.

3. Molly — The Versatile 🐟

  • Why: Adapts to freshwater and brackish water! Exceptional flexibility.
  • Types: Black Molly, Gold Molly, Balloon Molly, Dalmatian Molly.
  • Breeding: Easy to breed — a fun project for beginners.

4. Swordtail — The Elegant Fighter ⚔️

  • Why: Hardy and beautiful — the male has a distinctive sword-like tail.
  • Warning: Males sometimes compete — keep one male with 2-3 females.

5. Corydoras — The Handsome Bottom Cleaners 🧹

  • Why: Clean the aquarium bottom of leftover food, calm and peaceful.
  • Note: Buy 4+ because they are social and get stressed alone.
  • Size: 3-7 cm depending on the species.

Golden Tip from AQUAVO

Start with 6 Zebra Danios + 4 Platies + 4 Corydoras in a 60 L aquarium. This ideal mix gives you activity at all levels of the tank: Zebra Danios at the surface, Platies in the middle, and Corydoras at the bottom.

If you choose schooling fish from this list, the next step is selecting the species and quantity — Which Schooling Fish to Choose. If you choose livebearers like Platies or Mollies, expect fry without planning — Livebearers and Managing Fry Numbers.

data.title: Puffy or Floating Fish: Dropsy or Another Cause?
data.excerpt: Protruding scales resembling a pinecone are a strong sign of systemic fluid buildup. However, floating with a smooth body is not automatically a swim bladder diagnosis—it has multiple causes starting with water parameters.
data.content:
Puffy or Floating Fish: Two Entirely Different Conditions

These two conditions are often confused, and the difference between them is the difference between a simple digestive issue and a frequently fatal condition. There is one visual difference that clearly separates dropsy from other issues:

DropsyFloating or Buoyancy Problem
Body ShapeScales protruding like a pinecone when viewed from aboveSmooth body with normal contour
PresentationAbdominal swelling and general edemaFloating, sinking, or listing to one side
NatureA symptom of systemic fluid accumulation in tissuesA symptom with multiple causes—not a diagnosis in itself
PrognosisPoor—especially after scales protrudeDepends on the cause
Practical Check: Look at the fish from above, not from the side. Protruding scales are only visible from this angle. Protruding scales = Dropsy. A smooth body with a buoyancy issue means the condition is not dropsy—and doesn't mean the cause is known.

A Buoyancy Problem Is Not Automatically a "Swim Bladder Disease" Diagnosis

The most common mistake regarding this issue is labeling any buoyancy disorder as "swim bladder disease" and immediately moving to treatment. Floating or listing is a sign, and it has more than one potential cause, each requiring a completely different treatment:

  • Digestive tract fullness or air swallowing with floating food—the most common and simplest cause.
  • Poor water quality—a neglected and recurring cause that must be ruled out before anything else.
  • Internal infection that may affect the swim bladder itself or put pressure on it.
  • Pressure from an enlarged organ or a mass within the abdominal cavity.
  • Congenital deformity or injury—usually permanent.
  • Early stage of a systemic condition that may later develop into protruding scales.

Therefore, the rule is: check the water first, monitor the progression, and do not assume the cause is a simple mechanical issue just because the fish is floating. To differentiate from other conditions, refer to the Symptom Diagnosis Guide.

First Steps—In Order

  1. Check the water before any action. Ammonia, nitrite, and nitrate—Reading Your Test Kit, and Nitrite Spikes in Aquariums.
  2. Withhold food for a day or two if the fish is adult and otherwise healthy. This is a common supportive measure in the hobby and may help if the cause is digestive—but it is not a guaranteed cure and is not suitable for every situation.
  3. Soak pellets before feeding, or switch to sinking food—this reduces swallowed air at the surface.
  4. Review the overall amount of food—Fish Feeding Guide.
When withholding food is not advisable: with fry and juveniles, as their nutritional needs are continuous and their reserves are low; with small, fast-metabolism species; and with emaciated fish or those already not eating. If the fish is not eating on its own, the problem is not fullness, and fasting will not help.

If the problem persists for weeks without improvement, it may be a permanent injury or deformity, and some fish can live with it in a calm, low-flow tank.

Dropsy: Be Honest With Yourself

Dropsy is not a disease in itself but a symptom: systemic fluid accumulation in tissues and the abdominal cavity causes the scales to protrude outwards. It results from a fluid regulation imbalance, and its underlying causes include internal bacterial infections or organ failure. Therefore, there is no single "dropsy cure" that always addresses the root cause.

  • Protruding scales are a strong sign that the condition is systemic, not localized or digestive.
  • The prognosis is poor once scales are clearly protruding, even with treatment. We state this frankly because promising a cure here would be dishonest.
  • Isolate the fish immediately—for its comfort and to protect the others if the cause is infectious. Quarantine Guide.
  • Improve the water quality: this is the most you can practically do.
  • Do not treat by guesswork. Never use human medications—Dangers of Human Medicine for Fish.
We will not provide antibiotic dosages: antibiotic availability and regulations vary, and systemic treatment without accurate diagnosis does more harm than good. If you have access to a veterinarian specializing in fish, they are the correct resource.

What Usually Precedes Both Conditions

Both conditions often appear after a period of stress on the fish, not suddenly out of nowhere:

  • Deteriorated water quality over a long period—Ammonia Spike Emergency Treatment.
  • Chronic overfeeding.
  • Overstocking and constant stress—How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Handle.
  • Temperature fluctuations—Protecting Fish in the Iraqi Summer Heat (50°C).

Round-bodied species like fancy goldfish and bettas are more prone to buoyancy problems due to the shape of their abdominal cavity.

data.title: Setting Up Your First Aquarium: The Correct Order Step-by-Step
data.excerpt: Most people who lose their fish in the first month didn't buy poor equipment; they set it up incorrectly. Seven stages in order, and where the cycling stage, which everyone skips, fits in.
data.content:
Setup Matters More Than Equipment

Most people who lose their fish in the first month didn't buy poor equipment — they bought good equipment and set it up incorrectly. The most common mistake in the hobby: buying fish on the same day you buy the aquarium.

A new aquarium has clean water without bacteria. Bacteria are what convert toxic ammonia into less harmful substances, and building them up takes weeks, not hours. Adding a fish before this means letting it swim in its own poison. The mechanism is explained in the biological cycle.

The Correct Setup

StageWhat to DoDuration
1. SelectionA larger tank than you think, and a location away from direct sunlightBefore purchase
2. InstallationLevel and sturdy surface, rinse substrate with water only, install filter and heater1 day
3. FillingWater treated with a dechlorinator, pour it onto a plate to avoid disturbing the substrate1 day
4. OperationRun the filter and heater for 24 hours before anything else1 day
5. CyclingAmmonia source + patience + regular testingWeeks
6. First FishVery few, after ammonia and nitrite reach zeroAfter cycling
7. ExpansionSmall batches spaced weeks apartMonths

First Stage Decisions

  • Size: A larger tank is easier, not harder — a larger water volume resists sudden changes in temperature and chemistry. Choosing the Tank.
  • Location: Away from direct sunlight and windows (algae and heat), and on a surface that can bear the weight — one liter weighs approximately one kilogram, so a 100L tank exceeds 100kg with substrate.
  • Filter: Choose based on size, not price. Choosing a Filter.
  • Heater: And a separate thermometer. Heater Guide.
  • Do not buy fish yet. This is the most important point on the list.

Cycling: The Stage Everyone Skips

Cycling is the process of establishing the beneficial bacteria colony inside the filter. It needs an ammonia source to feed on, and time. You know it's complete when ammonia and nitrite both reach zero, and nitrates appear.

  • Test every two days — Reading Water Tests.
  • Do not perform large water changes during cycling; it slows the process.
  • Do not clean the filter at all during this stage.
  • The brown algae that appear in the first few weeks are normal and will disappear on their own — Algae Guide.

Your First Fish

Start with a much smaller number than the tank's final capacity, and choose hardy species — Hardy Fish for Beginners. Acclimate them properly when transferring: Acclimating New Fish. If you are choosing schooling species, calculate the full school size from the beginning: Schooling Fish.

Then add gradually in batches, because each addition increases the load before the bacteria can catch up — How Many Fish Can Your Tank Hold.

Routine After Stabilization

  • Daily: One feeding that finishes within two minutes, and a check of temperature and behavior. Feeding Guide.
  • Weekly: Testing, a partial water change, and gravel vacuuming. Water Changes.
  • Monthly: Rinse the filter media with tank water — never with tap water. Treating Tap Water.

In Iraq, add two considerations from day one: summer heat and power outages — Summer Heat and Emergency Tools.

Order of Introducing Fish After Cycling

Cycling is complete, and a crucial question is often overlooked: which fish should go in first? The answer significantly impacts the tank's success in the first month.

  • Add in batches, not all at once. The bacterial colony expands based on the existing load; adding all fish at once overloads its capacity, causing ammonia to rise — The Biological Cycle.
  • Hardiest first. Hardy species can safely navigate the fluctuations of the first few weeks, while sensitive ones should be added after readings stabilize — Fish That Don't Die Quickly.
  • Aggressive ones last. Fish that establish territory should be introduced after others have settled, otherwise, they will treat every new arrival as an intruder — Aggression and Chasing.
  • Test between batches. A slight rise in ammonia or nitrite after an addition means you should wait before the next batch — Test Reading.

And do not skip quarantine for any batch after the first, because the tank now has something valuable to lose — Quarantine.

If you are still in the stage of choosing the location and stand, that stage precedes all of the above — Where to Place Your Aquarium and On What.

data.seoDescription: Learn the correct step-by-step order for setting up your first aquarium, including the crucial cycling stage often skipped by beginners. Avoid common mistakes and ensure a healthy environment for your fish.

data.title: Cloudy Aquarium Water? Diagnose by Color and Treat Correctly
data.excerpt: Cloudiness indicates three different problems sharing one symptom. The water color tells you which one you have. A diagnostic guide: milky white, green, and yellow — and why excessive water changes worsen the first condition.
data.content:
Diagnose by Color Before Doing Anything Else

Cloudy water isn't a single problem; it's three entirely different issues sharing one symptom. The water color identifies which one you have and whether the solution is correct or will make things worse. The most common mistake in this regard is treating the first condition with the method for the second.

ColorCauseRisk to Fish?First Step
Milky White / HazyBacterial Bloom — heterotrophic bacteria multiplying on excess organic matterYes, indirectly: consumes a lot of oxygenIncrease aeration, do not do large water changes
GreenFloating microalgae feeding on excess light and high nitratesNo, not directlyComplete blackout for 3 days
Yellow / Clear BrownDissolved tannins from driftwood or Catappa leavesNo, and some fish prefer itActivated carbon, or leave it

Milky White: The Condition That Requires Patience

This is a bacterial bloom. Excess organic matter — uneaten food, waste, dead leaves — feeds bacteria living freely in the water, not the beneficial bacteria residing in the filter. This is common in new aquariums and after over-washing the filter.

Why excessive water changes worsen it: When you remove a portion of the free-floating bacteria, the remaining ones multiply faster to compensate. You end up with the same cloudiness after a day or two, having lost water stability for no benefit.

The real danger in this condition is not the cloudiness itself, but that this bacterial bloom consumes a large amount of dissolved oxygen. In the hot Iraqi summer, the water already holds less oxygen, so the fish are under double pressure. The first practical step: increase aeration, not water changes.
  1. Increase aeration — add an air stone or increase surface agitation.
  2. Reduce feeding to once a day, only an amount that is finished within two minutes.
  3. Do not clean the filter during this period.
  4. Wait 3 to 7 days; it will clear on its own when the organic matter is depleted.
  5. Test for ammonia and nitrite. If they rise above zero, the problem is bigger than cloudiness — see Sudden Ammonia Spike Emergency Treatment.

If your aquarium is new, the cloudiness is a natural part of cycling. Read The Nitrogen Cycle Explained Simply to understand where you are in the process.

Green: Excess Light, Not Dirty Water

Green water is floating microalgae. It cannot be removed by mechanical filtration because its size is smaller than the pores of filter floss. It feeds on two things: light and nitrates.

  • Complete blackout for 3 days. Cover the aquarium and turn off all lights completely. The fish will tolerate this without issue, but the algae will not.
  • Move the aquarium away from direct sunlight. A south-facing window in Iraq is enough on its own to perpetuate the problem.
  • Reduce lighting hours to 6–8 hours after the blackout, and keep it consistent.
  • Change 30% of the water after the blackout to reduce the nitrates that fueled the bloom.

If it returns quickly, the cause is nutritional, not light-related: accumulated nitrates from infrequent water changes or overstocking. Details in the Algae War Guide.

Yellow-Brown: Usually Doesn't Require Treatment

This is dissolved tannin from driftwood or Catappa leaves. The water remains clear but colored like tea — this is the difference from the previous two conditions, where the water is hazy, not colored.

Tannins do not harm fish, and blackwater fish like Bettas and Tetras benefit from them. If the color bothers you visually only:

  • Activated carbon in the filter — it absorbs tannins within days. Available in the filtration supplies at AQUAVO.
  • Periodic water changes will gradually reduce the color.
  • For next time: boil the wood and soak it before adding it. The full method is in Preparing Driftwood for Aquariums.

The Root Cause in Most Cases

Three conditions with different causes, but one cause underlies most of them: overfeeding. Food that is not eaten decomposes, feeds free-floating bacteria, and raises nitrates that feed algae. Reduce feeding, and half of your water problems will be solved before they even start.

  • One feeding per day, finished within two minutes.
  • 20% weekly water change — consistent, not large and sudden.
  • Rinse filter media with aquarium water, not tap water.
  • Keep lighting hours consistent, and use the Calculators to determine your tank size and water change volume.
