data.title: Comparison Between Tetra Food and Economic Feeds in the Market
data.excerpt: Is the difference between expensive Tetra food and cheap feeds worth it? A comparison of ingredients and their effect on the health and color of your fish.
data.content:
Introduction

In the world of ornamental fish, choosing the right food is crucial for the health and well-being of the fish. In Iraq, where temperatures reach 50 °C in the summer, power outages occur, and tap water is saturated with chlorine, selecting the correct feed becomes a greater challenge.

Tetra Food: Advantages and Disadvantages

Tetra food is an excellent feed for ornamental fish, as it contains all the necessary nutrients for fish growth and health. However, this type of feed can be expensive and is not readily available throughout Iraq.

  • Contains all necessary nutrients
  • Supports fish growth and health
  • May be expensive
  • Not readily available throughout Iraq

Economic Feeds: The Reasonable Alternative

Economic feeds offer a reasonable alternative to Tetra food, characterized by competitive prices and greater market availability. However, they may not contain all the necessary nutrients for fish health.

  1. Competitive prices
  2. Greater market availability
  3. May not contain all necessary nutrients
Golden advice from AQUAVO: When choosing fish food, consider the water quality and temperature in the fish tank, as these factors affect fish health and feed effectiveness.

Using Tetra Food and Economic Feeds in Iraq

In Iraq, where temperatures reach 50 °C in the summer, feed containing additional nutrients should be chosen to help fish adapt to extreme heat. Tetra food can be used as an excellent option, as it contains all the necessary nutrients for fish health.

AQUAVO's Role in Providing the Ideal Feed

When comparing one feed to another, read the ingredient order on the package: feed starting with fish meal or shrimp is better than that starting with wheat or grain meal. With delivery to 18 governorates, obtaining the right feed becomes easier.

Conclusion

When choosing between Tetra food and economic feeds, consider the water quality and temperature in the fish tank. With golden advice from AQUAVO and product quality guarantees, professionals and beginners in fish keeping can obtain the ideal feed for their fish, ensuring their health and well-being under Iraqi conditions.

data.title: Internal Parasites: A Fish That Eats But Doesn't Gain Weight
data.excerpt: Nothing is visible on the body, and the key sign is a combination of three: normal eating, weight loss, and stringy white feces. White feces alone is not a diagnosis.
data.content:
A Fish That Eats But Doesn't Gain Weight

Internal parasites differ from external ones in one fundamental way: you see nothing on the fish. The body is clean, with no spots, no dust, and no visible worms, yet the fish gradually weakens. Because the first sign is slow and gradual, most cases are discovered too late.

SignMeaning
Emaciation despite normal eatingFood is being consumed internally — the clearest early sign
Stringy white or transparent fecesThe intestines are not digesting as usual
Sunken belly and protruding spineAdvanced emaciation
Refusal to eat after a period of voraciousnessUsually a late stage
Short red threads protruding from the ventInternal worms in an advanced stage
The practical difference from external parasites: external parasites start with itching and behavioral changes, while these start with weight loss and abnormal feces. If the signs are on the surface, refer to External Fish Parasites.

White Feces Are Not a Diagnosis Alone

Stringy white feces is the most commonly mentioned sign, but it is not conclusive proof of worms. It has more than one cause, and some do not require medication at all:

  • A fish that hasn't eaten for a while — the feces become mucousy and light-colored because the intestines are emptying. A fish stressed from transport or being chased will show the same appearance.
  • Poor quality food or a sudden change in diet — temporary digestive upset.
  • Deteriorated water quality — appears in many forms, including this. Always start by reading your water test results.
  • Actual internal parasites — this is suspected when white feces are combined with persistent emaciation despite eating, not when it appears alone for a day or two.

In other words: the key sign is the combination — normal eating + weight loss + abnormal feces, over weeks, not days.

Why Is This Condition Harder Than Others?

Treating internal parasites is harder than external ones for two structural reasons:

  1. The medication must reach the inside. Adding medication to the water treats what touches the skin and gills; the parasite inside the intestines is not affected in the same way. Therefore, the common method is treatment via food — which completely fails with a fish that has stopped eating, which is exactly what happens in the later stages.
  2. The treatment window narrows over time. A fish that is still eating is treatable; a thin fish refusing food has much weaker chances. This is why early detection is more important here than any other detail.
We will not publish dosages or specific compound names: these medications vary in availability and regulation, and an incorrect dose for a thin fish will kill it faster than the parasite. The correct method — isolation, dosage, and duration — is in Correct Treatment Protocol, and never use human medications: Dangers of Human Medications for Fish.

Where Do They Come From?

Internal parasites usually enter with the fish itself, they do not spontaneously generate in the tank:

  • A new fish carrying the infection without symptoms. A seemingly perfectly healthy fish may carry an internal infection that appears after weeks. This is precisely why quarantine should last weeks, not days.
  • Unreliable live food — a known source for some infections.
  • Chronic stress turns a limited infection into a visible problem — overstocking and constant chasing.

To distinguish emaciation from other similar causes — such as a fish being prevented from reaching food by a tankmate — refer to the Symptoms and Diagnosis Guide and the Feeding Guide. Sensitive species like Discus are affected more clearly and quickly than others.

Hole-in-the-Head: A Different Form of Internal Problem

A condition that appears as small pits or erosion on the fish's head and around the eyes, known as "hole-in-the-head." It is often associated with large cichlids — such as Oscars and Discus — and is frequently accompanied by emaciation and loss of appetite.

  • What is agreed upon: It is linked to poor chronic conditions — deteriorated water quality, prolonged high nitrates, poor or monotonous diet, and constant stress.
  • What is debated: The exact role of parasites versus the role of environment and nutrition is not definitively settled in the literature, and we present it as is rather than making a definitive statement.
  • Practical approach: Improving water quality and diversifying the diet are essential regardless of the treatment, and early-stage cases are more receptive to improvement.

data.title: Cheap Heater vs. Good Heater: The Difference is in Failure Mode, Not Heating
data.excerpt: All heaters heat; the difference lies in the thermostat's accuracy and what happens when it fails. A heater that gets stuck on is more dangerous than one that turns off, and this is what determines your purchase.
data.content:
The Heater is Not for Warming — It's for Stability

Most people buy a heater to raise the temperature in winter. Its real function is more important: preventing fluctuations. Tropical fish can tolerate 24 or 27 °C, but they cannot tolerate dropping from 27 to 21 °C every night and returning every day.

This daily fluctuation is the primary trigger for white spot disease, which is why outbreaks occur in spring and autumn — not in the dead of winter — when people turn off the heater because the day is warm. Details in Treating White Spot.

Rule: Keep the heater running year-round on a thermostat set to 26 °C. It will automatically turn off in summer and only turn on during cold nights. Turning it off seasonally is wrong, not a saving.

How Many Watts Do You Need

The common rule is about 1 watt per liter. However, this is an approximation that assumes a moderate room temperature — the greater the difference between the room temperature and the tank temperature, the higher the wattage needed.

Aquarium SizeHeated RoomCold Room or Tank Near Window
50 L50 W75–100 W
100 L100 W150–200 W
200 L200 WTwo heaters instead of one

Two smaller heaters are better than one large heater in larger tanks for two reasons: if one fails, the entire tank doesn't crash, and if one gets stuck in the 'on' position, its wattage alone is not enough to cook the tank. To accurately calculate your tank size, use the calculators.

The Real Difference Between Cheap and Good

The difference is not in heating — all heaters heat. The difference is in the thermostat and the failure mode:

Poor HeaterGood Heater
Thermostat AccuracyWide deviation from the set pointNarrow, consistent, and stable deviation
Failure ModeOften gets stuck in the 'on' positionShuts off when malfunctioning
CasingThin glass that breaks from thermal shockQuartz or stainless steel

And the failure mode is the crux of the matter. A heater that turns off allows the tank to cool slowly, so you notice and can act. A heater that gets stuck 'on' quietly raises the temperature to 35 °C or higher, and you discover it when the fish are gasping at the surface — high temperatures suffocate because warmer water holds less oxygen. The mechanism is explained in Protecting Fish from Heat in the Iraqi Summer.

The Precaution That Saves Your Entire Tank

  • A separate thermometer, always. Do not trust the heater's own reading — if its thermostat deviates, you are reading its error, not the water's reality. Glass and digital thermometers are available at AQUAVO in the testing and monitoring section; they are the cheapest and most useful piece of equipment you can buy.
  • Check the thermometer daily, even a quick glance. A two-degree change is an early sign of a failing thermostat.
  • Do not operate the heater out of water, and do not pull it out of the water while it is running — thermal shock can break the glass casing.
  • Turn it off before a water change if the water level will drop below it, and wait after refilling before turning it back on.
  • After a long power outage, monitor the temperature when it returns — sudden changes in either direction are harmful. See Emergency Tools for Power Outages.

Conclusion

Buy wattage appropriate for your tank size and room temperature, two heaters instead of one if the tank is large, and a separate thermometer regardless of the heater. Then, leave it running year-round at 26 °C. Stability is the product; temperature is merely the means to achieve it.
data.seoTitle: Heater Guide: Cheap vs. Good - Failure Mode Matters
data.seoDescription: Understand the critical difference between cheap and good aquarium heaters. Learn why failure mode (getting stuck on vs. off) is more important than heating power and how to protect your fish.

data.title: Is This Stone or Wood Safe for the Aquarium? The Vinegar Test and What to Reject Immediately
data.excerpt: Some stones dissolve slowly, raising hardness and pH unnoticed. A simple home test, a list of items to reject immediately, and why fizzing doesn't always mean it's forbidden.
data.content:
Not All Stone or Wood is Suitable for the Aquarium

Decor is not just an aesthetic piece — it is a surface that interacts with the water for years. Some stones dissolve slowly, raising hardness and pH, and some woods rot, and minerals may leach substances that kill invertebrates before fish.

The problem is that the effect is gradual: you don't notice anything in the first week, then you find the pH has risen and the hardness has changed, and you don't know why.

Stone Test: Vinegar

The simplest and most useful home test. Place a few drops of vinegar on the stone in a dry, clean spot:

ResultMeansDecision
Fizzing and bubblesThe stone is calcareous and dissolves slowly in waterIt will gradually raise hardness and pH
No reactionRelatively inertSuitable for most aquariums
And fizzing doesn't always mean "forbidden": calcareous stone is actually beneficial for African cichlid tanks that require hard, alkaline water. However, it is disastrous for a Tetra or Discus tank that needs soft water. The issue is suitability, not permissibility. GH and KH Hardness.

What to Reject Immediately

  • Any stone with shiny mineral veins or rust — dissolved minerals are toxic, and invertebrates are affected first.
  • Painted or dyed stone, and home decor stones not intended for aquariums.
  • Shells and coral if your aquarium requires soft water — all are carbonates that raise hardness.
  • Fresh or chemically treated wood — furniture wood and wood treated against insects are strictly prohibited.
  • Stone from an unknown source near agricultural land — potential pesticide residue.

Wood: Preparation is Mandatory

Wood intended for aquariums requires preparation before introduction:

  1. Scrub with a brush and water only — no soap or detergents at all.
  2. Boil it if its size allows: it sterilizes it, reduces tannins, and helps it sink.
  3. Soak it for days, changing the water — it reduces water discoloration later.
  4. Expect color. Tannins color the water like tea and are harmless; some fish prefer it. Details in Wood Preparation and Yellow Water Fix.

AQUAVO offers natural wood for aquariums and aquascaping, volcanic rock, and dragon stone, in the substrate and decor section.

Edges and Gaps: Mechanical Hazard

  • Sharp edges tear the fins of long-finned fish, and the wound is an entry point for infection — White Fungus.
  • Narrow gaps trap small fish.
  • Unstable stones can collapse and break the glass. Build from the bottom on a stable base, and do not lean a large stone directly against the aquarium glass. Rock Arrangement.

The Practical Rule

If you are unsure about a piece: test it with vinegar, and soak it in a separate bucket for a week, monitoring pH and hardness, before introducing it to a tank with fish. A bucket is cheaper than a whole aquarium. Also, monitor the test results after introduction — Reading Aquarium Water Tests.

And after you confirm the material is safe, the question of appearance and arrangement remains: what surface and what substrate suit your tank and its plants — Aquarium Substrate and Decor Guide: Choosing Surfaces.
data.seoTitle: Aquarium Decor Safety: Vinegar Test for Stones & Wood - AQUAVO Iraq
data.seoDescription: Learn how to test aquarium stones and wood for safety using the vinegar test. Discover which decor items to avoid and how to prepare natural wood for your tank. Expert advice from AQUAVO.

data.title: Selecting a Healthy Fish Before Purchase: What to Look For at the Store
data.excerpt: The cheapest treatment is a fish you didn't buy. Look at the entire system, not just the fish, and ask to see it eat — this does not replace quarantine.
data.content:
The Cheapest Treatment is a Fish You Didn't Buy

Everything on this site about diseases starts after the fish reaches your home. But the biggest preventive decision is made minutes before that: while you are standing in front of the store's tank. A fish you don't buy cannot transfer anything to your tank.

However — and because this is always misunderstood — visual inspection does not replace quarantine. A fish that appears perfectly healthy may carry a latent infection that is not visible to the eye. Inspection reduces the probability; quarantine deals with what remains.

Look at the Entire Tank, Not Just the Fish

Most buyers overlook this point. Many stores run multiple tanks on a single filtration system, so the water circulates through all of them. If that's the case, a sick fish in an adjacent tank concerns you.

  • Ask if the tanks share filtration — a simple question that can change your decision. Not all stores operate this way.
  • A dead or dying fish in any connected tank is sufficient reason to postpone your purchase, even if the fish you want looks excellent.
  • Cloudy water or a strong odor in the system indicates an overload or neglect.
  • Fish rubbing against decor in any connected tank — scratching is a behavior that precedes visible symptoms, explained in External Fish Parasites.

What to Look for in the Fish Itself

SignWhat it Means
Fins folded against the bodyStress or illness — a healthy fish keeps its fins extended
Rapid or gasping breathingGill or water problem — do not buy it
Sunken belly or protruding spineEmaciation — may indicate internal parasites
White, stringy, hanging fecesA digestive sign worth postponing the purchase
Spots, dust, or growthsVisible parasite — the entire tank is suspect
Swollen or cloudy eyeEye problems — requires a known cause before purchase
Redness, sores, or bloody patchesInjury or infection
Spinal curvatureUsually a permanent deformity
Lethargy or standing at an odd angleObserve for a minute before judging

Do not judge from a single glance. Stand for a full minute and observe: a healthy fish moves confidently, explores, and reacts to the movement in the tank.

The Strongest Test: Ask to See It Eat

This is the best test available to you at the store, and the easiest. A fish that refuses to eat in front of you rarely improves after the stress of transport — and transport itself is an additional stress, explained in Transporting Fish and Aquariums.

  • Ask when it arrived. A fish that arrived today is still at the peak of shipping stress. Postponing for a few days gives you better information and gives it a chance.
  • Ask about its adult size — and verify yourself, as many fish are sold at a fraction of their final size. See Fish That Outgrow Home Tanks.
  • Ask about the store's water parameters if possible. A significant difference in hardness or temperature means slower acclimation — see Acclimating New Fish.

When to Walk Away and Not Buy

There is no shame in leaving without a purchase. The short list of reasons to walk away:

  1. Any sign of illness on any fish in the same system.
  2. The fish is not eating and there is no convincing explanation.
  3. Its adult size does not fit your tank — this is not a health issue, but it is the worst purchasing mistake in the long run. Calculate this using How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Hold.
  4. Your tank is not ready yet — still cycling — see The Nitrogen Cycle Explained Simply.

And if you do buy, the next step is not to put it directly into your tank: Quarantine then Acclimation. For choosing a seller in general, especially for online sales, see Avoiding Fake Fish Stores and Instagram Scams.

data.title: Dissolved Oxygen in the Aquarium: When is an Air Pump Necessary?
data.excerpt: Most sudden deaths are due to suffocation, not disease. How does oxygen actually enter the water, what consumes it, and why does temperature simultaneously reduce supply and increase demand?
data.content:
Oxygen is the First to Deplete and the Last to Be Noticed

Most sudden deaths in the aquarium are not caused by disease or poisoning – they are caused by suffocation. A fish gasping at the surface is not "hungry" or "being difficult"; it is trying to breathe from the only oxygen-rich layer available.

This article is about dissolved oxygen itself: how it enters the water, what consumes it, and how to know if it's low before you lose your fish.

How Oxygen Actually Enters the Water

It is a common misconception among hobbyists that "bubbles don't provide oxygen; surface agitation is everything." This is an oversimplification. The reality is more nuanced: gas exchange occurs at any surface of contact between air and water – the surface of the aquarium itself, and the surface of every bubble.

PathwayHow it WorksWhen it's Most Important
Aquarium SurfaceDirect contact with room airShallow, wide aquariums – large surface area
Bubble SurfaceEach bubble is a mobile contact surfaceTall, narrow aquariums
Upward Current from Air StonePushes deep water to the surface for renewalAlways – this is the most important role of an air stone
The practical outcome is the same regardless of the explanation: a stagnant surface equals a problem. Whether you agitate the surface with the filter outlet, an air stone, or a fan, the important thing is that the water at the surface is constantly renewed.

What Consumes Oxygen

Fish are not the only consumers, nor are they always the largest:

  • Fish – and in quantities that increase sharply with temperature.
  • Beneficial bacteria in the filter – ammonia oxidation is an oxygen-consuming process. Your filter breathes.
  • Decomposing organic matter – excess food, waste, and dead plants.
  • Bacterial blooms – cloudy white water consumes large amounts of oxygen, which is why aeration is the first step, not water changes. See Diagnosing Cloudy Water.
  • Plants at night – they consume oxygen in the dark instead of producing it.

Temperature: The Factor That Changes Everything

This is the most critical relationship, and it's particularly crucial in Iraq: warmer water holds less oxygen, while a warmer fish needs more. Supply drops and demand rises simultaneously.

The dissolved oxygen ceiling drops from about 9.1 mg/L at 20 °C to about 7.0 at 35 °C – a reduction of nearly 23% before a single fish even breathes. Meanwhile, metabolism roughly doubles with every 10 °C increase. Details and the full table are in Protecting Fish from Summer Heat.

Signs of Deficiency, in Chronological Order

  1. Gathering at the surface, especially in the early morning – before the lights come on, oxygen levels are at their lowest after a full night of consumption.
  2. Rapid breathing and visible gill movement.
  3. Lethargy and loss of appetite.
  4. Gathering near the filter outlet – the most oxygenated spot in the tank.

Note: High nitrite levels cause exactly the same symptoms because they prevent blood from carrying oxygen. So, before assuming a lack of aeration, test – see Reading Aquarium Water Tests.

The Air Pump: When it's Necessary and When it's Optional

In a tank with a wide surface area, few fish, cool temperatures, and a filter that agitates the surface well – the pump is an enhancement, not a necessity. However, it becomes necessary in:

  • Summer and any heatwave.
  • Overstocked or tall, narrow tanks – see How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Hold.
  • During medication treatments and when raising the temperature – see White Spot Disease.
  • Breeding tanks and sponge filters, as they operate on air power inherently – see Choosing a Filter.

Air pumps, air stones, distributors, and check valves are available at AQUAVO in the aeration and oxygen section.

During Power Outages

When the filter and pump stop, surface renewal stops – precisely when the aquarium needs it most. A simple manual procedure: scoop water with a cup and pour it from a slight height periodically; this agitates the surface and renews contact. Reduce feeding entirely until the power returns. Details in Emergency Tools for Power Outages.

Current Itself, Not Just the Pump

The air pump is one method of water movement, but movement itself is a broader environmental factor: oxygen distribution, stagnant zones where waste accumulates, and the effort a fish expends to stay in place.

Surface agitation, in particular, is more important than deep current, as gas exchange occurs at the surface. Full details – including how to detect dead spots and signs of excessive current – are in Water Flow and Movement.

Noise and Vibration

The air pump is the most common source of noise in an aquarium, and most of it is solvable:

  • Vibration transfers to the surface. Place the pump on a piece of sponge or folded cloth instead of directly on a hard surface – the simplest measure with the biggest impact.
  • Do not place it on the aquarium itself; the glass transmits and amplifies vibration.
  • A clogged air stone increases resistance, thus increasing noise – clean or replace it.
  • A taut airline transmits vibration. Leave it slack with a loop.
  • And don't place the aquarium in a bedroom if the noise bothers you – see Aquariums in the Bedroom.

data.seoDescription: Learn how oxygen enters your aquarium, what consumes it, and why temperature is critical. Discover when an air pump is necessary to prevent fish suffocation.

data.title: Changing Tank Water: How Much, When, and Exactly How
data.excerpt: Filters do not remove nitrates—water changes are the only way to get them out. Implementation steps, common mistakes that turn water changes into problems, and a decision-making rule to determine your schedule instead of a fixed percentage.
data.content:
Why Change Water in the First Place?

A filter doesn't clean water in the way you might imagine. Beneficial bacteria convert toxic ammonia into nitrite, and then into nitrate—and that's where the cycle ends. Nitrates accumulate and are not removed by any biological filter.

So, water changes aren't about "cleaning"; they are the only practical way to remove nitrates from the tank. Along with nitrates, dissolved organic compounds that don't show up on any test but accumulate and stress the fish are also removed.

The entire basis is explained in the Biological Cycle; this article is about implementation.

How Much and How Often? Let the Readings Decide

We won't give you a fixed percentage that works for every tank because it doesn't exist: it varies with the number of fish, the amount of food, the plants, and the tank size. Instead, use a decision-making rule:

Nitrate Reading Before ChangeMeansAction
Low and stable weeklyCurrent schedule is sufficientContinue it
Increasing from week to weekOutput is less than productionIncrease the percentage or frequency
Increasing rapidly despite changesThe bioload is too high for the tankReduce food and fish count first

Important point: Ammonia and nitrite must always be zero. If they appear, the problem isn't the water change schedule but the biological filtration itself—see Sudden Ammonia Spike. Test strips and ammonia/nitrite test kits are available at AQUAVO in the Testing and Monitoring section.

General rule: Small, frequent changes are better than one large, sudden change. The aquarium is a living system that thrives on stability, and any jump in temperature or chemistry is stressful in itself, even if the new water is cleaner.

The Steps

  1. Prepare the new water first. Treat it with a dechlorinator before it enters the tank, not after. Details on chlorine and chloramine in Treating Tap Water for Aquariums.
  2. Match the temperature. Ensure the new water is close in temperature to the tank water. A large difference is a shock, and during the Iraqi summer, tap water can be warmer than the tank, not cooler.
  3. Siphon from the bottom. Do not siphon from the surface: waste accumulates between the gravel, and the siphon removes it along with the water. Siphons and gravel vacuums are available at AQUAVO in the Maintenance and Cleaning section.
  4. Turn off the heater if the water level will drop below it, and turn it back on after refilling.
  5. Add water gently onto a plate or against the glass to avoid disturbing the substrate and clouding the water.

Mistakes That Turn Water Changes from a Solution into a Problem

  • Washing filter media with tap water in the same session. The worst possible combination: you remove stable water and kill beneficial bacteria simultaneously. Wash media with removed tank water, and in a separate session from a large water change.
  • Changing 100% or emptying the entire tank—rarely necessary and effectively resets the tank to an uncycled state.
  • Using untreated water "because it's a small amount." Chlorine harms bacteria regardless of the quantity.
  • Changing water only when a problem appears. Water changes are preventative, not emergency treatment; waiting until the water is cloudy means the fish have been living under stress for weeks.

Special Cases

  • New tank cycling: Change less water—frequent large changes slow down the establishment of the bacterial colony.
  • Heatwave: Smaller, more frequent changes, and pay attention to the new water's temperature. See Protecting Fish from Heat.
  • Cloudy white water (bacterial bloom): Here, large water changes worsen the problem. Details in Diagnosing Cloudy Water.
  • After a long power outage: Test before changing, and start small.

Use the Calculators to accurately determine your tank volume and the required water amount.

Remember that water changes are what truly remove waste, not "cleaner" fish—details in Best Aquarium Cleaner Fish. If the water quality deteriorates without apparent reason despite regular changes, consider an external source: Aquarium Airborne Toxins.

Your Nitrates Are High Despite Regular Changes

You change water regularly, yet nitrates remain high. This doesn't mean water changes are useless—it means the source of production is faster than what the changes remove, or the incoming water itself isn't clean.

  • Test your tap water. If it already contains nitrates, you are adding them with every change—a simple measurement can confirm this.
  • The bioload is higher than you think—see How Many Fish Can Your Aquarium Hold.
  • Overfeeding, the most common cause—see Aquarium Fish Feeding Guide.
  • Accumulated waste in stagnant areas that the siphon doesn't reach—see Aquarium Water Flow.
  • Fast-growing plants do consume nitrates, and this is a structural rather than temporary solution—see Best Low-Tech Aquarium Plants for Beginners.

As for chemical nitrate removers, they treat the number, not the cause, and hide the problem instead of solving it. Address the source first, and temporarily increase the change percentage—gradually, not all at once.

data.seoDescription: Learn the essential steps for changing aquarium water, how often to do it, and common mistakes to avoid. Maintain a healthy environment for your fish with AQUAVO's expert advice.

data.title: Planted Aquarium Lighting: Duration Before Intensity, and Watts Don't Measure What You Think
data.excerpt: With LEDs, wattage has become a measure of electricity consumption, not light reaching the plant. Why adjusting the number of hours is more important than anything, and why increasing lighting is often the worst first step.
data.content:
Watts Don't Measure What You Think

The question "How many watts do I need?" is a relic from the fluorescent lamp era. With LEDs, wattage has become a measure of electricity consumption, not the light that reaches the plant — and two lamps with the same wattage can yield completely different results.

What matters to the plant is the light intensity reaching the bottom of the aquarium, which depends on the lamp's power, water depth, distance, and reflection. Depth is a crucial factor: the same lamp above a deep tank will provide much less light at the bottom than it does above a shallow tank.

Duration Before Intensity

If you adjust only one thing, adjust the number of hours. 6 to 8 hours daily is sufficient for any home aquarium. More than that does not result in stronger plants — it results in more algae, as algae benefit most from excess.
SituationHoursNote
Tank without plants4–6Lighting for viewing only
Low-demand plants6–8Most suitable for most tanks
Densely planted tank8 maximumRequires balanced fertilization
Tank with algaeReduce, or blackout for 3 daysAlgae Guide

Use a timer. Consistency is more important than the number: intermittent, irregular lighting confuses plants and benefits algae.

Light Alone Does Not Grow Plants

Plants need three things together: light, nutrients, and carbon dioxide. A deficiency in any one makes an increase in the others harmful, not beneficial.

  • Strong lighting + low nutrients = algae.
  • Strong lighting + insufficient CO2 = algae.
  • Moderate lighting balanced with the other two = healthy plants.

This is why increasing the lighting is often the worst first step when plants fail. Refer to Plant Fertilization and CO2 Systems for Planted Aquariums.

Direct Sunlight: Not Free Lighting

A tank near a sunny window receives immense, uncontrolled light, and the result is almost certain: green water and persistent algae, no matter how you adjust your lamp. In Iraq, there's a second danger: direct heating through the glass.

Keep the tank away from direct sunlight, or isolate it with a curtain. Details on heat in Summer Heat and the green water problem in Diagnosing Cloudy Water.

Lighting and Fish

  • A continuous dark period is essential. Fish need rest, and plants consume oxygen at night instead of producing it — this is important in an overcrowded or warm tank. Dissolved Oxygen.
  • Do not turn on strong lighting suddenly in a dark tank; room light first reduces stress.
  • Shy fish prefer dimmer lighting and floating plants that break up the light.
  • After introducing a new fish, keep the lighting dim — Acclimating New Fish.

LED aquarium lighting is available at AQUAVO in the lighting section.

Limits of What We Can Say

We will not give you a single number for the required light intensity: accurate measurements require equipment not available to hobbyists, and values change with depth, distance, and plant type. The honest practical rule is: start with a short duration and moderate intensity, and increase slowly only if the plant requires it and no algae appear — algae are your most accurate indicator that you have exceeded the limit.

Plants that grow well require regular trimming, otherwise they shade themselves — Trimming and Propagating Aquarium Plants. And if you want to document the result with a photo that resembles what you see with your eyes, lighting is the primary factor — Aquarium Photography with Your Mobile.

data.title: External Parasites: Velvet, Visible Worms, and Itching Without Spots
data.excerpt: The first sign isn't something you see—it's itching and rubbing against decor. A guide to differentiate velvet from gill flukes from anchor worms, and why velvet affects gills before becoming visible.
data.content:
Itching Before Anything Visible

The first sign of external parasites isn't something you see on the fish—it's behavior. The fish rubs against the glass, gravel, or decor in a flashing motion, swims erratically, and sometimes gasps at the surface. This precedes any spots or dust by days.

Therefore, the rule is: If itching affects more than one fish, test the water immediately, then inspect thoroughly, and do not wait for something visible to appear. Itching in one fish might be normal; in several fish, it's a warning sign.

And the first thing to rule out isn't a parasite at all: poor water quality causes the exact same itching. Start with reading your test results and the symptoms diagnosis guide.

What Exactly Are You Looking For

What You SeeMost LikelyDistinctive Sign
White spots the size of a salt grainWhite Spot (Ich)Has a separate article—see below
Fine golden or rusty dustVelvetAppears at an angle of light, affects gills first
Nothing visible, but severe itching and flared gillsGill or Skin FlukesBreathing is faster and harder without spots
White/green thread hanging from the body with rednessAnchor WormVisible to the eye, attached at one point
A flat, transparent disc moving on the bodyFish LiceActually moves and changes position

White spot is the most common and clearest to identify, with a specific treatment mechanism explained in White Spot: Why Medication Doesn't Kill Visible Spots. The rest of this article is for non-white spot issues.

This table provides a likelihood, not a diagnosis. A single sign does not equal a single parasite: itching alone can be caused by poor water quality without any parasite, difficulty breathing can be caused by ammonia or lack of oxygen, and loss of color accompanies chronic stress. It's also possible for two infections to occur simultaneously, or for a secondary bacterial infection to appear over a parasite, confusing the picture. Read the signs in conjunction with water readings, not in isolation.

Velvet: The Most Dangerous Because It's Least Obvious

Velvet is very fine dust, much finer than white spot, with a golden or rusty color. It's not easily seen with the naked eye—the practical way is to look at the fish from an angle with light, and the surface will shimmer as if sprinkled with powder.

  • It starts in the gills. This is why respiratory symptoms—gasping, rapid breathing, lethargy—appear before you see any dust. A fish gasping in clean, well-oxygenated water is a situation that warrants a thorough inspection.
  • Fast and deadly. It progresses faster than white spot, so delay here is more costly.
  • Light-dependent. The parasite causing it has a stage that benefits from light, which is why dimming the aquarium during treatment is recommended as an auxiliary measure—auxiliary, not a substitute for treatment.

We do not provide dosages: medications and their concentrations vary between products and markets, and the wrong dose on a stressed fish can kill it. The correct method is in Correct Treatment: Quarantine, Dosage, and Duration.

Visible Parasites: Don't Pull Them Out Forcefully

Anchor worms and fish lice are visible to the eye, which tempts immediate manual removal. Removal is part of the solution, but with two conditions:

  1. The head remains if you pull. Anchor worms are embedded under the skin, and quick pulling will sever them, leaving the embedded part, which can then become inflamed. Removal should be done gently with a firm grip, and the attachment site should be treated afterward.
  2. Removal doesn't end the cycle. The unattached stages remain in the aquarium, which is why treatment targets the aquarium, not just the fish.

The resulting wound is an entry point for secondary infection—monitor it, and refer to Fin Rot and Fungal Infections if its appearance changes.

Where Do They Come From Originally

These parasites rarely appear out of nowhere. They enter with a new organism, plant, or water from a store bag:

  • Quarantine is the only effective barrier—Quarantine. Most parasite outbreaks are due to fish introduced directly.
  • Do not empty the bag water into the aquarium—Acclimating New Fish.
  • Stress opens the door. Overcrowding and temperature fluctuations weaken immunity, turning a limited parasite presence into an outbreak—How Many Fish Can Your Tank Handle and Summer Temperatures.
  • Be mindful of shrimp and invertebrates before any treatment—many parasite medications, especially copper-based ones, are lethal to them—Shrimp and Snails.
  • And scaleless fish—like loaches, corydoras, and small catfish—are mentioned with special caution in many medication instructions. Their presence in the aquarium changes the choice of product and dosage, not just negates it—Loaches.

And if the symptoms are internal—emaciation with normal eating or white, stringy feces—the course of action is entirely different: Internal Parasites.
